Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?

Not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley, helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.

"He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.

"He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world."

Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.

While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.

"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10."

While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?

BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.

Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.

He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.

He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.

He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.

When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.

He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.

While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.

But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.

The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".

He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.

Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.

"It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss said last month. "He's at an incredible level."

Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.

He briefly played at centre-back as a youngster at West Ham before establishing himself as a top-class defensive midfielder for the Hammers. But since joining the Gunners in 2023 he has taken his game to another level, adding significantly more attacking output.

Rice created 17 big chances in the Premier League last season, as defined by Opta, a total bettered only by Bruno Fernandes and Rayan Cherki.

The 27-year-old has also registered 14 assists in all club competitions since August 2025. While set-pieces have undoubtedly contributed to that tally, he offers much more.

He ranks among the top 4% of central midfielders across Europe's top five leagues for progressive carries, while posting similarly impressive figures for chances created, touches and expected assists.

The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner missed Spain's Nations League defeat by England this month through injury, and his absence was keenly felt as the hosts uncharacteristically struggled for control, at least against 11 men.

It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.

The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.

His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.

The former Manchester City player has slotted in seamlessly since joining Barcelona in August, and averages 106 successful passes per 90 minutes in La Liga - the second-highest figure, behind Vitinha, of any player in the top five European leagues.

The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top

Pedri may be six years younger than Rodri, his midfield partner at the Camp Nou, but he boasts extraordinary experience for a 24-year-old, having made more than 250 appearances for Barcelona, not to mention playing at two European Championships and two World Cups.

The Tenerife-born midfielder combines tigerish work-rate with quality in possession.

He has created 26 chances from open play in La Liga this season, the sixth-highest total across Europe's top five leagues, and wins possession an average of 7.6 times per 90 minutes, the 10th-highest figure.

However, such is Spain's wealth of midfield options that he is not even guaranteed a starting place for his country, with Fabian Ruiz preferred for their final three matches at the 2026 World Cup.

Paris St-Germain midfielder Ruiz, who finished 10th in this year's Ballon d'Or rankings, also deserves to be in any debate about the world's best midfielders.

He might not yet have the profile of Barcelona team-mates Rodri or Pedri, but on current form alone, versatile youngster Lopez is one of Europe's best box-to-box goalscorers.

The 23-year-old already has nine goals and seven assists this season. Counting only goals scored in Europe's top five leagues and the Champions League, no central midfielder has more.

While Lopez can also operate on the wing, the presence of Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon means he has mainly featured as a number eight or a number 10 this term.

The Barcelona academy graduate played only a bit-part role as Spain won Euro 2024 and was unfortunate to miss the World Cup after breaking a bone in his foot in May.

However, a summer off enabled him to hit the ground running this season, and he has not looked back.

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:46:17 GMT

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has challenged Andy Burnham over whether EU students in the UK could pay lower university tuition fees as part of his deal with the bloc.

The prime minister insisted the issue of tuition fees was "a separate deal", with discussions on this continuing.

Asked whether he could rule out EU students paying the same fees as British students, Burnham said this was "the European negotiating position" and "won't be put on the table".

At a UK-EU summit last Friday, the two sides agreed a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth travel scheme.

A joint statement said they would also work towards a "supplementing" agreement on tuition fees for EU students in the UK and British students in the EU, with negotiations concluding within six months.

EU sources had earlier suggested the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

But the UK has insisted the wider deal will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can reach an agreement on tuition fees.

At the moment, EU students at UK universities generally pay the same fees as international students, ranging from £11,400 to £38,000.

For British undergraduate students tuition fees are currently capped at £9,790 a year.

Universities have raised concerns that capping EU student fees at the same level could cost hundreds of millions a year, at a time when the sector is struggling financially.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Badenoch asked Burnham who would pick up the bill if EU and British students paid the same fees, "cash-strapped universities or cash-strapped taxpayers?"

In response, the PM said "the deal on tuition fees is not done", adding: "We will take that conversation forward always rightfully mindful of the challenges faced by higher education."

Pressed over whether the EU would still sign his wider deal if he refused to cut fees for European students, Burnham said legislation introduced in Parliament on Thursday would set a date for the implementation of deals on food, emissions and a youth experience scheme.

He added: "We will continue discussions with the European Union on the question of tuition fees."

Asked if he would rule out EU students paying the same tuition fees as British students, Burnham replied: "She is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position.

"That has not been put on the table. It won't be put on the table."

Asked if Burnham was saying EU students would not pay domestic fees, the prime minister minister's official spokesman told reporters he would not get ahead of the outcome of ongoing talks.

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:45:09 GMT

The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans.

The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by EU governments.

It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme.

Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move.

The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry.

The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others.

Germany and France had previously agreed a joint position under which UK involvement would have been conditional on matching EU import restrictions and tariffs on imports of Chinese electric cars and hybrids.

Alignment in this area with the EU would increase the price of increasingly popular Chinese cars in the UK, as well as raising the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on British-made cars.

Now Ireland, as first reported by the Financial Times, is suggesting the UK could join Made in Europe without the need to match the EU's tariffs.

The argument made in favour of this is the UK and EU car industries are so heavily integrated and interdependent.

The proposal, which would also apply to Switzerland and countries in the European Economic Area (EEA) such as Norway, would depend on the non-EU countries granting the EU access to their subsidy and procurement schemes.

However, the idea is still at its early stages. It will first be discussed by EU ambassadors, before it is considered by competition ministers from the EU's member states at a meeting next month.

The proposal would also have to be accepted by the European Commission and the European Parliament.

Andy Burnham has previously pushed for UK inclusion in the scheme to avoid "collateral damage" to British industry.

Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he claimed the government had successfully "removed the threat" from the Made in Europe scheme as part of talks over the EU deals he agreed last week.

Pressed later whether he had overstated how advanced talks were on the EU side, the prime minister's spokesman said: "We continue to engage on these issues with Europe in a genuine spirit of cooperation."

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said it had proposed a "pragmatic and balanced way forward" on the scheme, having "listened closely to all member states".

Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:42:11 GMT

Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.

However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.

Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.

The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.

Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.

Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.

Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.

Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."

Confusion and anger - Yoro red card rescinded, but row goes on

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:28:10 GMT

Leny Yoro will be available for Manchester United's game against Brentford on Saturday after his one-match ban was rescinded

Leny Yoro's overturned red card against Liverpool appears to have turned into an unseemly difference of opinion between Manchester United and referees' body Pro Ref.

Let's recap what happened on Sunday.

Yoro was sent off after bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield.

Referee Sam Barrott sent off the France international, and the decision was backed up by video assistant referee (VAR) John Brooks.

It split opinion among pundits and fans. Would Isak have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens? Was it really a clear goalscoring chance?

Then came the events of Tuesday.

First, a Football Association regulatory commission upheld United's appeal and cancelled the red card.

Then Pro Ref boss Howard Webb said the red card was not "clearly wrong" - just moments before United held a pre-match news conference.

Over to Red Devils head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who was fiercely critical of the decision, and in particular the VAR.

But how can Pro Ref still believe the decision was right when an FA commission said it was wrong?

BBC Sport looks at how the system works.

So United won their appeal. Pro Ref would disagree. Could the two sides not just agree to differ?

"You ask me a question and I need to defend our situation and our club and our players," Pochettino said about Yoro's red card.

It continued a theme from his post-match news conference.

You can see why Pochettino would be keen to talk about the red card, rather than the performance of his players. After all, United had just lost the first game of his tenure. Was the Argentine keen to create a siege mentality?

You can also understand United's frustration - two of their biggest games of the season so far have been defined by refereeing decisions.

The first was the VAR error to allow Erling Haaland's match-winning goal in the Manchester derby, when Enzo Fernandez clearly committed an offside offence.

As for the Yoro incident, Pochettino reserved much his criticism for the VAR. United felt he only took a cursory look at where the ball would run.

What about Webb's reaction?

It should be noted that Match Officials Mic'd up, on which Webb gave his views, was filmed on Monday evening - before the result of the appeal.

Would that change his opinion? Almost certainly not.

Webb acknowledged the argument against a red card, which was Isak would not get the ball. But he was adamant it was not such an egregious error that it required a VAR intervention.

So are we back to arguing about when VAR should get involved?

The VAR threshold is too high, until it is too low. Rinse and repeat.

It is the Premier League clubs, and not Pro Ref nor the FA, who set where the bar sits.

Take the last stakeholders' survey, which helps to shape how the game is officiated.

It found 65% wanted to maintain the current threshold for VAR intervention, 20% to increase it, and just 15% to lower it.

But, of course, where the Yoro incident sits is still a matter of opinion.

This video can not be played

'And the three points?' - Pochettino after Yoro red overturned

How confusing it must be for a supporter just watching on, hoping to understand.

An FA regulatory commission has said the red card decision was wrong. Case closed? Not so fast.

Pro Ref will not always agree with the decision of an appeal board, nor will they use it as a barometer for future decisions.

And the burden of proof for a VAR intervention is considered higher than for an FA commission.

Pro Ref places far more stock upon the judgements of the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.

The KMI Panel creates the merit table for referees, and helps shape how decisions are made in the future - especially for the VARs.

But surely the FA is the higher body? Not quite.

The FA is responsible purely for disciplinary measures and has no say on how games at the professional level are refereed.

If the Premier League tells Pro Ref the decision is right or wrong, that counts far more than any vote by an FA commission.

So how did United make their case?

BBC Sport understands the club argued that if Isak had maintained his top recorded speed, he would not have got to the ball first.

The club say that is objectively provable, within minutes, using data. This, they say, was not a subjective decision.

To argue it was not subjective goes completely against the nature of the decision - it required a referee's judgement.

Whatever this data was, it most definitely was not available to the referees. The VAR cannot call upon a 3D animation of each player, detailing their running speed and providing an objective result.

How much stock did the commission place on this evidence? We will not know until the written reasons are published in a few days' time.

But United are not going to let this lie, and Pro Ref is not going to bend.

Such is the way FA commissions work, you can never be sure who will win.

There are three panel members who are usually former players, but occasionally you might get a retired referee.

The role of the commission is not to "usurp the referee by re-refereeing the incident".

A designated referee delegate is present to answer questions on the laws of the game, but they cannot offer an opinion on the incident.

The only input Pro Ref has is the official's report - a short entry by the referee that says which law was used for the red card. There is no other context.

It will read something like this: "I have to report that I, as the referee, sent off Yoro, Leny of Manchester United FC Under Law 12 section: S5."

The burden is on the club to prove its case by submitting a body of evidence - videos, images and testimony.

There is no right of reply. The evidence is weighed up by the panel, a vote is cast and the majority wins.

It makes predicting the outcome notoriously difficult, as the system is an opinion poll based upon a club trying to persuade at least two people to agree with them.

Take a look at Aston Villa's successful appeal against Douglas Luiz's red card for violent conduct four years ago. Luiz had been sent off via a VAR review for a headbutt on Aleksandar Mitrovic.

The panel's written reasons stated the appeal was won partly because Luiz was "a few inches shorter than Mr Mitrovic so his forehead is naturally at the same height as Mr Mitrovic's nose/face as the two players come together".

So, when the two players bumped chests the headbutt was just an accident. Appeal upheld because Luiz was a bit shorter.

Some might think anything is worth trying.

US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:21:34 GMT

The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.

The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.

China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.

The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".

He claimed that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression" as well as "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base".

But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.

Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.

Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.

Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.

"The key message is that the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods... are also not subject to these new tariffs."

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.

The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.

The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the US's reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.

Wife drugged and raped by husband asked police if she was to blame, court hears

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:42:10 GMT

Warning: This article contains distressing content

A woman who had been drugged and raped by her husband for 20 years asked police: "Is it my fault he's done this?", a court heard.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's right to anonymity, has admitted a litany of offences against her - including rape, administering a substance with intent and inviting 13 other men to join the abuse.

Nine of those men have pleaded not guilty to sexual offences against her and are standing trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

Giving evidence in court for the first time, the woman also said claims she had been "pretending to be asleep" during the abuse were a "load of rubbish".

The victim, in her 60s, was formally interviewed by Greater Manchester Police on 7 November last year, around two weeks after officers had arrived at her family home to arrest her husband.

In the interview, played to the jury, she told Det Con Anouska Barker: "I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can't believe it's true, and I think you have made a mistake."

She told police at the time of her husband's arrest that as far as she knew, the pair had not had a sexual relationship for about nine years due to her experiencing symptoms of the menopause.

The husband, she said, had never complained about it and the pair never discussed it.

Asked how their sex life was before, the woman described it as "just normal, vanilla".

Asked by Barker what her husband had "been like" in the years they had not been in a sexual relationship, the woman said: "Is this my fault? Is it my fault that he has done this?"

"Absolutely not, I don't want you to ever think that," Barker replied.

Describing their relationship, she said they had been "a loving couple".

"We did things together, we went out with other people. We've always had quite a lot of friends and a good social circle and done things."

During the interviews she said she had never consented or agreed to anyone else being involved in their sex life, and it had never been suggested by her husband.

The woman said on a number of occasions she recalled feeling particularly "wobbly" and "weird" after drinking the previous night.

She told Barker she had messaged a friend to say: "I feel like I'm wasting the day and this is ridiculous, and I need to pull myself together and cook some dinner."

The woman said on one occasion in the summer of 2024, she felt so strange that friends suggested she "see a doctor".

Questioned about how much alcohol she drank, she said she would often drink a bottle of wine a night but was "usually fine" and would take herself to bed and remove her make-up, and would normally be up by 09:00.

Shown photographs of the men alleged to have abused her while she was unconscious, she told the detective she did not recognise any of them or remember speaking to them.

After the jury were shown the video of her police interviews, the woman was asked to take the stand in the courtroom.

Katy Thorne KC, representing 43-year-old paramedic Jonathan Kirk, said her client's case was that the victim had spoken to him and had her eyes open in the early hours of 17 August 2025 - when he allegedly raped her while she was unconscious in her bedroom.

Thorne said: "If I were to suggest to you - you were pretending to be asleep?"

The victim spoke calmly and directly and replied: "That's a load of rubbish is what I'd say."

Thorne said that Kirk's version of events was that the husband had explained that "you two as a couple had a sleep fetish; you had been pretending to sleep", asking the woman: "Is that something you recall?

The wife responded: "No."

Judge Maurice Greene interjected and asked: "Do you have a sleep fetish?"

The victim said she did not.

The jury also heard another of the accused, taxi driver Philip Wild, claimed that the victim had "greeted him at the door" on the occasions he is alleged to have sexually assaulted and attempted to rape her, in August 2023 and February 2025 respectively.

In response to Pierce Power, defending Wild, she said: "No. That's a lie".

She was also questioned by the barrister representing Jordan Wallace, 31, who is alleged to have raped her on 4 May 2025.

Rachel White, defending Wallace, said she was not suggesting the victim had been "telling lies" but said she may have "not remembered" speaking to Wallace.

"It didn't happen," she said.

Counsel representing the other six men on trial did not ask questions.

Earlier in the trial Louise Oakley KC, prosecuting, said the woman had been subjected to the "barbaric fantasies" of her husband for more than two decades.

"The sad reality of this case is that there are many, many men whose fantasy is an unconscious and unresponsive woman," she said.

"[The husband] found a large number of them."

An investigation into his offending began after a team of undercover journalists in Germany infiltrated a channel on the messaging service Telegram which was being used by some men to share images of unconscious women appearing to be raped.

One of the users was traced by police to the husband's address, where he was arrested in October 2025.

Oakley said more than a million photographs and videos of his wife being abused were found on a Samsung mobile phone, which she described as a "confession booth" of his "darkest secrets".

On trial with alleged "contact offenders" Wild, Kirk and Wallace are amateur football coach Alan Keelan, 42; recruitment consultant Mohammed Sabir, 28; sheet metal worker Richard Townsend, 37, and Robert Stewart, 70, who was retired.

Also in the dock are Daniel Rayner and David Graves, described as alleged "non-contact offenders" because they did not physically attend the home address, who deny conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent.

Four other men; Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee in Scotland; Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport; Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich in Cheshire, and non-contact offender Karl Lindsay, 55, from Taunton in Somerset, have already pleaded guilty to a number of offences.

How much has the Iran war put up your energy bills?

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:58:51 GMT

The latest increase in energy bills is hitting British households hard in the pocket.

Announcing a 26% rise in the energy price cap from January, energy regulator Ofgem said the hike is largely down to the conflict in the Middle East.

Ofgem estimates that around £404 of the £443 increase in the annual energy price cap from January is due to higher wholesale natural gas prices.

Natural gas is used for heating by around 85% of homes, according to trade body Energy UK, and by power companies to generate electricity.

This means that when the wholesale price of gas rises, its feeds directly into the costs British households pay when they use either gas or electricity.

While the price of gas puts pressure on energy bills, other costs including upgrading the electricity grid to cope with more sources of renewable generation, feed into what households pay.

However, Ofgem says that these additional costs made no contribution to the rise in bills in the latest period.

Around a third of Great Britain's natural gas comes from the UK's own North Sea fields.

But the rest is imported - some by pipeline and some by ship as Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) - which means the price paid is determined by international markets.

Since the US-Israel strikes on Iran began on 28 February the UK wholesale price of gas has more than doubled.

Analysts say this is a direct consequence of the Middle East conflict.

Around a fifth of the world's supply of LNG normally comes from the Middle East but key producers like Qatar have seen supplies badly disrupted by Iranian attacks.

After the country's giant Ras Laffan LNG plant was hit by an Iranian strike on 18 March it was estimated that repairs could take up to five years.

The same site was rocked by an explosion in June which killed 13 people. The Qatari energy minister said the blast would not affect the country's exports and it was "an accident and not sabotage or hostile in nature".

And while Middle East producers have been able to significantly restore flows of oil through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iranian threats to shipping - largely by using covert ship-to-ship transfers of oil - the same cannot be done with LNG.

The number of LNG tankers exiting the strait is well down on pre-war numbers according to data from maritime intelligence firm Kpler.

The removal of this significant supply of natural gas from global markets has pushed up international wholesale prices.

Analysts say there is no realistic prospect in the near term of new regional natural-gas pipeline infrastructure being built to bypass the Strait of Hormuz and compensate for lost LNG shipments.

This absence of alternative options means the wholesale price of natural gas is likely to be heavily influenced by the course of the US war with Iran - and whether it escalates or eases.

That means it's impossible to predict when wholesale prices might start to come down again - and when UK households might get some financial relief on their energy bills.

Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 13:57:12 GMT

Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has been given a suspended sentence after admitting dangerously driving his Lamborghini while inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon on a motorway.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, who later crashed into a metal gate during rush hour, gave no reaction as he was handed a 12-month jail term, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court.

Sterling had pleaded guilty to dangerous driving of a Lamborghini Urus and possessing nitrous oxide on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road on 28 May.

The judge said Sterling's use of the Class C drug had became a "maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period" in his career.

Sterling, who left the court without making any comment, was ordered to complete 100 hours unpaid work and was banned from driving for 24 months.

He was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire.

District judge Kirsty Allman told the court on Wednesday that Sterling was seen at 01:10 BST at a McDonald's in Hayes driving "erratically and at speed" while inhaling from a pink balloon.

She went on: "At 7.45am, having not slept, you made a deliberate and entirely selfish decision, to drive your vehicle without adequate sleep and whilst consuming a Class C drug, nitrous oxide."

She said this exposed a "large number of road users to a significant risk of serious harm by the manner of your driving on two motorways and in peak travel time that morning".

During the September hearing, prosecutor Simon Jones said a number of calls were made between 07:45 and 08:52 BST about a black sports car and the manner it was being driven.

Witness Christopher Jennings called 999 after driving alongside Sterling's car on the M25, and "he was shocked by what he saw", Jones said, and made clear "he sighted the defendant inhaling from the balloon".

Fiona Jennings – driving on the southbound M3 – described the driving as "absolutely horrendous" and "swerving in and out of lanes", the court heard.

The court heard Sterling strayed into the central reservation of the M3, exited at junction 4A, and veered off the A327, crashing into a metal gate near a layby.

His vehicle sustained "substantial damage to the tyres and bodywork and was no longer capable of being driven", the court heard.

Sterling was taken to Basingstoke police investigation centre by officers, where he disclosed he had a "problem with nitrous oxide", said Jones.

The substance is legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes but is frequently used as a recreational drug, commonly known as laughing gas.

Sterling complied with an impairment test, but for a blood sample, Sterling asked to obtain legal advice before making a decision.

In the police sergeant's view "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer".

Sterling was later interviewed by police with legal representation present where he accepted he had been the driver and provided no comment answers about the driving.

Defending Sterling on Wednesday, Jason Bartfeld KC said there was no dispute that this was a "top category case" because of prolonged driving and "at times" serious impairment which would have been short periods within the driving.

But the defence did not accept the damage to the car was serious and said there was "confusion" over the failure to provide a specimen.

District Judge Kirsty Allman said: "I accept that your character has been positively exemplary.

"You enjoyed a highly successful professional football career and were widely regarded as a role model for many young people through your achievements and public profile."

He was given credit for his guilty pleas.

Sterling most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, having left Chelsea in January, but made just eight appearances in the Netherlands.

In four years at Chelsea - including a season-long loan at Arsenal - he made 59 league appearances after signing from Manchester City in 2022.

With City he won four Premier League titles, having started his senior career with Liverpool before moving to Manchester in 2015.

He is currently without a club.

In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport.

Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 13:42:08 GMT

Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter.

A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem.

The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.

Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

Ofgem said the rise had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war. Wholesale gas prices, paid by suppliers, were up 33% in the last three months, the period used to set the January to March cap. They have more than doubled since late 2025.

The warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.

"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said it wrote to energy suppliers "reminding them of their responsibilities" to customers this winter. They have been told to identify people who need help early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable.

Campaign Groups Friends of the Earth and Global Witness said major oil and energy companies are making huge profits because of spiralling oil costs, hurting households.

Energy UK, which represents suppliers, said the firms which send your bill, have profits capped on a percentage basis and do not see the same benefit as international energy generating companies. However, higher bills will mean higher profits in nominal cash terms.

The increase is the biggest since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest.

People on prepayment meters will be hit as their spending comes when energy is needed, rather than the cost being spread over the year as with direct debits.

The cap sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, not the total bill. Those on fixed deals are unaffected until the end of their term, but for those on variable tariffs it means:

The cap is set every three months, based on the costs faced by suppliers as well as the cost of running the energy system.

It is based on a three-month period that ends about six weeks before the new cap comes into force. A fall in international wholesale prices in recent days will not be reflected in January's cap, but it will be in April's.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills.

"For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets," she said.

Andrew Bowie, shadow energy secretary, said: "It is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes onto bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher.

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, said dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.

She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house.

Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment from 4 January to help with their energy bills this winter, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales.

Citizens Advice said the money will disappear quickly, particularly for those on prepayment meters, leading to a wave of requests for emergency help.

Energy UK said the funding was poorly targeted and insufficient to stem rising levels of customer debt.

The government said councils had a £100m discretionary fund to support vulnerable households which fell outside of the main scheme.

Raheem Sterling - from national icon to suspended jail sentence

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:42:57 GMT

Raheem Sterling has scored 123 goals in 396 Premier League appearances and provided 65 assists

Raheem Sterling grew up a stone's throw from Wembley Stadium, and went on to start a European Championship final for England there.

At his peak, the four-time Premier League winner was earning £325,000 a week at Chelsea.

"Raheem is a huge player with a huge influence in the last few years in English football," said then Blues boss Thomas Tuchel when he signed a 27-year-old Sterling in a £50m deal in 2022.

"He is at the perfect age to take responsibility around the younger players that we have and be an example.

"He just needs to do what he did over the last few years and he will be a huge asset for us."

Sterling enjoyed a 10-year England career, also played for Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal, and commanded combined transfer fees of about £100m.

But his career at the top level looks to be in the balance at the age of 31 after he was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. Sterling has also been disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.

At an earlier hearing in September, Sterling admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before crashing a Lamborghini on 28 May.

The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.

Sterling also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

This video can not be played

How Sterling went from England star to court appearance

Sterling's life was touched by tragedy at a young age.

Born in Kingston, Jamaica, he was just two when his father was shot dead.

His mother, Nadine, was determined to give her children a safer environment to live in. She moved to England to lay a path for Sterling and his sister to join her once she had found a home and finished her education, while cleaning bathrooms and changing bedsheets in hotels to earn extra money.

Sterling grew up on a housing estate in Neasden, north-west London, and spent part of his education at Vernon House, where teachers attempted to help the football-obsessed youngster with behavioural problems.

In an interview with the Players' Tribune, external in 2018, Sterling said: "I was so naughty that they kicked me out of primary school. I just didn't like to listen to anyone but my mum. That was my problem."

He was 10 when teacher Chris Beschi told him: "If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or in prison."

Sterling would grow to become one of the standout English attacking talents of his generation.

This video can not be played

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash

Raheem Sterling: From school struggles to a class of his own

On 14 November 2012 - aged 17 years and 342 days - Sterling made his England debut on the night his Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard won his 100th cap in a 4-2 defeat by Sweden in Stockholm.

Sterling would go on to make 81 more appearances for his country, scoring 20 goals.

He featured at three World Cups - 2014, 2018 and 2022 - and two European Championships. He was one of the standout players as England reached the Euro 2020 final at Wembley, where they were beaten by Italy.

Sterling was now at the peak of his career - the former Queens Park Rangers youngster, who has a tattoo on his forearm of a young boy holding a football looking up at the Wembley arch, named in the team of the tournament by Uefa.

Liverpool had signed a 15-year-old Sterling from QPR for £600,000 in February 2010.

He made his senior Reds debut two years later and became the second-youngest goalscorer in their history - behind Michael Owen - when he scored the winner against Reading in October 2012 at the age of 17.

In 2015, Sterling joined Manchester City in a deal worth up to £49m, making him the most expensive English player at the time.

He had been under contract at Anfield until 2017 but turned down a new deal to move to Liverpool's rivals, with City boss Manuel Pellegrini describing the 20-year-old as "one of the best attacking players in world football".

Sterling went on to score 131 goals in 339 appearances in all competitions during seven successful years at Etihad Stadium.

As well as four Premier League titles, he helped City win five League Cups, one FA Cup and one Community Shield.

It was while he was at City, in 2021, that Sterling became an MBE in the Queen's Birthday Honours for his services to racial equality in sport.

"I am grateful to have been recognised," he said. "But my priority is to try to help to educate society and myself. I'm learning every day."

After City came the move to Chelsea, where his career began to stall.

Tuchel, now England manager, was sacked two months after signing Sterling, who made just 45 Premier League starts for the Blues over four years.

Off the pitch, he launched a scholarship fund aimed at closing the gap in the number of black British students who go to university.

On the pitch, he was finding it a struggle.

He spent 18 months as a member of Chelsea's so-called 'bomb squad', and a season-long loan to Arsenal in 2024-25 proved largely unsuccessful.

This video can not be played

Sterling: If you grew up in a certain area you feel like there's limits

'Sterling will look back and wonder'

As well as his success on the field, Sterling has made headlines off it too.

In 2015, when he was 20, reports began to surface about his behaviour away from the game.

Sterling was pictured apparently inhaling nitrous oxide and was also photographed smoking a shisha pipe.

That prompted then Liverpool boss Brendan Rodgers to warn Sterling he would "look back in 20 years and wonder what he was doing".

Sterling also made headlines while on duty for England at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

The Sun ran a story titled "Raheem shoots himself in the foot" as pictures emerged of a tattoo of an M16 assault rifle on his leg.

Sterling explained on social media: "When I was 2 my father died from being gunned down to death I made a promise to myself I would never touch a gun in my life time. I shoot with my right foot so it has a deeper meaning."

The incident led to a widespread discussion in the UK about the treatment of black athletes in the media, with comparisons drawn between how Sterling's life was covered compared to others.

Sterling spoke out a number of times on the issue and wider racism in society, which was reflected in him being made an MBE.

Five years after his MBE, Sterling's career has stalled. He has not played since appearing for Feyenoord on 17 May, after agreeing a short-term move to the Netherlands.

Eleven days after that game, he was arrested after crashing a Lamborghini near the M3 in Hampshire.

This video can not be played

Watch: Sterling joins PL 100 club - best goals & stats

Listen: From Wembley schoolboy to playing for England at Wembley

Sterling was riding the crest of a wave when he moved from Manchester City to Chelsea in the summer of 2022 for £50m.

His medal cabinet was already fit to burst with 10 major trophies under Guardiola and, alongside Harry Kane, he was arguably England's most important player for then head coach Gareth Southgate.

Tuchel viewed Sterling as his number one target that summer and Chelsea's new ownership - Behdad Eghbali and Todd Boehly - delivered as the club entered the post-Roman Abramovich era.

Two months later, Tuchel was sacked and Graham Potter was in situ.

Sterling's career has not been the same since.

It is, of course, senseless to suggest the troubles Sterling has had on and off the pitch in recent years are simply down to the sacking of Tuchel in 2022.

But speak to those close to Sterling and they will explain Tuchel was among the key factors behind the winger's decision to swap Manchester for west London.

He was captivated by Tuchel's vision, not only for the team, but his role in it.

'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:12:11 GMT

Domestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.

With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?

The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.

Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.

The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000.

She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.

The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.

To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill.

The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.

They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.

"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E. On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year.

Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.

She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.

She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.

"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."

Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.

"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.

"At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."

To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.

Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.

Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.

Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.

Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell & Bernadette McCague.

Hundreds complain about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu 'aggressive'

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 11:57:31 GMT

More than 800 people have complained to the media regulator about an episode of ITV reality show I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! in which Mariella Frostrup accused her campmate AJ Odudu of being "aggressive".

Ofcom said 887 people had filed complaints about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.

An Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."

The pair were seen clearing the air on Tuesday, with broadcaster Frostrup saying she was "sorry for calling you aggressive" and Odudu telling her it is "a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".

Relations between the pair became fractious when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode.

Tensions flared further as they and other campmates discussed their friction and the cooking arrangements the following morning.

After fellow celebrities Wayne Rooney and Claire Sweeney tried to smooth the strained relationship in Sunday's episode, Frostrup told Odudu she was "making a drama out of a crisis" and that she had been "thrilled there was another person" who said they could cook.

Odudu responded: "You have a funny way of showing it, that's all," before Frostrup replied: "You see, that's just aggressive and that's what keeps happening."

Odudu said she felt being called aggressive was "very harsh".

Both women later had tearful conversations with other campmates, with Odudu saying "aggressive" was "an insane word" to use about her, while Frostrup said the pressure in the camp was "too much".

Many viewers defended Odudu after the encounter.

They included former BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo, who said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."

Singer Beverley Knight wrote: "The word 'aggressive' feeds directly into the 'angry Black woman' trope. It IS hurtful and offensive."

Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".

It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing."

Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation in Tuesday's episode.

Odudu told her being called "aggressive" was "triggering because in this world, navigating it as a person who looks like me can be difficult sometimes because my experience is that my emotions and my intent are completely misconstrued".

She added: "In same way that you are allowed to express yourself, I can't express myself in the same way. We're not granted the same freedom.

"You're allowed to be emotional and passionate, and I automatically go to 'aggressive'. There's no in-between. It's like I'm 'dramatic' and 'aggressive' and that's it.

"Whereas I feel like someone like you gets to go through all the emotions of life and all of those emotions are accepted and embraced and valid."

Frostrup replied that she thought being labelled "aggressive" was "a woman thing more than anything else".

"I think women who speak their mind and are forthright, that's 'aggressive', whereas a man who speaks his mind and is forthright is a 'strong man'," she said, but added that "I totally get that there's more" when race is involved.

Odudu responded: "I do definitely see your point and agree with it, but those words stick as well. Those words can stick for us. The moment passes for you and it doesn't pass for me."

"But hopefully it has?" Frostrup asked.

Odudu replied: "Well, I wasn't being aggressive, so it shouldn't have been there."

Signs of friction resurfaced when Frostrup told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well".

Odudu replied that "of course" she had accepted her apology, before Frostrup accepted that "it's really important to me to understand why it's triggering".

Odudu added: "It's good you asked, but it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women."

"Good to know," Frostrup concluded.

An ITV statement said: "The production monitors everyone in camp 24/7 and if at any time we feel someone has overstepped the line by using inappropriate language or displaying unacceptable behaviour, we would take steps to intervene and speak to everyone involved.

"The duty of care for our contestants is of the utmost importance to us. We take the welfare of the celebrities very seriously and have measures in place to ensure they are supported at every stage of the process: before, during and after filming."

Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 10:03:12 GMT

Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?

Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned. Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards.

Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.

Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban.

Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump.

There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues.

For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal.

But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms.

As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes.

"Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X.

Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable.

Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks.

So how on Earth did he manage it?

Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a company that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position.

Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI.

Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them.

So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known.

He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.)

Working for Huang isn't easy.

Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else.

When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders.

Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it.

Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses.

For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (£137).

In addition, Huang has powerful allies, and they are mostly powerful men. US President Donald Trump personally pushed for his return to Nvidia, while Elon Musk said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.

He is one of very few people who knows both Trump and China's President Xi Jinping personally - and somehow he has surfed the geopolitical tension between the two continents.

He has said he thinks both China and the US can win the AI race and called on them to pull together.

And finally there's the bottom line, which is always money.

Huang's brief departure from Nvidia caused economic turmoil. The firm's value sank by a whopping $1tn before it climbed back up again.

It affected not only pension funds and investors around the world, but also Nvidia's own staff.

Tech employees often get to own valuable stocks in the company they work for as part of their pay packages.

Nvidia employees have been sitting on a goldmine. It wasn't really in their interests to see that drain away because of the boss's love life.

With a firm grip on the company he co-founded, cult-like status in tech circles and friends in high places, Jensen Huang created a situation where even national security concerns over the US's biggest rival couldn't topple him.

Missed chances to save boy, 2, murdered by grandparents despite dad's concerns

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 10:00:14 GMT

Opportunities to protect a two-year-old who was murdered by his grandparents were missed by multiple agencies, a review has found.

Ethan Ives-Griffiths died on 16 August 2021 after suffering a "catastrophic" head injury at his grandparents' home in Garden City, Flintshire. He had been beaten, starved and deprived of fluids.

North Wales Safeguarding Board apologised "unreservedly" after a review found attempts by his dad to raise concerns were not acted upon.

Michael Ives, 49, and Kerry Ives, 47, were jailed for life in 2025. Ethan's mum, Shannon Ives, 29, was jailed for 12 years for causing or allowing his death and child cruelty.

Flintshire council said it "failed" Ethan and was "deeply sorry".

Warning: This article contains details of violence and abuse that some may find distressing

When Ethan died, he was dangerously dehydrated and severely underweight, with 40 visible bruises or marks.

After his grandparents were found guilty, Mr Justice Griffiths said the pair had engaged in a "campaign to break him" and text messages from Michael Ives said the toddler would have to "learn the hard way".

Ethan was "a shadow of the chubby healthy child he had been" in the days before he fatally collapsed, the judge said.

Co-chair of the safeguarding board, Nicola Stubbins, said the child practice review, published on Wednesday, made "difficult reading".

She said: "We apologise unreservedly that those multi-agency systems did not protect Ethan as they should have.

"We owe it to Ethan to ensure that the vital lessons from this case lead to lasting changes in our professional practice."

The Ives family was well known to health and education services, Flintshire council's children's services, and North Wales Police, because of issues surrounding "significant domestic violence", substance abuse and homelessness - with 36 referrals and concerns raised about Ethan or his immediate family since 2016.

The review, which refers to Ethan as Child E, noted a history of "non-engagement" with services by Ethan's mother and her family, but found there was "no escalation of concern", with a high proportion of cases closed with no further action.

It also found wider communication between agencies was impacted by IT systems which did not share all the historical information held on file regarding previous referrals.

When his mother and father, Will Griffiths, split on 9 June 2021, police in attendance noted that Ethan's father was "begging" the social worker not to take him to his grandparents, but there was no record that was shared with the children's service.

The family were initially sent to Shannon's sister, where staff thought Ethan would be safe, but later - unbeknown to the council - went to live in the home of Michael and Kerry Ives, in Garden City.

At the time, the review noted school staff, the social worker and the police officer involved thought they were instrumental in sending the children to safety, "little did they know this was the first step in [Ethan's] demise".

The "impact of this knowledge continues to be felt by these staff, who have noted the lack of support they have felt from their respective agencies since this time", the report added.

When Shannon Ives informed children's services on 7 July that Ethan was living with his grandparents, there was no record of any checks being made about his welfare and his address was not changed on the IT system, the review found.

Griffiths told reviewers he had contacted the council to express concerns about Ethan's mother and her parents, but "no one listened".

The report states it was "well documented" that there were concerns about Ethan's grandparents' care and highlighted a "missed opportunity" by Flintshire children's services to "gain valuable information".

Though national guidelines set out in Wales Safeguarding Procedures state that children on the child protection register should been seen by social workers every 10 days, the last time Ethan was seen was 22 July 2021 - more than three weeks before his death - despite a number of attempted home visits.

During a visit on 5 August, a social worker waited on the doorstep for 45 minutes, but did not see Ethan because Shannon and Kerry Ives said he was asleep. CCTV footage later revealed Ethan had already been a victim of physical abuse at this point, which his mother and grandmother were attempting to conceal.

Several attempts to see the children by a social worker and health visitor occurred over subsequent days, but access was denied each time.

The review also considered the effect of the Covid19 pandemic on the provision of social services - with social workers having to isolate and some agency workers brought in from outside the local authority area.

It noted an "unprecedented increase" in referrals by 76 per cent in the three months between March 2021 and June 2021 had also placed an "additional significant pressure" on services.

However, the review concluded a repeated feature of the case was the "missed opportunities" by the various agencies to hear the voices of the Ives children, especially Ethan.

It said there was little information about him in reports and discussions, and files did not "capture his needs, his character, his likes or dislikes".

In one police report, which recorded the events of 9 June 2021 - when Shannon Ives and her children were moved from their family home, there was no mention of him, despite being present.

"From the information shared," reads the report, "it is safe to say that [Ethan's] voice was not heard."

The report set out 16 recommendations to "strengthen safeguarding practice across agencies" with Fôn Roberts, chair of the review, stating Ethan must remain "at the centre".

"He was a young boy who needed safety, care and protection," he said.

"His voice was not heard, and historical information was not consistently brought together."

He stressed new policies, training and systems "must translate into consistent practice".

"The priority must be to embed the learning and demonstrate that it makes a meaningful difference to the safety and wellbeing of children," Roberts said.

In a statement, Flintshire County Council said the "profound impact" of Ethan's death had left a "lasting effect on the professionals and teams responsible for safeguarding children in Flintshire".

It said the child practice review "highlighted areas where information recording and sharing, professional curiosity and co-ordinated intervention could have, and should have, been stronger".

The council apologised to Ethan's father and said it would work to strengthen its approach to "engaging with fathers and male carers in our work with families".

"We recognise that our services were part of the safeguarding response and accept our responsibility for the shortcomings identified by the review.

"We are deeply sorry for the areas where we failed Ethan."

Chief executive, Neal Cockerton, said the Ives made "sustained effort" to "mislead and misdirect", providing false information to professionals seeking to support and protect Ethan.

"While the responsibility for Ethan's murder lies solely with the people convicted of that crime, as a council we deeply regret that opportunities to do more were missed and that he did not receive the level of protection he deserved.

"We have never lost sight of the fact that a young child lost his life, in circumstances where opportunities to protect him were missed," he said.

"While we cannot change what happened, it has strengthened our collective determination to do everything possible to protect vulnerable children.

"However, no amount of learning or improvement can change the outcome for Ethan or lessen the grief experienced by those who love him."

Craig MacLeod, director of social services, was asked if Ethan would still be alive if there had not been the missed opportunities.

He said that "whether interventions would have made a difference I don't know..."

MacLeod was also asked why the father's concerns were not acted upon.

"We were focusing on domestic violence and emotional harm.

"We weren't fully attuned to the risk presented by the grandparents."

A Welsh government spokesperson said: "We expect all those involved in safeguarding children to carefully consider the findings and recommendations of this review and take the necessary action to strengthen practice, improve working together and keep vulnerable children safe."
