What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 09:54:32 GMT

Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.

The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.

It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.

The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.

It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months.

It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.

Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.

The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill.

Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.

Customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy they use and how they pay for it.

From January, for those on variable tariffs:

The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs will not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.

Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.

As well as how much energy you use and how you pay for it, where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.

The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.

The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.

In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.

Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.

Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.

This is especially important when prices go up.

Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.

Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region and payment method.

Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers are 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.

From January, daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.

The electricity standing charge is lower than the amount charged over the previous three months, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.

Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.

The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen

Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.

You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind.

Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees.

Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills.

Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households.

However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising.

In December 2025, Ofgem approved a £28bn investment to improve the electricity and gas grids in Great Britain to strengthen energy supplies and protect customers against volatile energy prices. It will also reduce Britain's dependence on gas.

Customers will pay part of the cost of the upgrade, through an additional £108 added to energy bills by 2031.

These charges started to appear from April 2026, adding about £6 a month to the bill for a typical household covered by the energy cap.

Suppliers must offer customers affordable payment plans or repayment holidays if they are struggling to pay their bills. Most also offer hardship grants.

Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, and since then unpaid bills and charges have shot up.

Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, has advice for people who may be struggling:

Energy UK has a list of support schemes.

Heating oil is not covered by the energy cap. About 1.5 million UK households use heating oil and they have already seen a sharp increase in bills since the Middle East conflict triggered a jump in oil prices. Some users have seen costs more than double.

The issue is particularly acute in Northern Ireland, where about 500,000 homes use heating all, almost two-thirds of all households.

In March, the government announced a £53m support package to help low-income households in rural communities who use heating oil.

Blade Runner 2099 not just about AI, say star Hunter Schafer and series creator

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 06:28:22 GMT

"What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.

The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicted a technologically advanced yet dystopian version of Los Angeles in the then-distant future of 2019.

While the movie's flying cars haven't - quite - materialised yet in the real world, Blade Runner's themes of technological progress and the threats it poses feel just as relevant.

At least that's what the cast and crew of Blade Runner 2099, a new TV series set in the same universe, are hoping.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to stars Hunter Schafer, Lewis Gribben and Dimitri Abold, plus showrunner Silka Luisa, to ask why they think themes of artificial consciousness and existential threats still resonate.

The original Blade Runner, directed by Sir Ridley Scott, is considered a sci-fi classic that had a long-lasting influence on the genre.

It told the story of Detective Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, who hunted down synthetic humans known as replicants.

Schafer says her first exposure to the series was actually marketing for Blade Runner 2049 - the film sequel starring Ford and Ryan Gosling in 2017.

"I never thought I'd have the opportunity to make an addition to the world," she says.

"And so when that opportunity came along, I was quite thrilled."

Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the original film, and portrays a Los Angeles where replicants have taken over.

Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive human forced to team up with replicant Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh), as she tries to track down an artefact that could save humanity.

The series lands at a time when there are disagreements about the nature of the threat AI could pose to humans.

"I think it's particularly relevant right now, especially for the youth and young people who are inheriting a world that's asking a lot of the same questions that the show asks," says Schafer.

"I think that's timely and hopefully helpful to some degree."

But Blade Runner 2099 isn't "necessarily about just AI", says showrunner Luisa.

"It's this bigger question of what is the world going to be in 15 years and how can you plan for it?" she says.

The first Blade Runner also touched on themes of corporate greed and environmental damage, which are evident in the new series.

Luisa hopes the theme of a future that "is not going to be what you were promised" resonates with viewers today.

"The idea that you were born into a world and you thought you were expecting certain aspects of your life just to roll out," she says.

"That system is collapsing. And so what will be your place in whatever comes next?"

Blade Runner 2049 won awards and scored well with reviewers, but reports suggested it didn't hit box office targets.

This was partly blamed on marketing for the film trying to appeal more to existing fans than new ones - so what would the cast say to get younger viewers on board?

"It's just a very rich world," says Gribben, who plays Cora's younger brother Elias.

"It makes you want to learn more."

Gribben also points out that Blade Runner 2099, which employed "hundreds of artists and craftspeople" according to its makers, is a celebration of traditional film-making despite its themes.

"I think a lot of people crave human stories," he says.

"They crave new kind of worlds and new things.

"And I think studios will rely more on technology to make better-looking movies, but they won't have that soul."

Abold, who plays Cora's human ally Bebeto, says one of the show's key messages is about "the connections that you make".

"And the connections that you make are the foundation of humanity," he says.

"Because at the end of the day, all we have is ourselves and each other, right? And that's what feeds any human emotional experience."

Reviews for Blade Runner 2099 have been mostly positive, with a score of 72% on Rotten Tomatoes and an average of 65% on review aggregator Metacritic.

There was praise for the lead performances, the show's visual style and the way it updates the themes established in previous series entries.

The most common criticism was the show's pacing, with several critics describing it as a slow-burn and questioning whether Blade Runner worked as well off the big screen.

Schafer says she felt a lot of pressure when she signed up for the show,

"It's something that we were all aware of when making this show," she says.

"Everybody who was working on this show loves Blade Runner.

"Most people who love film-making love Blade Runner, everybody brought their best to work.

"It upped our game a bit."

Blade Runner 2099 is available on Prime Video from 25 November.

She spent decades as an FBI agent and this is the case she could not let go

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 02:48:53 GMT

Jane Collins had spent 30 years as an FBI agent, but there was one case that haunted her long after retirement.

Michael Donovan was a fraudster, former minister and multimillionaire she had pursued for years, and even in her retirement she could not escape him.

He was regularly featured in the news and on the radio, appearing as a spokesperson for a number of causes, from migrant rights to anti-racism and justice reform.

He and his husband, Richard Moore, lived about an hour's drive from her, in Augusta County, Virginia, on the edge of the Appalachian Mountains.

Together they owned a business, Libre by Nexus, which had made more than $200m (£152m) from migrants seeking release from US immigrant detention centres - but it was a scam, government regulators said.

To Collins, they were the ones who got away.

She had investigated Nexus from 2016 until her retirement from the FBI in 2021. But the only federal criminal charges either faced - after almost six years of her investigation - was a tax charge against Moore.

So when Collins left the bureau, there were still a few strands left of her investigation that she could not let go - like the case of Zach Cruz, the brother of the man who killed 17 people in Parkland, Florida.

They had fronted his $500,000 bail bond, personally picked him up from jail, given him somewhere to stay, and made media appearances on his behalf.

Investigators later found they also took $400,000 from him, proceeds from his late mother's life insurance. Last month, the pair were found guilty of stealing it - with Collins playing a key role as a witness during the trial.

Collins told the BBC in her only interview about the case that she saw it as her final chance to face them in court.

"It means something when people are held to account," she said.

Collins says she was still a young girl when she first thought about joining the FBI.

"I've always been very interested in justice, making things right, and I think all of those things just fell into place," the 64-year-old recalls from her home in Charlottesville, Virginia, where a picture of her late golden retriever named Yogi hangs on the wall and a vintage car is parked in the driveway.

She was accepted to Quantico, the FBI training academy, soon after finishing university, and began to climb the ladder at the bureau, conducting surveillance on suspected Russian spies and crack dealers. In the late 1990s, she began working more on white-collar crimes, which really excited her - "much to my surprise," she adds. What she liked about these cases was the paper trail, and the way they presented themselves as puzzles to solve.

"There's a lot more in those cases that are concrete. As we say, documents don't lie," she says. "It was more challenging."

It also changed her perspective on crime, and victims. Although there was no trail of blood, there was an undeniable ripple from the fraud to the people and families hurt by it.

"People getting defrauded of money, some people their life savings," she explains. "There's a lot of psychological issues that go with that for a victim. They have been duped, so they're very hard on themselves."

Weeks after his older brother gunned down 14 students and three staff members at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Zachary Cruz went to the campus to "reflect on the school shooting and soak it all in".

But when police found him there skateboarding, they arrested the then 18-year-old, charged him with trespassing and put him in jail. On the heels of his brother's massacre, a judge set his bail at $500,000.

His friend called Nexus, looking for help to get him out. But Donovan and Moore did more than that - not only did they pay his bail, but they picked Cruz up from jail and took him to a hotel room.

Cruz later told the court that when he met them for the first time, it felt "like a movie".

During dinner that first night, the couple asked Cruz if he wanted to move to Virginia and work for Nexus.

The Florida judge overseeing his probation called it a "wonderful opportunity".

Soon he was living with them, and sharing in their media spotlight. Donovan and Moore accompanied him on interviews where the young man spoke about trying to understand his brother's crimes.

The couple even helped produce a short-lived online reality show called "Being Zach Cruz", which chronicled what it's like to be the brother of a famous killer.

"It was not ordinary," he later said.

According to Moore and Donovan, in an interview with the BBC in 2022, Cruz had become part of their family. They called him their "son" and said they had spent lavishly on his pursuit of a skateboarding career.

But they were deeply in debt, fighting off creditors - and the IRS. And through it all, Collins was doggedly on their tail.

Donovan and Moore had spent their wealth extravagantly - a fleet of luxury vehicles, a $500,000 wedding and a million-dollar self-published book titled Not Free America: What Your Government Doesn't Want You to Know.

But they owed millions to several state insurance boards, which had fined them for operating an unlicensed bond company. They owed a former business partner, RLI Insurance, millions for their failure to pay back bail that was lost when clients skipped court. And Moore owed more than $3m to the IRS.

Prosecutors alleged it was this tax debt that spurred Moore and Donovan to dupe Cruz out of his inheritance. Donovan declined an interview, through his attorney.

Collins initially focused her investigation on Libre by Nexus, and whether the company had broken any laws.

But her case took a turn when she received a tip that Donovan and Moore may be personally exploiting Cruz.

Bank records showed that $428,000 - the insurance money Cruz was entitled to after his mother died - was transferred into a joint account held by Cruz and Moore, and then into Moore's personal account, in 2019, according to the county's search warrant.

Collins tried to interview Cruz, who was still living with Moore and Donovan.

Driving up to their house one evening, Collins says she saw an armed security guard stationed outside, while barricades blocked the entrance to the front door and driveway.

"People can't easily come and go," she thought to herself. Cruz never came to the door.

Since 2016, Collins had been working on the case in conjunction with the Internal Revenue Service and Homeland Security Investigations, which oversees immigration law. The agencies were investigating whether Nexus defrauded people and brought migrants illegally to work for their company, as well as the allegations involving Cruz's insurance money and tax fraud.

But by the time she was due to retire, the federal prosecutor in charge of the case had narrowed the focus to just tax fraud, which he passed onto another prosecutor.

Collins was disappointed.

Ultimately, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau - a federal agency with the power to bring civil, but not criminal, cases to court - took legal action against Nexus, leading to an $811m judgement against the company.

The agency provides a much-needed service, helping to pursue corporations when other avenues have failed, said Ted Mermin, executive director of the Berkeley Center for Consumer Law & Economic Justice.

To bring a criminal case, "you have to show that beyond a shadow of a doubt they violated the law", he said.

A civil case, on the other hand, only needs to show that it is more likely than not that they violated the law.

Meanwhile, Collins was running up against the clock: the FBI has a mandatory retirement age of 57, and she had already been extended. She retired in the summer of 2021 at the age of 59.

A few months later, Cruz, Donovan and Moore sued her, alleging she had "conspired to create a fake 'joint investigation'" with a local agency, and that her career was "cut short after she violated department policies and/or laws in connection with her rogue investigation".

The bureau's attorney repudiated those claims, and a federal judge dismissed the case. The lawsuit did little to dissuade Collins, who brushed it off as "frivolous".

"I was not intimidated by them," she told the BBC. Through his attorney, Donovan declined the BBC's request for comment. Moore, who is serving a seven-year prison sentence for filing a fraudulent Nexus tax return, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Before she left the bureau, Collins sat down with her bosses and the agent assigned to take the case over from her, she said. She still had hope that it would be prosecuted.

But more than a year went by, and there were no charges.

It seemed, at least for a while, that her case was finished. Then, in October 2022, local police and Virginia State Police stormed Moore and Donovan's home in Fishersville, and their offices in Verona.

It was not the feds, as Collins had hoped. But this was still a chance at holding the men to account.

They seized laptops, mobile phones, body cameras and thumb drives. Donovan and Moore were arrested and charged, and then released on bail.

Evidence of the raid was still clear in the shattered glass of the front door, when the BBC went to Nexus offices to interview the couple several days after police stormed the property.

In the interview, Donovan and Moore said they had not taken advantage of Cruz and had done nothing wrong.

Zach, who was still living with them at the time, told the BBC he had spent all his inheritance willingly. But he is no longer living with the couple, and appeared as a witness for the prosecution during the trial.

After Collins retired from the bureau in 2021, she began working for a state agency. She plans to retire for good in a few years, when she hopes to spend more time with her husband and three children and travel around the world.

Looking back, she thinks of this chapter at the end of her career in federal law enforcement as discouraging. She had wanted to declare "case closed" years ago.

"I enjoyed my career immensely. I wouldn't trade it. I felt like I made a big difference in a lot of ways," she says. "But this case, it caused me a lot of frustration."

Still, she says, she feels grateful that someone did take this case on.

When she heard the jury had convicted them on all counts, she thought: "Finally, justice".

"It had been a long time coming," she said. "But we needed to wait until the house of cards fell down."

My family were killed in Ukraine. My mum blamed Zelensky's troops - the truth is complicated

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 00:54:13 GMT

I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.

It turned my world upside down.

Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

We stopped speaking.

Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground.

I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.

But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.

I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.

I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.

Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.

This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.

It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.

"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.

With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse.

"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.

Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.

I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.

She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones."

She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.

"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her.

She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.

The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.

She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions.

With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.

Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.

"If they had seen me they would have killed me too."

Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.

"Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.

Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

The new local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.

These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.

The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.

Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.

He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.

As for my grandfather, it said his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.

I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.

I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents.

He said he did not know anything about who killed them.

"I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

I examined military maps from DeepStateMap. Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.

My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.

I turned to the Ukrainian military.

A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.

Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.

We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

It said it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.

We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.

However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.

Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.

There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.

Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.

She is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place

At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.

"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.

"Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.

Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe

BBC News Wed, 25 Nov 2026 00:34:05 GMT

Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.

"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.

In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.

In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.

Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.

In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.

"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.

Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."

However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."

These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.

"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.

Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offences. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.

This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.

"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.

Tiny car sales rose strongly till 2024 although they have flattened since in France with the withdrawal of subsidies for electric models.

Curiously, the arrival in this niche market of a giant competitor in the shape of Stellantis brand Citroën was actually good news for existing French manufacturers like Aixam and Ligier.

"We're specialised in this niche market and we're very good at what we do, but of course, we didn't have the communication strength of a multinational like Stellantis. They helped us to make people understand that it was possible in France to drive this product from 14-years-old, in Germany from 15-years-old. They gave a lot of visibility to our market," says Aixam sales and marketing director Tom Faget.

Aixam has invested €30m (£25m; $33m) in expanding its production capacity in France. And its sales are growing in other European countries, even as the French market slows.

Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them.

"We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence.

"Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."

There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.

Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location

New Scientist November 25, 2026

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Advertisement

Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets (Morus bassanus) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters (Puffinus mauretanicus) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.

Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.

“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.

In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.

The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.

Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro, also at BirdLife International.

Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.

“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aeh2224

AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it

New Scientist November 25, 2026

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

Advertisement

This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please.

It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

If two chromosomes are better than one, why not three?

New Scientist November 25, 2026

If two chromosomes are better than one, why not three? Wouldn’t this give a better chance of surviving environmental change?

Hazel RussmanLondon, UK

Living creatures with three sets of chromosomes do exist and are known as triploids. However, they are sterile because of the way that chromosomes behave during the formation of gametes (ova and sperm).

Advertisement

During this process, matching chromosomes pair up and exchange genetic material, then separate again. Eventually, gametes with a single set of chromosomes are produced. Because of the gene exchange that took place earlier, each gamete is unique, with a different combination of gene variants (alleles). This is good for providing raw material for natural selection, but it would obviously not work with an odd number of chromosome sets.

Among plants, tetraploids with four sets of chromosomes and hexaploids with six do exist. Bread wheat is a hexaploid. As long as the chromosome number is even, the system works as described.

RÓisín LongTrinity College Dublin, Ireland

Humans usually have two copies of each autosomal (i. e., non-sex) chromosome, and so two copies of each gene. This has many benefits. If one gene copy has a disease-causing mutation, the other can sometimes buffer this. Further, during meiosis (the process by which sex cells with one copy of each chromosome are created), genetic material is shuffled between chromosomal pairs, promoting genetic variation and facilitating environmental adaptation. So, would having more chromosomes be even better?

Having full extra sets of chromosomes is termed “polyploidy”. Many lineages across animals, plants and fungi experienced polyploidy in their evolutionary history, before returning to having two chromosome sets, and some species are currently polyploid. These polyploidy events correlate with times of environmental stress, and so polyploidy probably conferred an immediate survival advantage under specific conditions. Extra genetic material also presents the opportunity for novelties to evolve over time. However, polyploidy rarely becomes established in lineages, and has many immediate disadvantages.

Polyploidy disrupts cell size and the ratio of surface area to volume, disturbing regular cellular functioning. The significant increase in genomic material interferes with usual cellular processes and gene expression. Polyploidy can also disrupt even division of chromosomes into sex cells during meiosis. While polyploidy is more common in plants, it is rarely observed in animals. Polyploidy is a common cause of miscarriage in humans.

Further, having extra copies of individual chromosomes (termed “trisomy”) alters balanced gene expression and development and also often results in miscarriage. Down’s syndrome (trisomy of chromosome 21) is the most common autosomal trisomy among live births, one reason for this being that fewer extra gene copies are present on this small chromosome.

So, while there can be advantages to having three or more chromosome copies, the consequences at the gene- expression, cellular and organismal level are complex.

Is The Time Traveler’s Wife the perfect audiobook to experience on shuffle?

New Scientist November 25, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Reader Jenny Ozanne writes to tell us of a horrific incident that befell her partner. He had bought Audrey Niffenegger’s novel The Time Traveler’s Wife as a CD audiobook, to listen to on long car journeys.

“After a while, he complained that the plot was completely impossible to follow,” writes Jenny. “It was only when I checked his player that I realized he had accidentally set the CD to ‘shuffle’. “

Advertisement

Jenny raises two points, which Feedback heartily endorses: “I’m still not sure what’s more impressive: the story’s ability to survive total chronological chaos, or the fact that he listened to three random chapters before suspecting anything was wrong.”

Feedback would suggest that The Time Traveler’s Wife might be the ideal novel to experience on shuffle, since the narrative is heavily non-linear. The main character hops uncontrollably back and forth through history. This led us to wonder: would any similarly chrono-displaced stories survive the experience of being played on shuffle, or even be improved by it?

We wondered, for instance, about David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas. This has six stories set in different periods, including a future in which human clones are used as cheap labour, and a more distant future in which everything has gone a bit Mad Max. The stories are linked by characters in later timelines reading about the earlier ones, and by subtle coincidences. What would it be like on shuffle?

However, after careful reflection, we realised there is only one correct answer to this, and that is Shane Carruth’s 2004 film Primer, which tells the story of two tech bros who invent a time machine in their garage. At first, they use it to go back in time and make money on the stock exchange, only to become caught up in an escalating web of betrayal and deception as they endlessly rewrite their lives.

Primer is so overcomplicated, so mind-wreckingly confusing, that some poor soul once went so far as to draw a diagram trying to convey its timeline. Posted on Reddit by u/Clawz114, the diagram looks like a cross between a metro map and a flowchart of the inner workings of a chemical factory. It is therefore possible that playing the scenes in random order might actually cause the film to make more sense.

It’s that time of year when many of us are thinking, “Oh blimey, I need to buy everyone presents” and then having a meltdown when we can’t think of anything. The last refuge of the true gift scoundrel is, of course, the scented candle. This item might as well come with a note saying, “Sorry, I couldn’t think of anything”.

Readers looking to step up their scented candle game may wish to investigate JD + Kate Industries, which is run by a pair of humour writers with a sideline in themed scented candles. They have taken these tedious items to new and different places.

For instance, consider the Late Bronze Age Collapse scented candle, which “commemorates everyone’s favorite late 13th century [BC] widespread societal collapse”. Happily, it doesn’t smell of violence and decay, but rather of “burning cedar”, since “Lebanese cedar was a popular building material in the Late Bronze Age”.

Those with more contemporary tastes may wish to consider the AI scented candle, which has a little sculpture of a data centre on the top, “surrounded by a post-apocalyptic, bombed-out city”. What does it smell of, you ask? “Diesel generator exhaust fumes”.

Finally, those nostalgic for the headier days of space exploration might appreciate the Apollo 11 scented candle. Disappointingly, this doesn’t smell of moon dust, which, as we understand it, basically smells of burning because it reacts with oxygen on contact. Instead, its scent mimics “a certain powdered orange drink mix often associated with the space program, but that was not brought on Apollo 11. The astronauts brought a generic, grapefruit-flavored powdered drink mix instead, because they selfishly did not consider us and our desire to market candles.”

Feedback has no idea if these candles are any good, but we enjoyed JD + Kate’s website a lot.

Let us foray once again into the wonderful world of scientific acronyms. First, two reader claims that, for reasons that will become obvious, we cannot verify.

Michael Berkson tells us: “As a solicitor my late wife was involved in development of insurance for doctors. The firm had to tell the client that they needed to choose a better name. Their original choice was Professional Indemnity Support Scheme.” Michael says the clients were open to replacing “scheme” with “service”, which helps not at all.

Likewise, Jim Taylor asserts that he was once confronted with a military programme intended to ensure that spare parts would always be available for key equipment. It was called the Contractor Repair Advanced Provisioning System.

Finally, a story we can confirm is true because we looked it up. Reader Geraldine Beare is an indexer, which is one of those jobs that we often forget about but would swiftly notice if it wasn’t done. “I am at present indexing a book on goats,” says Geraldine. Through this assignment she has learned the acronym “OMAGOD”, which she recommends saying “quickly, or perhaps in a vaguely Scottish accent”. It actually stands for ovine mouth and gum obscure disease.

Our verdict on Dark Eden by Chris Beckett: ‘Holy cow. Chapter 44!’

New Scientist November 25, 2026

Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden, a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013.

Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too!

Free newsletter

It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It really got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – very different flora and fauna.”

Advertisement

Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in Dark Eden. I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an essay Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here.

Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world

There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image.

“I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.”

The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers.

“Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.”

Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”.

Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed Dark Eden – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex.

“Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”.

But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, Audrey Niffenegger and Emily St. John Mandel).

What is the world actually like, if what we see is just our brain’s interpretations? part 3

New Scientist November 25, 2026

If the world we observe is just our brain’s interpretation of the electrochemical signals it receives from our eyes, what is the world actually like? (continued)

James FentonClachan Seil, Argyll and Bute, UK

Surely a camera puts the lie to the idea that the world exists only when we are present? A picture taken from a remote camera, without any humans present, shows us the same world as our eyes do. The geological record shows that the world existed before us and that the natural forces we experience today have been present for billions of years. Our senses tell us that rock is solid; the geological record tells us that rocks have always been solid.

Our senses tell us that rock is solid; the geological record tells us that rocks have always been solid

The geological record can be used to infer the past landscapes and processes before humans evolved, and we infer this without using our senses – only our intellect. The structure of animals and plants that were present before humans tells us that they reacted to the same forces (such as gravity and light) as we do today. This implies that there is an objective reality out there – whether observed or not – and that our senses, and those of other animals, are quite good at describing it.

Wairarapa transport funding: Rural projects risk missing out under BCR rules

New Zealand Herald November 25, 2026

The Waihenga Bridge into Martinborough often closes in severe weather events. Photo / Sue Teodoro

Wairarapa’s vital transport links risk missing out on funding because investment rules favour metropolitan routes over rural lifelines, mayors say.

At Greater Wellington’s Regional Transport Committee meeting on Tuesday, South Wairarapa Mayor Fran Wilde and Carterton Mayor Steve Cretney raised concerns that the region’s low traffic volumes put it at a permanent disadvantage.

To be included as a priority in the 10-year Regional Land Transport Plan, projects must score well on a benefit-cost ratio (BCR) – a formula heavily driven by daily traffic counts and commuter time savings.

“My problem is the BCR, and I know we can’t change that ... but the fact is a small population area can never get a high BCR,” she said.

“You just cannot do it under this formula ever.”

The Regional Land Transport Plan guides regional transport investment and helps inform national funding decisions by NZTA.

In the previous plan, only three of the 39 listed programmes had specific ties to Wairarapa.

Wilde said Wairarapa’s strategic transport links were in need of investment, but because of relatively low traffic volumes and affected populations, projects were not included in the RLTP as a priority.

“If someone in Wellington was to say the suburb of Karori with 17,000 people now is going to be cut off completely for ‘x days’ or so many times a year, that would be a major issue for Wellington City,” she said.

“We have 50,000 people in Wairarapa.

“We have a bridge just south of Pūkaha on SH2 which is in dire need of replacement, and we have a road at the southern end that if there is a large event like an earthquake we will be completely cut off with no fuel supplies.”

She said the critical routes into Martinborough, such as the Waihenga Bridge on SH53, also close frequently, but “the traffic volume on normal days will never hit the BCR rate”.

“It’s very frustrating because if you had an equivalent population cut off in a metropolitan area that would be huge.

“But apparently that doesn’t matter in a rural area. I just wanted to say that.”

Cretney agreed with Wilde.

“I am concerned around the methodology and the fact that rural and interregional projects might be disadvantaged because they fall outside the metropolitan strategic network,” he said.

“How will the qualitative benefits be assessed where a traditional BCR does not adequately reflect on the resilience and rural accessibility or consequences of a network failure?”

Under the framework, projects were weighted 50% for regional priority, 20% for regional alignment and sequencing, and 30% for national strategic alignment.

The regional priority portion was based on Greater Wellington Regional Council’s transport investment priorities, which had a weighting of 30% for public transport, 30% for resilience, 20% for strategic access, and 20% for health, safety, and the environment.

Regional alignment was based on how soon it would be phased into the council’s Future Network Plan.

National strategic alignment was based on whether it aligned with the Government Policy Statement on land transport and its BCR.

BCRs indicate whether activities will generate more benefits than they cost, make it possible to compare activities, and enable prioritisation of activities under funding constraints – all within a well-defined framework.

For this reason, they remain the primary measure of economic efficiency NZTA uses when assessing an activity from a purely monetised point of view.

More than 10,000 students expected to re-sit NCEA English exam after disruption

New Zealand Herald November 25, 2026

More than 10,000 students are expected to sit an extra NCEA Level 2 English exam on December 4 after a nationwide outage disrupted the original sitting. Photo / Brett Phibbs

More than 10,000 students are expected to sit an extra NCEA Level 2 English exam next week after the original digital exam was disrupted.

An unknown number of students were unable to log into the online version of the exam, while others lost their work during or at the end of the assessment.

Schools had told the New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA) by midday on Wednesday that 10,516 students were likely to sit the exam on the morning of Friday, December 4.

NZQA arranged the extra session after the November 12 disruption.

A statement said it will send schools enough exam papers to accommodate students who decide to sit the exam after the initial count.

Contact reporter Rachel Maher

NZQA deputy chief executive for assessment Jann Marshall encouraged those students to tell their schools as soon as possible.

“Students eligible for Special Assessment Conditions will be able to receive that support if their school is aware they intend to sit the exam.”

Marshall said the paper had been in development for 2027 and had gone through NZQA’s usual development process.

“We know students have worked hard this year to prepare for their exams. This additional exam opportunity gives students another chance to demonstrate their knowledge and skills.”

Of those expected to sit the English exam, 156 have another exam scheduled for the same morning.

NZQA will use its usual exam clash process so they can sit both.

December 4 is the final day of the 2026 NCEA and New Zealand Scholarship exam period.

NZQA’s digital exam platform went down nationwide about 10am on November 12, midway through the NCEA Level 2 English exam.

Some students reported losing up to 1400 words of their essays, while others switched to pen and paper where schools could provide it.

NZQA said the issue was resolved at 10.35am and was linked to the overnight transfer of student responses from its exam platform to its marking system.

About 37,500 students were registered to sit NCEA Level 2 English digitally on November 12, while another 7500 sat it on paper. NZQA chief executive Christian Hawkesby told Herald NOW it was unclear how many students had to abandon the exam after the platform crashed.

The impact varied between schools. At some exam centres, students waited up to 40 minutes before being given extra time to finish.

A 16-year-old Manawatū student told the Herald he was about 20 seconds from finishing an essay when the system shut down.

NZQA said schools could submit derived grades on behalf of affected students using evidence from mock exams or other work for the same standard.

Hawkesby said NZQA would also compare results with previous years to gauge the impact of the outage.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said students had been “badly let down” and asked NZQA to have a backup ready for the following week’s exams.

Rachel Maher is the education correspondent for the New Zealand Herald. She also covers other topics such as Auckland issues, crime and local government. She started at the Herald as a breaking news journalist in 2022, before joining the Auckland team this year.

Fibre optic cable reveals hidden structure of Alpine Fault in new study

New Zealand Herald November 25, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Researchers have used a fibre optic telecommunications cable running across Haast Pass to gain an unprecedented look inside one of New Zealand’s most significant earthquake faults.

The study used laser light sent down an unused optical fibre to measure tiny changes in the cable as seismic waves passed through it.

The technique, known as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS), effectively turned the cable into a long line of sensitive earthquake sensors, allowing researchers to examine the Alpine Fault’s internal structure in greater detail than conventional seismometers.

The findings, published in the journal Science Advances, reveal the fault is not a single fracture but a complex band of damaged rock about 200m wide, containing six narrower zones of intensely crushed and sheared rock.

Professor John Townend, of Victoria University of Wellington, an author of the study, said the research had allowed scientists to use ordinary telecommunications infrastructure to look inside the fault.

“We’ve used an ordinary telecommunications cable to look inside one of New Zealand’s most significant faults.

“By sending laser light down an optical fibre in a cable crossing the Alpine Fault near Haast, we turned it into a long line of sensitive earthquake sensors.

“Seismic waves from small earthquakes nearby travelled along the fault as distinctive energy pulses that reveal its internal structure.”

Townend said the signals showed the fault was a band of damaged rock rather than a single clean crack.

“Within it, we found six much narrower zones of more intensely crushed and sheared rock. We call these ‘cores,’ and we think the most prominent core is where the fault slipped during recent large earthquakes.”

The main core runs for about 180km, with the researchers finding that despite bends and kinks in the fault at the surface, its main slip zone appeared to be largely continuous underground.

“This matters because an earthquake’s size depends mainly on how much of the fault breaks,” Townend said.

“Understanding the fault’s structure helps us work out how much could break at once, and so how large the next big earthquake might be.

“That helps Aotearoa prepare for the hazard and reduce its impacts.”

University of Otago Centre for Sustainability Research director Professor Caroline Orchiston said the research represented another leap forward in Alpine Fault science.

She said the technique had revealed significant detail about the complexity of the fault zone near the surface, and what that could mean for earthquake magnitude, ground movements and aftershocks.

The research also confirmed that boundaries between the Alpine Fault’s South Westland, Central and North Westland segments acted as barriers to the way earthquakes travelled along the fault.

Larger earthquakes of magnitude 8 or above were more likely to jump those segment boundaries, Orchiston said.

“All together, this new science can really help us understand what a future Alpine Fault earthquake could be like, e. g. do most large earthquakes on the fault turn into magnitude 8+ events, or could we expect some in the magnitude 7 range that stay within one segment of the fault?

“And what does this new knowledge mean for how we might forecast aftershocks one day? These are all questions for the future, but we need this fundamental research to help us get there.”

Orchiston said DAS was still an emerging technique and further research funding would help advance scientific understanding.

She said the work also highlighted how Alpine Fault research was helping scientists around the world better understand mature plate boundary faults, which had produced earthquakes over thousands or millions of years.

Earth Sciences New Zealand seismologist Dr Emily Warren-Smith said the remote sections of the Alpine Fault, including South Westland, were hugely influential in determining what the next earthquake might look and feel like.

“While much of the Alpine Fault is inaccessible and sparsely populated, like in South Westland, these often-forgotten remote sections are actually hugely influential in determining what the next earthquake will look and feel like.”

Warren-Smith said how an earthquake rupture travelled through the Haast section of the fault could be the difference between a devastating event with nationwide impacts and a much smaller earthquake limited to the lower South Island.

“DAS now offers an incredibly detailed way of studying these complex and remote sections of faults to unparalleled scales, all while using existing infrastructure.

“These detailed observations are vital in helping us build better earthquake models to help prepare for the next Alpine Fault earthquake.”

The Alpine Fault is capable of producing a major earthquake, with scientists working to better understand the likelihood, size and potential impacts of a future rupture.

The research adds to efforts to improve understanding of how earthquakes might propagate along the fault and the risks they could pose to communities and infrastructure.

Man admits concealing body of 21-year-old Braydon Hepworth

New Zealand Herald November 25, 2026

Braydon Hepworth's body was found buried in a shed in Linwood on October 8 after he disappeared in early September. Photo / NZ Police

By Adam Burns of RNZ

A Christchurch man has admitted concealing the body of Braydon Hepworth.

The 21-year-old’s body was found buried in a shed in Linwood on October 8 after he disappeared in early September.

A 34-year-old, one of two men charged with concealing Hepworth’s body, appeared in the Christchurch District Court on Wednesday.

He pleaded guilty to interfering with human remains.

Judge Jane Farish extended a temporary order for name suppression before releasing him on bail.

The man will be sentenced in April.

A 60-year-old man, whose name is also suppressed, pleaded not guilty tomanslaughter, concealing Hepworth’s body and making a false statement. He appeared in the High Court at Christchurch last week and was remanded in custody with a trial tentatively set for late next year.

An independent review is being carried out into the care Hepworth received at the Christchurch City Mission after he was told to leave its Whakaora Kāinga transitional housing complex less than two months before he disappeared.

Mission board chairwoman Jane Evans earlier said the review would examine Hepworth’s time with the mission and the decision-making involved in his care.

“We take our responsibilities to our clients, our staff and the wider community very seriously,” she said in October.

“The mission is open to improving how it supports people in its care and looks forward to the outcome.”

Wellington barrister Andrew Scott-Howman, who was leading the review, was due to report to the board at the end of the month with a summary of findings and response to be released soon after, “subject to privacy and legal limitations”.
