Child trafficking in New Zealand: Oranga Tamariki gets referrals almost daily

New Zealand Herald November 25, 2026

Child trafficking is increasing in New Zealand at alarming rates, Children's Commissioner Jane Searle says.

New Zealand is increasingly recognised as a destination, transit and source country for child trafficking, according to government documents.

Material obtained under the Official Information Act by Newstalk ZB has revealed Oranga Tamariki receives referrals about suspected cases on an “almost daily basis”.

Human trafficking involves the recruitment, transportation, transfer, harbouring or receipt of people for exploitation through force, fraud or deception.

The documents show years of warnings about gaps in adoption and immigration settings while Children’s Commissioner Jane Searle said the country has been “asleep at the wheel”.

“Most New Zealanders would be shocked if they knew child trafficking was occurring in New Zealand and knew the problem is growing,” Searle said.

She cited an estimate of up to 8000 trafficking victims a year in New Zealand “and we know from international statistics, at least a third of them will be children”.

Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee – who led urgent reforms to adoption law last year – said there had been some “horrific” stories and it was disappointing previous Governments hadn’t acted to fix the issues raised.

Oranga Tamariki said it was estimated that 1.2 million children are trafficked every year and every country is affected, including New Zealand.

Searle said she believed the figure was much higher.

“The problem is larger than can be measured because this offence happens in the shadows. Children can be completely invisible.”

With a career in law and as a police detective, Searle’s background includes sitting on government agency and sector advisory groups, including the Human Trafficking and Worker Exploitation Advisory Group.

She said many New Zealanders wrongly assume it only happens overseas or across international borders.

Searle said domestic trafficking can occur online and “we’ve had cases of that”.

She said one of the concerning issues is that trafficking would be happening much more than we would ever know.

“We don’t have enough data, but what we do know from those working on the front line is it’s increasing in New Zealand at alarming rates.

“It is time for New Zealand to catch up and understand this is happening both domestically and across borders ... and that this issue is not going to go away.”

Oranga Tamariki’s International Child Protection Unit manager Sharyn Titchener said there was “a lack of research into child trafficking within a New Zealand context” and the agency has no data collection or codification system that accurately captures the main forms of child exploitation.

Social workers at Barnardos Aotearoa have noted concerning situations over the years, particularly involving children who have been brought across the border or moved through “transient placements” between caregivers.

Barnardos Aotearoa operations manager Sarena McNaught said the issue was “hidden in plain sight”.

“We cannot, as an organisation, prove that this is child trafficking, but what we can do is provide thorough assessment and make sure we place a referral for investigation.”

She said what her staff can measure is closer to “domestic servitude”, asking themselves whether the tamariki (children) are placed in education or if their core role in the home environment is akin to household slavery.

McNaught said “if there’s a lack of continuity or stories that don’t add up in regards to that young person’s life”, that raises flags.

She said people can help spot signs in their own backyards, encouraging people to notice children who stay removed from social connection or community play.

“We don’t want people assuming the worst, we just want people to have the heart of the children at the centre and be curious.”

Searle said “someone who’s been trafficked internationally may not speak English, they’re totally isolated from anyone that would protect them, they’re used as a commodity, have huge trauma, [have] trust barriers with authorities and [are] in a country they don’t know”.

“Traffickers prey on fear and that’s how they keep people from getting help. Because of that, it can be difficult for agencies to be able to identify and connect with the victims.”

High-profile cases before the courts in recent years have included a Fijian national sentenced in 2018 to 10 years and three months’ jail after selling her 15-year-old daughter into sex slavery more than 1000 times.

In 2020, Samoan national Joseph Matamata was sentenced to 11 years on trafficking and slavery charges. Two of his 13 victims were children adopted from Samoa and trafficked to New Zealand for labour exploitation.

The documents show officials spent years warning ministers about vulnerabilities in international adoption and immigration settings.

A December 2020 briefing stated “there is a risk that adopted children may be entering New Zealand into existing harmful environments”.

Officials also advised that New Zealanders with significant Oranga Tamariki care and protection records had been able to adopt children in an overseas court and have those adoptions recognised for immigration purposes.

Agencies warned that international adoptions can carry welfare risks including trafficking, forced labour, domestic servitude, coerced marriage and sexual exploitation.

Intelligence assessments found children entering through “non-genuine” adoptions may also face increased risks.

Officials define a non-genuine adoption as one motivated mainly by secondary gains, such as immigration opportunities, education, employment or residency, rather than a permanent parent-child relationship.

One briefing said “many non-genuine adoptions are being entered into purely for the purpose of obtaining a residence visa” and another warned that “the incidence of non-genuine adoptions ... is expected to increase over time”.

Immigration New Zealand’s acting general manager of refugee and migrant services, Alejandra Mercado, said officials encounter these cases and they are “a long-standing challenge”.

She confirmed joint-agency intelligence work involving police, Oranga Tamariki and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment “has identified cases of child trafficking”.

Until urgent reforms last year, Immigration New Zealand was legally required to recognise overseas adoptions that met the criteria in section 17 of the Adoption Act.

This meant officials could not consider concerns about the adoption or the adoptive parent, with no character checks for parents seeking to bring adopted children to New Zealand under the Dependent Child Category and no provisions to assess parents’ risk profiles, including criminal histories.

Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast as soon as the issue had come across her desk she had asked for it to be dealt with “immediately and urgently”.

The Adoption Amendment Act 2025 was passed under urgency in September last year, and the new Government would be able to pick up a piece of legislation “that will absolutely make sure that children cannot be trafficked through New Zealand in this way without some protections for them”, McKee said.

Most of the 1000-plus children adopted from overseas went into good homes in New Zealand, but “quite a number” didn’t.

“We’ve had some very horrific stories come through over the last few years.”

It was disappointing the problem hadn’t been fixed by previous Governments.

“It’s not just about me fixing the adoption law. It’s about Immigration looking at their settings, Oranga Tamariki working well with police, MBIE.

“We now have a trafficking plan in place that Minister Costello put in. So there’s a lot of work along multiple agencies that will help fix this problem.”

For the fifth consecutive year, the US State Department has ranked New Zealand Tier 2 in response to efforts to combat and counter trafficking in persons.

That means it “does not fully meet standards but is making significant efforts”.

By contrast, New Zealand’s Five Eyes partners Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States and several OECD countries are Tier 1.

But Searle said New Zealand used to be Tier 1 and the fall went largely unnoticed.

“That means we’re actually going backwards,” Searle said, “we were really asleep at the wheel.

“There are many countries overseas that have been dealing with these issues for years with much greater awareness than we have.

“We need to understand why we dropped, why we weren’t putting enough intentional resources and focus on this.

“We need to do better.”

Concerns have also been raised about traffickers using children to illegally obtain welfare payments, including the Unsupported Child’s Benefit and the Youth Payment.

As part of efforts to identify trafficking risks earlier, Titchener said assessors for the Unsupported Child’s Benefit and the Youth Payment have received specialist training.

“This has meant there is greater screening to ensure that children and young people are with caregivers who are protective.”

Oranga Tamariki’s International Child Protection Unit also sits on multi-agency groups providing advice, operational support, tracking emerging risks and identifying trafficking concerns.

It also delivers training to the New Zealand Police, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment.

Barnardos developed its own training module with Titchener’s Oranga Tamariki unit and it is now available to practitioners nationwide.

Barnardos’ McNaught echoed the importance of a multi-agency approach.

“We don’t want it to only sit with Oranga Tamariki or border control ... we want to ensure even teachers or GPs have an understanding as a cross-sector solution to close some of those gaps,” she said.

In September 2025, Parliament passed the Adoption Amendment Act under urgency, temporarily suspending New Zealand’s recognition of some overseas adoptions for citizenship and immigration purposes.

The Government said the changes were necessary because New Zealand’s international adoption laws had not provided sufficient safeguards for children and young people.

It acknowledged evidence that some children brought to the country through international adoption had been neglected, abused or exploited.

The measures remain in place while broader reform is developed through the proposed Overseas Adoptions Legislation Bill.

The Government has also adopted a Trafficking in Persons National Action Plan 2027–2031, aimed at strengthening prevention, victim support and enforcement.

Searle credits the progress, noting there was more awareness and focus than ever within government agencies.

“But there is no doubt we still want more,” she said, “we’re playing catch-up all the time.”

Searle said there was a need for more resources, more training for agencies, better data and more support for victims once identified.

“We need to wake up and understand this is here and it will only grow if we’re following overseas trends.

“The urgency is that there are victims there right now.

“We simply, as a country, can’t accept that this goes on in our shores.”

Rosie Leishman is a reporter and multimedia journalist based in Ōtautahi, Christchurch. She joined Newstalk ZB in 2025, after experience working at the Bangkok Post in Thailand.

Rotorua landlords Stephen and Jasu Bhana ordered to pay $11,250 in exemplary damages

New Zealand Herald November 25, 2026

Stephen and Jasu Bhana, controversial sibling landlords from Rotorua. Photos / TVNZ, NZME

Rotorua’s controversial Bhana siblings have been ordered to cut $200 from the rent they charge tenants of three poorly maintained flats, after “egregious” tenancy rule breaches.

The Tenancy Tribunal has also ordered Stephen and Jasu Bhana to pay the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment $11,250 in exemplary damages after the agency’s five-year fight to have the landlords fix the flats.

The tribunal made a three-year order restraining the Bhanas from further similar “unlawful acts” under the Residential Tenancies Act. Breaching a restraining order is a criminal offence.

Details of the case, relating to flats at 92A, 92B and 92C Ranolf St, are revealed in a just-published tribunal order decision dated August 20.

It comes after the Rotorua Daily Post revealed last week that two of Stephen Bhana’s other properties are up for mortgagee sale.

The Bhanas have been subject to several tribunal orders relating to the Ranolf St flats over the past two years.

The latest tribunal decision said the ministry took action against the Bhanas after the landlords failed to comply with a tribunal order to repair the flats.

This was despite two compliance deadline extensions.

The decision said the “extensive” background to this case started in September 2021, when the tribunal found the Bhanas had failed to maintain the three flats.

The landlords were ordered to fix the flats and pay the tenants at the time more than $16,000 in exemplary damages.

They were required to fix issues with the guttering, weathertightness, bay window, flashings, water-damaged timber, a toilet, kitchen tap, defective light fitting, door handles, kitchen cupboard doors and drawers, a ranch slider and the oven.

The Bhanas made lengthy appeals against those orders through the courts but were unsuccessful.

Some of the required repairs were made, including to a toilet, ranch slider and oven. In April 2024, the tribunal issued a further order for the remaining work to be done within three months.

Again, the Bhanas objected. Their request for a rehearing was refused, so they appealed, unsuccessfully.

In an affidavit to the tribunal, an investigator for the ministry said the landlord failed to respond to messages asking if the work was done after the July deadline passed.

The inspector came to inspect the flats in January 2025, but reported that six minutes after arriving, Stephen Bhana turned up and demanded she leave.

In the short time she was there, she noted the required work to the living room, kitchen and exterior was not done.

In July last year, the ministry filed an action against the landlord for not complying with the repair orders.

The Bhanas were granted two adjournments, delaying the hearing. One was because Stephen Bhana had a conflicting matter and a second because he was sick.

Their third adjournment request was declined, with adjudicator Rex Woodhouse recording in his order that he was concerned there was a risk of “continuing, significant, health and safety breaches at these premises”.

The hearing was scheduled for August 19. Early that morning, the Bhanas applied for Woodhouse to be recused, making general claims that he had breached obligations in previous hearings.

Woodhouse said there was no basis for him to recuse himself and he was certain he could consider the matter with an independent mind.

His decision said the Bhanas did not attend the hearing or offer any submissions.

Woodhouse found there was “no doubt” the landlords’ failure to comply with the tribunal’s work order was intentional.

They had “several years” to make the repairs, and their obligations were “crystal clear”.

Woodhouse referred to ministry evidence about a prior tenant of one of the flats, who had reported it was leaky and the cold, damp conditions – even in summer – made his children sick.

The tenant stayed despite the conditions because he wanted somewhere stable and to avoid emergency housing.

Woodhouse said he agreed with the ministry’s evidence that “the circumstances of the case make the matter egregious”.

He ordered the landlords to pay $3750 in damages per tenancy, totalling $11,250.

The $200 rent reduction would start from August 20 and apply to each flat until the work was proven finished. The decision did not say how much rent was being charged.

Woodhouse also made orders restraining the landlords from failing to maintain the premises and failing to comply with a work order for the next three years.

“The breaches are egregious, they have continued over a long period of time, and the matter is aggravated given the landlord has been obstructive with the (ministry) officers in ensuring that the work has been completed,” his decision said.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 30 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Fatal crash on Desert Rd near Waiouru; one person dead

One person has died following a crash on State Highway 1 near Waiōuru.

Police were called to the two-vehicle crash on the Desert Rd around 4.30pm yesterday.

One person was airlifted to Waikato Hospital in a critical condition but died early this morning, police said.

NZ Transport Agency (NZTA) said the crash happened between Waiōuru and Rangipō.

The road was closed while the Serious Crash Unit investigated and reopened just after 10pm yesterday.

Inquiries into the crash are ongoing.

I drew a line in the sand at Bondi Beach to stop writing about Gaza – I couldn’t stop crossing it

Sydney Morning Herald November 26, 2026

This is a book I was never going to write, and a book I was probably always going to write. I was never going to write Light Sleeper: Memoir of a Troubled Jew – about the unending tragedy of Israel and Palestine – because, when it came to the Middle East generally, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict specifically, I never felt I’d read enough, or knew enough, to do the subject justice. The more I knew, the more I knew I didn’t know, and what I didn’t know seemed vast and dense and well beyond my reach.

I was neither a Middle Eastern academic, nor a historian, nor a linguist specialising in the Middle East. I’d never served as a diplomat in the region, or as a policy or intelligence adviser to anyone trying to grapple with the realpolitik of what was possible, rather than what was just.

My résumé was slim by comparison. I’d been raised as a secular Jew, I’d had my bar mitzvah as a 13-year-old, I’d studied Middle Eastern politics as an undergraduate, and I’d visited Israel and the occupied West Bank, both as a tourist and as a journalist, many times over half a century.

In the late 1970s, I’d been mesmerised enough by an Egyptian president offering peace to the Israelis that, 10 years later, I’d gone to Jerusalem as a young correspondent, still under a Middle Eastern spell, hoping to understand my Jewishness better by basing myself in the “City of David”.

Once again, though, I never became what I would have called a Middle Eastern specialist, certainly not in the way I thought of many distinguished Israeli and Arab journalists, or, indeed, western journalists such as The Independent’s Robert Fisk, The Guardian’s David Hirst, The New York Times’ Thomas Friedman, The Sunday Times’ Marie Colvin, or our very own Pulitzer Prize-winning Geraldine Brooks.

I dearly wanted to be one of those journalists, but that was not the direction my life would take. When I went to Jerusalem in late 1986 as a fledgling correspondent for the South China Morning Post, part of me imagined living there for years, learning to speak Hebrew and Arabic fluently, travelling regularly with my notebook and laptop from Jerusalem to Cairo, Beirut to Damascus, Ramallah to Amman, befriending people on all sides of the political and religious divide, perhaps even falling in love with an Israeli or Palestinian woman, then raising a family in Jerusalem.

But just before leaving Sydney for Jerusalem, I fell in love with an Australian woman and, after our ill-fated trip to Gaza, we decided to get married and return to Sydney to build a life far from the faultlines of history.

On my return, I was initially at a loss to know what to write about, such was my obsession with the Middle East and all that it seemed to reveal about the human condition. Eventually, I found my way into profile-writing and – even though I could never have articulated this at the time – discovered that in writing about people’s internal tensions and struggles, I was sometimes witnessing the raw material for larger conflicts.

Betrayal. Bitterness. Humiliation. Fear. Wounded pride. A refusal to forgive. A desire for revenge. Memory … and the stories we told ourselves repeatedly. The universal was all there in the personal. What was a family feud if not a mighty struggle over different perceptions of fairness, belonging and memory? What was a bitter divorce if not a contest over competing narratives?

For years, I wrote about politicians, artists, poets, singers, lawyers, philosophers, actors, corporate leaders, dreamers and a good many rogues and scoundrels, too, and the more I did, the more difficult I found it to truly know someone.

People were never one thing, and if you listened to them explain their lives for long enough, you could see the way pain and damage had sometimes transmuted into a lifelong grievance, and how the certainty of that grievance had often led to a lifetime of blame. Multiply that by millions, then add history, religion, ideology and weaponry to the mix, and you had all the makings of a conflict of Middle Eastern proportions.

From profile-writing, I turned to subjects like immigration, asylum seekers, climate change, feminism, gendered violence, raising boys, health, travel, music, the media, even sport on a few occasions. All this by way of saying that I was never going to write a book on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict because it was too complicated and my attention had so often been elsewhere.

Also, I didn’t feel sufficiently well-versed in Jewish studies to think I could do justice to my own heritage. Did I understand Jewish traditions, culture and background well enough? Could I explain the political and religious movements that had informed Judaism? What did I know, say, of the “Days of Judges”, or how the 12 tribes of Israel had united? Or the secession movement of the 10th century BCE? Could I name any of the Zealots who had opposed Roman rule? Did I understand the Kabbalah movement of the 16th century? Had I read the psalms of David or Solomon? What about the wisdom of the Talmud?

And when was the last time I’d actually observed the Jewish sabbath, or said the kiddush for wine? Could I still read in Hebrew? Barely. When had I last entered a synagogue? Probably in 2016 when, together with my mother, sister and brother, we’d gone to the Temple Emanuel in Sydney to observe my father’s yahrzeit, the one-year anniversary of his death. (Later that evening – and every year since the day he died, October 13, 2015 – we’d light a memorial candle to honour his memory, and, in my case, toast him with his favourite double whisky on the rocks.)

And yet for all my gaps and deficiencies, there was this. From the age of 21, there’d been no subject that had absorbed my interest more than the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

In 1986, when I’d chanced my arm on becoming a freelance correspondent in Jerusalem, I’d done so, in part, to try to work out my Jewishness in the context of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. How could we, as a people, inflict such indignities on another people after everything we’d endured? How did Jewish people reconcile themselves to this? How did I?

Every time I’d been to Israel – and, indeed, when I’d lived there in the late 1980s – I could see how easily a Jewish person could lose sight of that question in the day-to-day thrill of this great in-gathering of fellow Jews from all over the world – Yemenites and Iraqis, Moroccans, Lithuanians and Poles, Germans, Russians, Ethiopians and Americans, orthodox and secular, Middle Eastern and European, pious and carnal, some holding prayer books, others assault rifles.

To visit Israel was to encounter one of the most dynamic, boisterous and unruly societies on Earth, one teeming with difference but bonded by connection, one beset by constant disputation but suffused with an electric life force that probably only occurred in a nation living on a knife edge.

There was much that I loved and admired about the place, particularly when I chose to forget how it had all come about, or, more particularly, what had been done – and was still being done – in the Jewish people’s name. That’s partly why, each time I went to Israel, I would travel into the West Bank – into towns like Hebron, Bethlehem, Ramallah, Nablus and Jericho – to meet Palestinians living under a brutal, ceaseless occupation, and to visit some of the refugee camps dispersed throughout the territory.

That’s also why my library gradually filled with books on the subject – biographies of Palestinian and Israeli leaders, volumes of history explaining Hitler, Zionism, the Jewish people, the Palestinian people, the Holocaust, the birth of Israel, the Nakba or Palestinian Catastrophe, Jewish literature, Palestinian literature, the failed peace processes, the so-called “War of Independence”, the Six-Day War, the Yom Kippur War, the Lebanon War, the changing face of the Middle East, the unchanging face of the Middle East, stories of courage and great suffering on both sides, the Old Testament, the New Testament, the Koran …

Most of these books were in my bedroom library, their spines glinting at me last thing at night, first thing in the morning, always beckoning me, it seemed, back into their dusty pages. Some I’d devoured two or three times, some I’d read once, or just glimpsed at. Some I’d skim-read, some were only half or quarter completed. But as former NSW premier and Australian foreign minister Bob Carr once wrote, “you own a book and absorb its contents by osmosis”, and by osmosis I’d absorbed all these books into my nervous system for a good part of my life.

Which is why, shortly after October 7, 2023, I decided to move all of them out of my bedroom and into my upstairs office. That way, I told myself, I would feel less haunted by what was unfolding in the Middle East, and less tempted to try to write about it.

Better to wake up to the Confessions of Saint Augustine and the teachings of Lao Tzu, the Dalai Lama and Thich Nhat Hanh. Better to know that in my dreamscape, there were all the poetry anthologies that I’d collected – and that had soothed me – over recent years and were possibly lulling me still in my nighttime reveries – most notably the Irish poets, including David Whyte, Seamus Heaney and John O’Donohue, but also my perennial heartthrob, American poet Mary Oliver.

I’m sure I began to sleep better with those books dispatched to another room, but, try as I might, I still couldn’t stay away from the daily news from Israel and Palestine, nor quieten the great disturbance that this war was igniting inside me.

I felt so tormented by the need to write about what was happening – and the need to not write about it – that one morning, I went down to Bondi Beach with my friend Jeremy Meltzer and, together, we drew a line in the sand to set an intention. On the south side of the line was the Middle East and all its ancient torments. “Don’t go there. Don’t write about it. Enough already.”

On the north side – stretching the entire length of the beach – were all the other things I could read and write and celebrate – music, poetry, philosophy, spirituality, nature. “Go there. Don’t cross to the south side, keep heading north. There lies eight million ways to happiness.”

Senior freelance writer

But I kept drifting south. I kept returning to the conflict that had obsessed me for half a century, and I felt was approaching some kind of shocking denouement. Was this the end of the Palestinian people? Was this the end of Jewish nationhood? Where did I stand on all this?

I knew in my bones that I was carrying some kind of untold story inside me and that it was becoming an unbearable weight not to try and tell.

The events of October 7 had made me feel more Jewish than I’d ever felt before, both for better and for worse. They’d made me think about the ongoing tragedy of the Jewish people, but, strangely enough, about all the Jewish authors who had informed my life – Philip Roth, Saul Bellow, Franz Kafka, Norman Mailer, Joseph Heller, Primo Levi, Viktor Frankl, Isaac Bashevis Singer, Amos Oz, David Grossman, Elie Wiesel ...

They’d also made me think of some of my favourite Jewish singer-songwriters – Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen and Paul Simon, in particular, but also Carole King, Billy Joel, Neil Diamond (a remote cousin, I think) – and the songs they had gifted the world.

And they’d made me think of the comedians – past and present – who had brought me undone, who had made me laugh from somewhere deep down in my kishkas – Mel Brooks, Groucho Marx, Lenny Bruce, Larry David, Jon Stewart, Sacha Baron Cohen, Billy Crystal …

I was proud of my Jewishness, but I was also appalled at what was being done in the Jewish people’s name – the deliberate starvation and denial of food, water and medicine, the elimination of entire bloodlines, the intentional targeting of children, the calculated mass murder – and I knew the essence of the Torah, the central Jewish holy book, as it was summed up by Hillel, the 1st-century BCE Jewish sage: “That which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. This is the whole Torah. The rest is commentary.”

And I think it was from that universal instruction that I began to write about what Israel was doing to the Palestinians in reprisal for October 7. And in the act of writing, I began to know better what it was that I was thinking, what it was that I was seeing and feeling and fearing. Like most writers, I didn’t know it properly until I committed the words to the page, and so these were the writings that became a series of columns in The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age – stories that would prove the most personally painful I’d ever undertaken.

In August 2025, Ann Mossop, the then artistic director of the Sydney Writers’ Festival, said to me, “Why don’t you write a book based on those columns? Use them as the spine of the book and create some connective tissue between them.”

We were at the opening night of the Byron Writers’ Festival – a festival which was to be washed out the next day – and I was standing next to my agent and friend Jane Novak, who replied sardonically: “That’s what I keep telling him.”

So, without saying a word – not to Jane, not to my partner, not to my family or friends – I began to write, slowly at first, then in a compulsive rush. Five thousand words, then 10,000, then 18,000, at which point I hesitated long and hard before sending them on to Jane.

“Great,” she said. “Keep going.”

And that’s when I thought, “Maybe if I don’t keep going, it will get worse. It will keep churning away inside me, and I’ll never get any rest.”

So that’s what I did. I kept going.

Steelers reportedly cut Rodgers after QB accuses coach McCarthy of sleeping during meetings

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 20:21:30 GMT

Quarterback was benched by team this week

Veteran due to retire at end of season

Aaron Rodgers launched an extraordinary attack on his head coach, Mike McCarthy, on Wednesday after the Pittsburgh Steelers benched him in favor of backup quarterback Mason Rudolph.

ESPN have reported that the Steelers have released Rodgers after his outburst. If no other team claim Rodgers on waivers, he will become an unrestricted free agent. Several teams, including the Indianapolis Colts and New England Patriots, are in need of a starting quarterback at the moment.

McCarthy, who was also Rodgers’ coach with the Green Bay Packers, had said on Monday that the 42-year-old was still the team’s starter despite recent struggles. On Tuesday night, the Steelers changed course and said Rodgers, one of the greatest players in NFL history, would be deactivated for Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos.

On Wednesday, Rodgers appeared on The Pat McAfee Show and set fire to whatever remained of his relationship with the coach. Rodgers first said he would not return to the Steelers, stating: “That ship has sailed”. He then accused McCarthy of falling asleep during meetings.

“Last Wednesday, we were in a quarterback meeting. Mike came in late, sat down, and within 10 minutes began snoring. Woke himself up, was rattling his papers,” Rodgers said. “We all looked around. Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again. And less than five minutes after that, he walks out of the room like nothing happened.”

Rodgers added that he only found out about McCarthy’s decision when his teammate Pat Freiermuth told him. Rodgers said Freiermuth had called him and said “I can’t believe they’re doing this.” To which Rodgers replied: “Doing what?”

Rodgers, who said this summer that he will retire at the end of the season, also alleged that McCarthy appeared to think he was still coaching the Packers during Sunday’s defeat to the Philadelphia Eagles. “The nail in the coffin for so many of us was at halftime, towards the end of it, we’re kind of on the offense on one side of defense on the other side,” said Rodgers. “And there’s some rambling or something [from McCarthy] and without even a heads up, he says, ‘All right, one, two, three Packers.’ That’s what he broke it down on in the locker room … [We] looked around going, ‘What the fuck? What is going on? Where’s his head at at this point?’” ESPN reported that multiple sources agreed with Rodgers’ version of events.

Rodgers said he had spoken regularly to McCarthy over the last few days, and the coach had not mentioned the possibility of being benched. He did, however, say they had discussed McCarthy sleeping during meetings. “[I told McCarthy], we can’t even have an honest conversation. I’m telling you, you snored in the meeting twice, in a quarterback meeting, that’s unacceptable,” Rodgers said. “And you’re telling me you’ve never slept at a facility before. And I’m telling you, I have a hundred witnesses and collaborating people who would support what I’m saying. I’m not saying that to fucking bury you.

“I’m saying that because this behavior and these habits are not healthy and they’re not becoming of someone intimately involved in the game plan. And that’s my whole point. And so, I left it with him that if you try and bench me or don’t change the play call, then you should just release me because I feel like at this point, I’m doing what’s right for the organization”. Rodgers said after his comments to McCarthy that the coach decided he was “getting rid of me”.

The Steelers (6-4) have lost their last two games but are still clinging on to the final playoff place in the AFC. NFL Next Gen Stats gives them a 62% chance of making the postseason, although the model does not take into account players flambéing their own team’s coach on live television.

Rodgers is considered one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time, someone whose single Super Bowl win does not match his natural talent. He is all but guaranteed to be a first-ballot Hall of Famer. His NFL records include highest passer rating for a quarterback with a minimum of 1,500 attempts (102.5), highest passer rating in a single season (122.5 in 2011) and lowest interception in a season (0.3% in 2018).

This season, however, has arguably been the worst of Rodgers’ career. His QBR of 45.6 ranks him 26th out of 30 qualified quarterbacks, ahead of only Deshaun Watson, Baker Mayfield, Justin Herbert and Daniel Jones. His completion rate of 60.9% is the second-lowest for any season of his career in which he has started more than one game and he leads the league in yards lost in sacks.

All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, police say

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 20:20:23 GMT

Unclear if ‘hostage-taker’ who was killed may have been a hostage as daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre ends

Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one man police described as a hostage-taker was killed.

Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.

When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8am on Tuesday local time, customers and employees were taken hostage – the president initially said there were 30 hostages, but after the final count, police put the number at about 70.

Many of them could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.

When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested.

One man was killed, whom De la Espriella and police described as one of the criminals who had allegedly resisted.

“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” said De la Espriella in a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year.

Local media identified the dead man as Haider Muñetón Zapata, 51, whose wife had spent the day searching for him as one of the hostages. She gave an interview to Blu Radio on Tuesday, saying they lived near the supermarket and that he had gone there to buy buñuelos, a type of fried dough ball, before picking her up to take her to work, but had stopped responding to her WhatsApp messages at 8.12am.

Zapata reportedly had no criminal record. Cartagena’s mayor, Dumek Turbay, told local media that when special forces stormed the supermarket, Zapata had allegedly resisted and attacked one of the officers, prompting police to shoot him dead.

In a video released shortly after the operation, De la Espriella described the police action as “extraordinary”, speaking with a gun tucked into his waistband, as he has done on several other public occasions as part of his populist tough-on-crime rhetoric.

The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.

More than 20 people were injured, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.

The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.

As the lengthy negotiations continued into the night, police used water cannon to disperse dozens of onlookers who had gathered outside the supermarket.

Cartagena’s mayor said that when police stormed the supermarket, some of the hostage-takers tried to blend in with the hostages by removing their hoods and changing out of their black clothes into civilian clothing.

According to Turbay, police then had to screen the hostages before eventually identifying the four who were arrested.

Supermarket employee Héctor Puello, who was taken hostage, told Caracol Radio that he had started his shift in the store’s bakery about two and a half hours before the gunmen arrived.

“First of all, I felt like I had come back to life because those armed men were mistreating us,” he said.

Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, said that when he realised what was happening, he hid inside a cold-storage room with four other employees. “After four hours, we couldn’t stand the cold any longer and came out,” he said, at which point they were captured and taken hostage.

Commenting on the rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.

The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.

In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.

Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.

On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.

“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

Judge orders transfer of Thomas Markle to face formal charges in California

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 20:06:57 GMT

Father of the Duchess of Sussex currently being held in Florida is charged with possession of child pornography

A judge in the US has ordered the transfer of Thomas Markle, the Duchess of Sussex’s father, to California to face formal charges of possessing child sex abuse images.

The move comes after a federal grand jury on the west coast paved the way for the prosecution of Markle Sr, who is currently being held in custody in Florida. He was charged with two counts of possession of child pornography.

The transportation of Markle Sr to the charging jurisdiction was ordered by the magistrate judge Lindsay Griffin in Florida on Wednesday, according to documents seen by the Press Association.

The 82-year-old is expected to appear before a Los Angeles judge in the coming weeks, where he will hear the charges against him and is likely to be asked to enter a plea.

The grand jury filing alleges that on or about 30 October and 4 November of this year, Markle Sr “knowingly possessed 35mm film negatives that contained child pornography”.

The negatives are alleged to include images that “involved a prepubescent minor and a minor who had not yet attained the age of 12 years old”. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in prison on each count.

Markle Sr was detained by FBI agents on 6 November after they seized a cache of material from two Los Angeles storage units that he rented for nearly two decades.

He came under investigation after he was reported to police in the Philippines and the FBI last month by his son, Thomas Markle Jr, who allegedly found illegal images in his father’s belongings in Cebu City.

Markle Jr told the Sun newspaper he had tipped off the authorities about the LA storage facilities.

The US attorney’s office for the central district of California stated: “Every defendant is presumed to be innocent until and unless proven guilty in court.”

After initially being released on conditional bail following his arrest in Florida, Markle Sr was detained just days later after removing his electronic monitoring tag.

During his interview for this, Markle Sr claimed not to understand the allegations against him and that he did not have “any child porn” and “no pictures of naked kids”.

Meghan, who moved back to the UK with the Duke of Sussex in August, has said previously she was “deeply distressed” at the accusations against her father, from whom she is estranged.

She revealed she was sent a letter via the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection in 2019 which made “troubling and disturbing allegations” about her father, but she was given assurances these were being investigated.

The Met has admitted it never shared the details with other law enforcement agencies, with the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct, now investigating the force’s conduct.

Which gaming headsets are worth the cost? I put 20 to the test – here are the best for 2026

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 20:00:35 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Wired, wireless, noise cancelling and budget … here are the headphones to level up your PC and console gaming

The best gaming chairs

We talk a lot about graphics in video games; we know how important it is to play on a decent screen so we can see what we’re shooting at … or running away from. But what about sound? Explosions, dialogue, the wheezy breathing of a nearby monster – arguably, audio quality is just as important.

Many modern games now support 3D or spatial audio, which lets you detect exactly where a sound is coming from in the game world. In survival horror adventures, you can hear the zombie lurking in the next room, and in popular shooters such as Fortnite and Apex Legends, you can pinpoint the footsteps of approaching enemies.

Sadly, most of us can’t afford elaborate surround sound speaker systems for our living rooms, but that’s where gaming headsets come in. They not only let you play without disturbing anyone else in the house (or office), but are also brilliant for spatial audio. I’ve tested an array of models to suit most budgets and needs, and, hopefully, with my help, you’ll never be surprised by a zombie again.

Best gaming headset overallSteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni

Best budget gaming headsetTurtle Beach Atlas 200

Best for multiplayer gamesRazer BlackShark V3 Pro

Best for comfortCorsair Void V2 Max Wireless

Best gaming headset for audiophilesAudeze Maxwell 2 ANC

I have been playing video games for 45 years and writing about them for my entire career as a journalist, so I really understand what makes a good piece of gaming hardware. During that time, I have reviewed hundreds of joypads, monitors, keyboards and, yes, headsets, developing a range of tests to sort the quality gear from the overpriced gimmicks.

I tested 20 headsets, paying close attention to comfort, which is vital for long gaming sessions, as well as sound quality, noise-cancelling capabilities and any other special features. As someone who plays video games every day for a living (it’s a tough job, etc), I was able to put every headset through hours of testing with a variety of games. I wore them while blasting strangers in Call of Duty, scoring volleys in EA Sports FC and building scale reproductions of Norman castles in Minecraft.

I also made sure I was getting good spatial information to detect exactly where my next opponent/victim was coming from. And naturally, the microphone has to make your voice crystal clear when talking to (or yelling at) teammates in the heat of battle.

To gauge the overall build quality, I put them through the ultimate trial: lending them to my teenage sons. If anything came back in one piece, I knew it was well constructed. My aim was to find headsets that felt light yet sturdy, sounded good, and aided – maybe even improved (if that’s possible) – my gaming performance.

Once tested, the headsets were donated to SpecialEffect, a charity that makes video games accessible to people with disabilities.

Danish manufacturer SteelSeries makes a range of highly acclaimed headsets, and this is the centrepiece of its collection, featuring 40mm drivers, active noise cancellation (ANC) and a high-bandwidth omnidirectional microphone for clear, natural speech. Instead of a basic USB dongle for connecting to a PC or console, it comes with a base station that plugs into your games machine and lets you tweak your sound settings via a monochrome screen.

Why we love it As soon as you load up a game, you know what you’re paying for. The Nova Pro Omni produces a lovely wide soundstage, making you feel immersed in the environment. While playing Elden Ring, I really felt the rumble of dragons flying overhead and the whoosh of arrows whizzing past my ears. The ANC is effective, easily filtering out the electric fan in my games room. The mic made my shouts of “There’s a sniper on that rooftop!” easily discernible to my Call of Duty teammates, but also picked up regular chatter with decent clarity. It’s comfortable, too, with plump earcups finished in a soft vegan leather, and the adjustable suspension band nicely cushions your head. It also uses neodymium, a compact, lightweight and highly magnetic material, in its drivers, reducing the headset weight while also producing precise, detailed sound.

It’s the base station that sets the SteelSeries apart. There are three USB ports at the back, so you can plug in a PC, PlayStation and Xbox simultaneously and easily switch between them (you can also connect your phone via Bluetooth if you want to watch TikTok videos while you’re waiting for a game to load). There’s even a charging port in the side for the removable battery that powers the headset. Better still, two rechargeable batteries are included in the box, so you’ll never run out of juice in the middle of an all-day Minecraft session.

For tinkerers, free smartphone and PC apps let you intricately modify the sound settings or choose from hundreds of preset options designed for specific games.

It’s a shame that … the earcups did get sweaty after several hours of Warzone, and it’s expensive. But if you have a PC and/or multiple consoles and want decent movie and music performance all from one headset, it’s definitely worth it.

Compatibility: PC, Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo Switch, mobile Weight: 339g (with mic arm attached Battery life: up to 30 hours per battery Drivers: custom 40 mm neodymium magnetic ANC: yes Sustainability: SteelSeries says all its products have parts that can be recycled and repurposed, and it sells replacement parts such as new earcups and headbands

Turtle Beach is among the best-known brands in the gaming headset world, and it’s a master of affordable-yet-hardy models. The Atlas 200 comes in three variations: multiplatform (PC, mobile and Xbox), PlayStation and a dedicated PC version that comes with a USB adaptor providing 24-bit resolution high-fidelity sound and support for the Waves 3D audio processing technology. It’s a no-nonsense wired headset with bass-loving 50mm drivers and a flip-to-mute mic, which means you just lift it up into its upright position to turn it off.

Why we love it At 280g, this is a light headset and comfortable to wear. The headband puts barely any pressure on your skull, and the earcups have good cushioning, yet dissipate heat well. I wore it for hours without it feeling sweaty or heavy. The sound is a little crunchy and unrefined, but it does the job, and it handles spatial audio reasonably well, although I found it difficult to tell if ambient sounds were above, below or on the same level as me. The mic is clear. While the Atlas 200 can’t compete with top-end models, it’s incredible value, outperforming other budget models. And it lasts surprisingly well: my sons have owned Atlas headsets for years, and somehow they’re still functioning. It’s a great option for casual gamers who just want a reliable headset they can throw on and forget about.

It’s a shame that … the mesh fabric that covers the headband feels fragile, but for the price, we’re not complaining.

Compatibility: PC, PlayStation, Xbox and mobile Weight: 280g Drivers: 50mm Nanoclear ANC: no Sustainability: Turtle Beach has reduced plastics in its packaging and claims on its website to be using post-consumer recycled plastic in some of its products. It sells spare parts for its current headsets

I’m a big fan of Razer, and my trusted neon green Kraken headset is still going after five years of heavy use. The BlackShark V3 Pro is the company’s high-end model, aimed at esports athletes (and wannabes), featuring ANC, a large detachable boom mic and 50mm drivers. It’s built for long sessions – lightweight but very comfortable with soft, breathable fabric covering the cups. If you are getting continually blasted by 12-year-olds in Fortnite, it’s not because your ears are too sweaty.

Why we love it The sound is punchy and precise, allowing you to catch every distinct rumble, roar or intriguing snippet of dialogue, no matter where it’s happening. Want to hear a pin drop in your game world? You’ve come to the right place. The default setting is tuned toward higher frequencies (perfect for footsteps), but a button lets you select from a range of pre-set EQ (equalisation) levels designed for specific games or for movie watching.

If you pair the headset with Razer’s apps (Razer Audio and Razer Synapse), you can customise all the EQ settings yourself. The mic is crisp, reliable and actively suppresses background noise, and there’s a handy scroll wheel to fine tune the mix of game sound and chat volume. The buttons are tactile and easy to use while playing. You can also connect to your phone via Bluetooth to take calls and view social media. The BlackShark V3 Pro feels like a high-end piece of sports equipment – like an expensive tennis racket or a pair of fancy football boots – in the same way, they will make you aspire to be a better player.

It’s a shame that … I could never get the sound just right for listening to music, but that’s a small issue. The dongle is on a weirdly long lead, too.

Compatibility: separate models for PC, PS5 and Xbox Weight: 367g Battery life: up to 70 hours Drivers: 50mm ANC: yes Sustainability: headset contains 24.67% post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic

Sitting comfortably in the mid-range of prices, Corsair’s Void V2 Max Wireless is a lightweight model styled with teen gamers in mind. It features 50mm drivers and support for Dolby Atmos spatial audio, and the boom mic can be flipped up or down to switch it on and off. There are four ready-made EQ settings such as Bass Boost and FPS (first-person shooter) Competition, which accentuates the sound of footsteps and gunfire, accessible by pressing down on the volume button. You can also use Corsair’s iCue app to customise the EQ and mic settings, as well as tweak the colour patterns of the snazzy RGB lighting on the earcups.

Why we love it For a start, it’s comfortable. The earcups are made of a particularly soft, squidgy memory foam, and they’re roomy, which helps to keep you cool through long periods of play. On top of this, the Void Max produces a surprisingly complex, textured audio experience with hefty bass that doesn’t impede higher-frequency sound effects.

The boom mic is nice and clear, too, although it’s a shame you can’t remove it. Plus, there’s Bluetooth support so you can connect to your phone and listen to Spotify – or take calls – while piloting a F-15 Strike Eagle in Ace Combat 8. My 18-year-old son grabbed this headset as soon as it arrived and absconded with it, so he’s definitely a fan.

It’s a shame that … it’s plasticky, so don’t sit on it. Also, the flashing RGB strips are not for everyone.

Compatibility: PC, PS5, Nintendo Switch, mobile. Separate model for Xbox Weight: 303g Battery life: up to 70 hours Drivers: 50mm ANC: no Sustainability: a Corsair spokesperson said: “Corsair does not take products back for recycling. Corsair offers a two-year warranty for all our gaming peripherals. If the headset is not operating in accordance with its published technical specifications, it will be replaced at Corsair’s expense. We offer replacement parts such as earpads, USB dongles and charging cables; these are complimentary, and you just need to pay for shipping unless it is under warranty.”

Designed for gaming audiophiles, the Maxwell 2 uses 90mm planar drivers rather than the more common dynamic drivers. While the latter use a vibrating cone to produce sound, planar drivers use a thin diaphragm, which produces a more precise, authentic sound with less possibility of distortion. To accommodate them, the earcups are rather large – my son said they look like dumbbells, but thankfully they’re not quite as heavy. It comes with an app if you want to tinker with the sound levels, and you can connect to your phone via Bluetooth to listen to music.

Why we love it If you take pride in your high-end PC and widescreen 4k monitor, you want a headset to match – and this is it. The Maxwell 2 has absolutely gorgeous sound, achieving eardrum-bludgeoning bass, but also lots of mid- to high-frequency detail and a wide acoustic space for a truly cinematic feel.

Playing sci-fi shooter ARC Raiders, I could hear the wind whistling above me, the thudding footsteps of giant killer robots and the distant pings of far-off gun fights – all with impressive spatial precision. It also supports head tracking (with the relevant software and compatible games), for even more accuracy. The noise cancellation is very good, easily blocking out my noisy PC and the TV blaring in the next room, and the mic is so clear, I sounded like I was recording a podcast. A serious and sublime headset.

It’s a shame that … it is heavy, although the wide suspension band helps take the pressure off. When connected to a gaming device via the wireless dongle and a mobile phone via Bluetooth, the headset automatically prioritises audio sources. Users can’t manually switch between the two wireless audio sources or listen to both simultaneously.

Compatibility: available in separate Xbox/PC and PlayStation/PC versions. Both versions also support Mac, Nintendo Switch, Switch 2 and mobile devices. If not, it will ask the customer to send in the headphones to be repaired. Repairs are free under warranty, but customers may need to cover postage costs for any needed beyond 30 days of purchase

Best for: wired

For those who just want a straightforward headset that gets the important stuff right, the MMX 300 Pro is the perfect option. It’s a wired model with impressive sound, deep bass and accurate spatial detail, and the mic is crystal clear. As you’d expect from a company specialising in studio headphones, it’s wonderful for music too.

The soft, velvety earcups are comfortable, so you can wear the headset for hours, and I like the accessible in-line controls for the mic and volume, so you don’t have to fiddle with the headset mid-game. I tested the closed-back MMX 300 Pro, but if you’d prefer an open back, consider the MMX 330 Pro. Beyerdynamic also has cheaper models – including the wireless MMX 130 and MMX 230 – that are extremely good too.

It didn’t make the final cut because … there are slightly more feature-rich options at the price.

Compatibility: PC, PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch and smartphone; Weight: 314g; Battery life: not applicable, wired only; Drivers: 45mm Stellar 45 dynamic; ANC: no; sustainability: the earpads, headband and cable can all be easily replaced, but the company provides no specific recycling guidance

Best for: wireless on a budget

At 212g, this is one of the lightest headsets I tested, but it’s resilient and comfortable thanks to the flexible plastic frame and soft memory-foam earcups. It offers both 2.4 GHz wireless connectivity and Bluetooth, so you can use it with your PC, any console and a smartphone, and the sound quality is decent with strong detail and an acceptable oomph to the bass. The volume controls are on switches rather than a dial, which isn’t ideal, but I found the buttons big and tactile, so they’re easy to find by touch. All in all, a great-value wireless headset.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the mic is embedded in the ear cup, so it’s not quite as clear as headsets with a boom mic attached.

Spare parts and guides are available via the Logitech Repair Hub

Best for: an immersive experience

The flagship model in the Turtle Beach range has rich cinematic sound (certified Hi-Res by the Japan Audio Society), while picking out those all-important footsteps and other environmental signals via excellent implementation of Dolby Atmos spatial audio. I tested with the epic adventure Ghost of Yōtei and loved how it captured the swirling winds, crackling fires and clashing blades – it was like being inside a Kurosawa movie.

Owners of multiple gaming systems can easily switch between four devices, including PC, PS5, Xbox and smartphone, and the supplied base station charges one of the two supplied batteries so you never run out of power. Add in the powerful ANC, extremely good detachable mic and comfortable, sturdy build, and you have a truly top-end headset.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Omni is marginally better, but it’s close.

Compatibility: PC, PlayStation, Xbox (Xbox-specific model) and smartphones via Bluetooth; separate models for Xbox and PS5/PC; Weight: 393g; Battery life: up to 40 hours per battery; Drivers: 60mm Eclipse Dual; ANC: yes; Sustainability: see Turtle Beach Atlas 200

Best for: style

In a market filled with identical black headsets, the Nova 3 offers a selection of lovely soft colours such as lavender and aqua. It’s a comfortable option too, with an adjustable suspension strip beneath the headband and gentle fabric earcups.

Even the audio is mellow, providing a nicely balanced sound stage that allows you to pick out important noises without being blasted by a wall of bass. As well as the usual 2.4GHz low-latency wireless connectivity via an included USB-C dongle, it also offers Bluetooth connectivity for your smartphone, and you can easily switch between them, just in case you fancy some TikTok action between Fortnite scuffles. There’s also an app to access custom EQ settings for different games.

It didn’t make the final cut because … there’s strong competition in this price range, and it’s so delicate my sons were worried they’d break it.

Compatibility: PS5, PC, Nintendo Switch, Xbox and mobile devices; Weight: 253g; Battery life: up to 30 hours; Drivers: 40mm neodymium magnetic; ANC: no; Sustainability: see info on Arctis Nova Pro Omni

The first decision you’re likely to make is between a wired and a wireless headset. The former tends to be a little cheaper; they’re also convenient and don’t require batteries. Wireless headsets free you from the tyranny of cables and often offer a range of connectivity options, including the standard 2.4GHz radio frequency, which will require a dongle receiver to be plugged into your PC or console, and Bluetooth for your smartphone. They do introduce a tiny amount of latency (the delay between your game generating a sound and you hearing it), but it is extremely low (about 10 milliseconds) in modern headsets.

Another key decision is whether to buy open-back or closed-back headphones. The former have grills or holes in the back of the ear cups to allow sound to move through and create a more natural audio experience. Closed-back headphones tend to create a seal around your ears so sound can’t escape: they’re better for booming bass and privacy, but can create distorted extraneous sounds – and make your ears hot. Most gaming headsets are closed-back, and this would be my recommendation for most gamers, as they put you right inside the virtual environment with no distractions. Many also offer active noise cancellation (ANC), a technology that emits sound waves to counteract and reduce incoming noise – great if you’re playing in a loud environment.

Audio quality is dictated by the drivers, which sit in each earcup, turning electric signals into sound waves. They come in different sizes, ranging from 40mm to 90mm, with the latter being the loudest, but not necessarily the best. Smaller drivers cope better with high frequencies, so they’re good for hearing footsteps; larger drivers provide heavier bass, so they’re great for games with pounding soundtracks or lots of cool explosions. Another important specification is frequency response, which is the range of audio frequencies a headset can reproduce: gaming headsets are usually in the 20–20,000 Hz range.

Spatial sound is important because it immerses you in the game world and helps you locate nearby enemies or loot chests – the good news is that many headsets support it, because the processing is done by the PC or console via software such as Dolby Atmos or Windows Sonic. However, accuracy is affected by the driver quality and the acoustic tuning in the headset. Some headsets come with apps that let you fine tune the range of the frequencies within the audio signal – ie the EQ (equalisation) settings – so that you can boost the bass, mid-range or treble.

Decent headsets that offer acceptable comfort, build quality and audio start at about £40 for a wired model and £60 for wireless. At about £100-£150, you’re getting a headset made with better materials and higher-quality drivers, as well as other features such as Bluetooth connectivity for your phone. At the top end, £250 upwards, you can expect highly configurable, studio-quality audio, supreme comfort and often the ability to connect to multiple consoles, switching seamlessly between them.

The problem with headsets is that they have a lot of delicate parts. They’re quite an intimate piece of equipment. Earcups will trap grease, sweat and skin particles from previous users, so unless these can be replaced, it’s unhygienic, to say the least. Also, you won’t know whether they’ve been looked after well simply from looking at a photo online. If you’re determined to buy secondhand on a site such as eBay, make sure the seller has excellent feedback and offers returns so you can inspect the headset when it arrives. Otherwise, look at stores and marketplaces such as Back Market or CEX that offer warranties on used goods.

Alternatively, Corsair sells refurbished headsets on its website. Honestly though, if money is an issue, I’d rather buy the best new budget or mid-range headset I can afford rather than a secondhand model with no warranty and an unknown hygiene history.

Keith Stuart is a veteran video game journalist with 30 years’ experience of testing, rating and breaking hi-tech gadgets. He has been wearing gaming headsets almost every day throughout his career, much to the frustration of anyone else in the house who needs to speak to him

Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 19:57:49 GMT

Chip Wilson said men importing brides from Thailand was due to women waiting too long to have children

The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.

Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.

Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.

There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.

According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.

“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.

“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”

The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.

The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.

On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.

Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn, has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.

He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.

Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.

“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”

Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.

More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.

“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”

Greg Fisilau to make England debut start in blockbuster All Blacks rematch

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 19:31:08 GMT

Borthwick makes five changes for New Zealand game

Head coach says he likes Pollock’s impact off the bench

Steve Borthwick has admitted he considers Henry Pollock most dangerous in his role of supersub after again leaving him on the bench against New Zealand and instead handing Greg Fisilau a surprise first start.

The 23-year-old Fisilau came into the autumn uncapped but has impressed off the bench in all three of England’s victories and is rewarded with his first start as Borthwick’s side bid for a third straight win over New Zealand for the first time.

Borthwick revealed Fisilau has been selected due to his physicality at the breakdown, having highlighted the All Blacks’ ability to slow England’s ball down last weekend, with Ben Curry dropping to the bench as one of five changes made by the head coach. Elsewhere, Tommy Freeman comes back on to the wing, Freddie Steward replaces George Furbank at full-back while Ellis Genge and Luke Cowan-Dickie get the nod in the front row.

Pollock, meanwhile, remains on the bench. He will win his 17th cap but has made just two starts for England to date – the disastrous Six Nations defeat by Ireland and the emphatic win over Japan earlier this month. Against Japan, Pollock impressed defensively but all eight of his England tries have come as a replacement, including two when deployed on the wing against Australia this November.

Citing the examples of Marcus Smith, who has emerged as Borthwick’s favourite for the No 23 jersey as part of a 6-2 bench, and George Martin, Borthwick revealed he favours unleashing Pollock in the latter stages of matches when explaining why Fisilau had seemingly leapfrogged the Northampton player in the pecking order.

“I enjoy what Henry has done off the bench,” said Borthwick. “Another one, George Martin, a number of us could say, ‘George Martin has had so much impact, he could start’. It’s not just Henry, there’s a number of people. Marcus – every time Marcus comes on, how well does he play? Every time. These guys are doing such a good job at the end of games. They do such a good job in that latter third of the game.

“There is always the question of balance. The balance of how many changes, the balance of what changes. I talked about the breakdown, which is significant, and suits Greg’s skill set. I also like Henry coming on and playing against tired defenders with a bit more space.”

England team: F Steward (Leicester Tigers); T Freeman (Northampton Saints), H Slade (Exeter Chiefs), S Atkinson (Gloucester Rugby), W Joseph (Gloucester Rugby); F Smith (Northampton Saints), J van Poortvliet (Leicester Tigers); E Genge (Bristol Bears), L Cowan-Dickie (Sale Sharks), J Heyes (Leicester Tigers), M Itoje (Saracens, capt), A Coles (Northampton Saints), O Chessum (Leicester Tigers), G Fisilau (Exeter Chiefs), B Earl (Saracens).

Replacements: J George (Saracens), F Baxter (Harlequins), W Stuart (Bath Rugby), G Martin (Saracens), B Curry (Sale Sharks), H Pollock (Northampton Saints), A McParland (Northampton Saints), M Smith (Harlequins)

The Exeter back-row Fisilau, whose father, Keni, played for Tonga, was first called into England camp in late 2024 but has had to bide his time for a first cap until this autumn. Handed the No 7 jersey, however, he now has the chance to further advance his claims for a place in Borthwick’s World Cup squad next year.

“Greg has been with the squad for a number of campaigns and didn’t get an opportunity in Test match 23,” added Borthwick. “And I think he’s then seized his chance. It’s interesting how opportunities come around, where a couple of knocks and bangs to a couple of players, and he’s into the matchday 23.

“Tom Curry in that week one, when his hip tied up, opportunity arises and he [Fisilau] has grabbed his chance and taken it with both hands. I’m delighted for him, delighted for his family. I think I said to you before that his dad always said, until he plays for England, his dad’s the best rugby player in the family.

“Well, Greg’s now the best rugby player in the family, and I think he’s very proud of it. I’m delighted for him. I’ve got an email from [Exeter’s director of rugby] Rob Baxter just now, who’s said the same thing. I’m just absolutely delighted for what Greg’s done.”

Borthwick’s decision to omit Furbank from the matchday 23 is a surprise, given how impressive he has been against Australia – on his first England appearance for two years – and in the record victory against the All Blacks last weekend. Steward shone when starting against Japan, however.

“George Furbank has played very well and I thought he was very good last weekend,” said Borthwick. “And at the same point in time, as I said, I want to develop a squad as well as a team.

“Freddie Steward’s been playing really well. And I thought against Japan, I thought he played to a really high standard, did exactly what the team needed of him. And he keeps adding dimensions to his game. And so I was delighted to name him in the starting team.”
