UK food inflation could hit 5% next year, Bank of England says

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 19:25:57 GMT

Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño

Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war.

The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.”

But she said the Bank expected food price inflation to rise sharply from the current level of about 1.3%. “We think that … it will go up to 3 to 5% in the middle of next year. I mean, obviously that’s quite uncertain, but that pressure is there,” Lombardelli said.

Lombardelli was being questioned by MPs alongside other members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC).

The MPC raised interest rates by a quarter-point to 4% at its last meeting earlier this month to tackle above-target inflation, and suggested further action could be necessary.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the MPC was also monitoring the potential impact of this year’s unusually large El Niño weather event on future food prices.

“There is uncertainty around this. You know, we still don’t know what the impact of this El Niño effect is going to be, for instance, because it will take time for it to manifest,” he said.

Surging oil and gas prices have pushed up the annual rate of inflation, which hit 3.6% last month, with the cost of petrol and diesel up by more than 33% over the past year.

But so far there have been fewer knock-on effects beyond energy prices. Food inflation has fallen well short of the peak above 17% seen in 2023, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exacerbated the supply squeeze as the global economy emerged from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Catherine Mann, an external member of the MPC who voted for a half-point increase this month, pointed to fierce competition in the food retail sector as a reason price rises had been constrained.

“We all go shopping ourselves. I can say that Aldi price match in my stores is apparent. Now, it wasn’t apparent four years ago. So that’s, I think, important,” she said.

Oil prices have fallen sharply since the Democratic party’s sweep in the US midterms brought hopes of an end to the Iran conflict, and as alternative sources of supply start to come onstream.

Bailey said if these lower prices continued, they would moderate the Bank’s predictions for UK inflation – which it had expected to peak at almost 5% next year.

“The prices are volatile … if these current prices were to stay what they are, the peak of inflation mechanically would be lower,” he said. However, Bailey and other MPC members underlined that some inflationary pressure for next year is already baked in – pointing to the 26% rise in the price cap for household energy bills due in January as an example.

The two-hour hearing underlined the divisions within the committee. The more dovish Swati Dhingra suggesting she saw this month’s rate rise as a one-off “insurance” measure, while Mann said she feared the MPC had undermined public confidence by failing to move more aggressively.

Dhingra compared the muted impact of rocketing oil and gas prices this year on the wider economy with the effects of the surge in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine.

At a similar point in that year, the prices of 70% of goods included in the consumer price index had risen, she said – but just 20% of prices have reacted so far this year.

But Mann pointed out that inflation had now been consistently above the Bank’s 2% target for five years.

“If we let inflation expectations drift away from 2% in the longer term, then monetary policy is going to have to work harder, meaning a higher rate for longer,” she said, adding: “The optimal response is to hike more and sooner.” The MPC’s next rate-setting meeting is on 17 December.

Ministers can’t control gas prices, but they can be more ruthless on other energy costs

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 19:21:16 GMT

Louise Haigh talked the right talk at the CBI this week, but greater ambition and tighter timelines are needed

Shocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the regulator, Ofgem, will set the price cap at £2,000-plus in every quarter of 2027.

Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. Gas prices, the overwhelming culprit in the £443 hike in the cap announced on Wednesday, can always fall – and might do so if calm returns to the strait of Hormuz.

But EDF’s outlook for next year currently reads: £2,254 for the second quarter, which will include about £100 extra in the “network costs” line in bills that includes paying for the upgrade of the electricity grid – demonstrating that gas prices are not the only story on a medium and long-term horizon. Then £2,078 in the quarter starting in July and £2,035 from October.

To repeat, projections can change, albeit an increasing slice of the electricity side comprises fixed costs, such as those network charges, that are nailed down in advance. The point, though, is that no one – certainly not government ministers – can claim to be surprised if this crisis lasts a while.

There are two points to make. First, the government no longer has an excuse to dodge the vexed question of a “social tariff” for energy – a scheme to give financial support to struggling households on a properly targeted basis.

The aim would be to get off today’s rickety practice of the chancellor giving 11th-hour handouts without a meaningful effort to ensure the money goes where it is most needed. This time it was £100 for council tax payers in lower bands – an inadequate proxy for poorer households or energy hardship.

The misnamed energy independence bill would give the government powers to do the necessary data-sharing work to design a proper social tariff. It’s time to hurry up with a job that has been talked about since the energy crisis of 2022 that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Next winter should serve as a hard deadline to get a workable social tariff in place.

The second point is this. Even as the government under Andy Burnham has emphasised cheaper energy as a new priority, its specific target is not terribly ambitious. It is to lower UK energy costs to bring them in line with other European countries within 10 years.

The goal is more credible than Keir Starmer’s empty (or cynical) promise of “£300 off bills” in the life of this parliament. But a decade to get in line with European averages? That is not speedy. Energy costs are, by a distance, the most pressing concern for UK industry. Yes, there are discounts for a limited number of heavy users, but how is wider “re-industrialisation” meant to happen if the UK remains uncompetitive on energy for another nine years?

A more encouraging way to look at things is that the government’s emerging new thinking on energy is bolder than a 10-year timeframe would suggest. The speech at the CBI this week by Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, offered three clear lines of attack: take more costs off bills and into general taxation; accelerate electrification and grid connections and get “wasted wind” costs under control; and go after the excess profits earned not only by gas plants at moments of high system stress but also by clean power generators with revenue arrangements tied to gas prices.

All are worthwhile strategies, but in combination they ought to be capable of delivering something better than European norms sometime around 2036. If not, the Treasury’s new “cost control framework” on energy levies will have to be sweated harder.

Being charitable, one might say the loose “within 10 years” phraseology was used because every government goal at the moment is framed within Burnham’s yet-to-be-unveiled 10-year plan. One hopes so, because the war on energy costs is more urgent for businesses and households alike.

There is nothing the government can do about wholesale gas prices, of course. But the necessary transition to clean power can be pursued with far more ruthlessness on costs. The 10-year plan, when it finally arrives, should also set a few five-year targets.

Critics of the trend says influencers are in danger of being used by the political machinery of government.

Poundland collapses, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:50:54 GMT

Do you work for Poundland? Tell us how you’re affected

Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk in “devastating news” for staff in the run-up to Christmas.

Administrators at AlixPartners have been appointed to the retailer, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, by Poundland’s directors. The chain is now expected to be broken up, with significant job losses and store closures after its owners rejected at least two last-ditch bids for the budget retailer.

AlixPartners said a sales process “did not identify a viable solvent solution for the business as a whole”. It said Poundland employed more than 10,000 people, which the Guardian understands is about 2,000 fewer than were in the business just a month ago.

It has been suggested that as many as 30,000 jobs in total could be at risk in Poundland’s stores, supply chain and at other affected businesses on high streets around the country.

Poundland would continue to trade with all stores and distribution centres remaining open while administrators pursued “all options including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part, from administration”, AlixPartners said.

Bally Auluk, a national officer for shopworkers’ union Usdaw, said: “This is devastating news for our members, who were only recently praised by management for helping to turn the business around.

“There is never a good time for this to happen, but just before Christmas has to be the worst. This decision has been made by the owners, Gordon Brothers, despite failing to engage with Usdaw, which is a disgraceful way to treat our members.”

The US finance firm, which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from the European retail group Pepco last year, has been under pressure to accept an offer that would save jobs and protect thousands of the retailer’s suppliers.

Gordon Brothers said on Wednesday afternoon it had “explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company” but that Poundland was “still vulnerable to inflationary pressures or any downturn in sales and margin”.

It said: “Poundland has faced several years of instability. In July 2025, Gordon Brothers supported the company’s restructuring plan – stepping in when no one else was willing to finance the business.”

In notes seen by the Guardian, Poundland’s directors wrote to staff and suppliers on Wednesday expressing “sincere sadness and intense regret” that they had been forced to call in administrators after Gordon Brothers said it would not provide more funds to keep the business operating as there was “no prospect of an acceptable solvent offer”.

Poundland’s managing director, Barry Williams, told suppliers: “We know this outcome will be as disappointing to you as it is to us.” About 2,000 suppliers will lose significant business and millions of pounds in payments for stock already supplied.

High inflation and heavy competition from budget stores, online specialists and supermarkets have left the 36-year-old retail chain – the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer – struggling.

Poundland’s board filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators last month – which was later extended – protecting the retailer from the demands of creditors until 26 November while a solution to its problems was sought.

Just two bidders interested in the whole company remained in talks right up until this week’s deadline.

Martin Property Group, a Northern Ireland family-owned company, which has been working with the existing management for about two months, remained interested.

It was joined by a last-ditch bid from Germany’s Zachert Private Equity, a fund founded by a former Bloomberg journalist that specialises in acquiring mid-sized companies.

Other bidders for the whole group included the little-known finance group Xyra Group Holdings, and the Irish investment company Innovest, which both fell out of the bidding race over the past week.

AlixPartners said: “We would encourage anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole, as well as UK retail operators with open employment opportunities, to contact the administrators.”

Poundland’s board was forced to appoint administrators before Thursday’s deadline as shelves began to empty because the company was running short of funds to restock during its peak Christmas trading period.

Gordon Brothers’ UK director, Mark Newton-Jones, held the latest of several meetings with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, on Monday, more than a week after giving evidence to the business select committee. MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said: “Poundland is a part of the fabric of high streets across the country and the news it has gone into administration just weeks before Christmas will be deeply concerning for workers and their families. We will make every effort to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps as many shops open as possible.”

MPs have accused the Poundland owner of extracting millions of pounds from the retailer when it was on a “knife-edge”.

Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland.

Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the business select committee, said he had recalled Newton-Jones to give public evidence. He said the committee was seeking assurances that Gordon Brothers or any related party would not act in any “insolvency capacity in relation to Poundland”.

Poundland, which was founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, has endured a rocky history under a string of different owners as it has faced rising costs and heavy competition from chains such as Savers, Home Bargains and B&M, as well as from the big supermarkets. Poundland co-founder Steve Smith said he was “gutted” about the chain’s administration.

It is now expected to be broken up with retailers such as Poundstretcher, B&M and The Range taking parcels of stores but leaving potentially hundreds empty.

Gordon Brothers rejected an initial management-backed rescue bid financed by Martin Property Group for the discount chain.

The US-based finance company said it could raise more from a breakup of Poundland – selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers – than through the solvent bids. Those bids promised only a small upfront payment for the £30m in shareholder debts that Gordon Brothers took on with its fellow shareholder – Poundland’s former owner Pepco – at the time of buying the chain.

Nasa knocked an asteroid off course. New closeup photos shed light on aftermath

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:48:33 GMT

Images of Dimorphos four years on from crash could help scientists design potential planetary defence system

Humanity may not yet have a means of fending off a Vogon constructor fleet – the destroyers of Earth in The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy – but its prospects of surviving an encounter with a rogue asteroid are looking considerably brighter.

Four years after Nasa deliberately slammed a spacecraft into a roughly 160-metre-wide asteroid called Dimorphos to knock it off course, scientists have released the first closeup images of the aftermath.

They suggest the asteroid now has one face flattened with a stadium-sized crater and is tumbling chaotically. Meanwhile, hundreds of previously unknown boulders encircle Dimorphos and its larger companion asteroid, Didymos.

As well as shedding new light on what happened to the asteroid after the collision, the images, captured by the European Space Agency’s (Esa) Hera spacecraft, could help scientists design more effective missions to deflect potentially hazardous space rocks in the future.

“Nasa’s Dart [Double Asteroid Redirection Test] mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid’s orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself,” said the Hera mission manager, Ian Carnelli, at Esa. “By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet.”

Nasa’s mission aimed to test-drive a planetary defence system that could prevent humanity from going the same way as the dinosaurs, should an asteroid or comet threaten Earth.

Neither Dimorphos nor its larger companion asteroid, Didymos, posed such a threat, but their movements provided scientists with a convenient means of assessing whether the strategy of trying to knock an asteroid off course might work.

On 26 September 2022, the roughly half-tonne Dart spacecraft ploughed into Dimorphos at more than 13,000mph, blasting a vast cloud of rocky debris into space.

Observations by telescopes on Earth revealed that the mission had succeeded in shortening the time it took Dimorphos to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. Before the collision, Nasa officials had said a change of 73 seconds or more would be considered a success.

But how much of the asteroid was displaced and precisely how it responded to the collision have remained open questions.

To investigate, Esa launched its Hera mission on 7 October 2024. After a two-year journey, the car-sized spacecraft reached the asteroid pair this month and has been surveying them from a distance of 15-18 miles (25-30km).

“Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same,” said Dr Patrick Michel, Hera principal investigator and director of research at the CNRS Côte d’Azur observatory in France. “Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once. The face struck by Dart has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid’s entire width.”

While the rest of Dimorphos appears to be relatively unchanged, the impact has also left Dimorphos “tumbling wildly in its orbit”, added Dr Michael Kueppers, the Esa’s Hera mission scientist.

“Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few metres in size,” Kueppers said.

Dr Michaël Marsset, an astronomer at the European Southern Observatory in Germany, described the release of the images as “a major milestone for both planetary defence and asteroid science”.

Unlike naturally occurring asteroid collisions, scientists knew precisely the mass, velocity and trajectory of the projectile and now had images of the asteroid before and after the impact, he said. “This offers a unique opportunity to study the physics of impacts at the scale of an asteroid.”

The Dart impact may also have exposed pristine material beneath Dimorphos’s weathered surface, offering scientists a rare glimpse of its interior, Marsset added.

Over the coming months, Hera will venture progressively closer to the asteroids and deploy two shoebox-sized satellites, one of which will use radar to peer inside Dimorphos.

The ultimate aim of these investigations is to transform asteroid deflection from a successful one-off experiment into a reliable means of planetary defence.

“The initial idea of deflecting an asteroid is not as straightforward as it sounds,” said Dr Ian Whittaker, a senior lecturer in physics at Nottingham Trent University. Although the momentum transferred by a spacecraft colliding with an asteroid should alter its motion, much also depends on how the asteroid responds to the impact, including how much material is blasted into space.“These images will help with understanding what is present after the impact and make for more accurate calculations in the future,” he said.

Asteroids are also remarkably diverse, ranging from relatively solid bodies to loose piles of rocks held together by their own weak gravity, said Marsset. “If we ever have to deflect another asteroid, this time on a collision course with Earth, we need to know what we are shooting at.”

The other major challenge is detecting potentially hazardous asteroids sufficiently early. Given years or decades of warning, even a tiny change in an asteroid’s velocity could be enough to make it miss Earth. “If it is discovered only months before impact, our options become considerably more limited,” Marsset said.

However, he added that major advances in asteroid detection were expected from the Vera C Rubin Observatory in Chile and Nasa’s forthcoming Near-Earth Object Surveyor space telescope. “These two complementary surveys will greatly improve our ability to discover potentially hazardous asteroids and, crucially, give us more time to respond.”

Whereas Douglas Adams’s Earth inhabitants were given mere minutes’ warning of their destruction, such advances could afford us both the time and the technology to avert our own.

The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:33:21 GMT

Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.

Mr Burnham correctly identified the transmission mechanism by which geopolitical problems feed domestic political resentment. “I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia,” the prime minister said.

The truth of that observation was painfully clear on Wednesday, when Ofgem, the energy regulator, announced that the price cap applied on domestic bills would rise in January. That means around 22 million UK households will pay an average equivalent to £2,166 a year for gas and electricity, up from £1,723 under the current cap.

International conflict and the climate emergency are driving up costs for British homes. Gas supply has been made volatile by uncertainty in the strait of Hormuz, while European reserves were depleted by exceptional energy usage to mitigate the effects of the summer’s ferocious and prolonged heatwave.

That leaves the continent poorly resourced to face what might be an unusually cold winter caused by the disruption of the polar vortex, plausibly accelerated by anthropogenic climate change. Many British households will face painful choices between heating their homes and affording other essentials. That hardship will exhaust the cost of living “breathing space” already offered by Mr Burnham – a VAT cut to bills and a one-off £100 payment to some households.

Meanwhile, the Conservatives and Reform UK claim that high bills are a function of environmental policies and look for solutions in the abandonment of Britain’s commitments to net zero – an approach that combines economic illiteracy with international irresponsibility. A dash to get dwindling North Sea oil on to a global market where the price is determined more by Mr Trump’s caprices or Vladimir Putin’s territorial aggressions is no shortcut to cheaper British bills.

Hastening the transition away from fossil fuels is the strategic route to energy security and the stability that permits other interventions to help with the cost of living. That argument must be central to the analysis that Mr Burnham offers when he moves on from “breathing space” policies to the more ambitious vision promised in a 10-year plan.

The prime minister has advertised that document, due to be published next month, as a blueprint for fixing “broken” markets, and restoring public control over utilities and other services on which people depend. What that means in practice will decide the fate of the Labour government. His focus on the cost of living is the right one, given how quick voters are to punish incumbents who fail to appreciate the scale of the problem or are perceived to lack credible solutions. Mr Burnham has passed the first of those tests. He cannot afford to fail the second one.

The Guardian view on the next UN secretary general: sacrificing principles will damn the institution, not save it

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:32:49 GMT

The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one

The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends.

Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight. With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time.

A female secretary general is long overdue, while the unofficial regional rotation would suggest a Latin American or Caribbean candidate. Rebeca Grynspan, a former Costa Rican diplomat and UN insider, was the clear frontrunner, but is thought to be opposed by the US and Russia over her criticism of Israel and stance on Ukraine. Lana Nusseibeh, a United Arab Emirates minister and former ambassador to the UN, entered the race late, but has now emerged at its centre, with Russia and the US backing her, while China, Britain and France are understood to have “discouraged” her. A third candidate, Rafael Grossi of Argentina, heads the International Atomic Energy Agency and is opposed by Russia. Another late entrant could still appear.

Mr Guterres has been a powerful voice of conscience, but many want a more active deal‑broker to reinvigorate the UN. Easier said than done. Ms Nusseibeh’s backers argue that she is the kind of political operator needed. But her nomination has rightly caused outrage in Sudan and among human rights groups and MPs, because she has been at the forefront of whitewashing UAE involvement in the devastating civil war – including dismissing UN findings.

Both sides have committed atrocities, but the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have a particularly grim record, with a UN mission reporting “hallmarks of genocide” in the ethnic killings and sexual violence that it perpetrated in El Fasher last autumn. Many outside players have Sudanese blood on their hands, but the UAE was first into the fray, inflaming the war. It denies supporting the RSF. But there is mounting evidence that its role – including supplying arms and mercenaries, according to UN and other reports – is far more extensive than that of others, sustaining this brutal war. Ms Nusseibeh says that she would act independently as secretary general. The UAE is lobbying energetically on her behalf.

This is a test for the Burnham government’s foreign policy. Some in Whitehall fear displeasing the US, and cherish the economic and security benefits of UAE ties. But this is not, as such officials suggest, a choice between principle and pragmatism. There would be nothing pragmatic about installing the nominee of a disruptive, adventurist state that fuels conflict at the heart of the multilateral system. And Ms Nusseibeh will surely be further compromised as more evidence of Abu Dhabi’s part in multiple wars emerges. To pick her would entrench moral taint and impunity in the UN, which could not then stand for something better, however imperfect, in a world of aggression and turmoil. It would not revive the institution, but risk condemning it. Britain must not falter.

Ten years on … the Bad Boys of Brexit are back in town

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:27:07 GMT

It feels as if we’re destined to hold the same referendum every decade. Nige, Arron and co are up for the fight

Roll back the years. The Bad Boys of Brexit have reformed and are back in town. Andy Wigmore on comms. Arron Banks on lead vocals and money. Nigel Farage on doing whatever the hell he likes. Apart from spending his own cash on security.

This time round, though, a woman has joined the band. Step forward, Catherine McBride. Probably the only woman alive who Nige thinks he can trust not to be totally pissed by 3pm. Even so, you can sense that this is a relationship destined to end in tears. Give it a couple of months and Catherine will be wishing she had never met Nige and Arron.

So we’re pretty much back where we were 10 years ago. Fighting the same battles over Europe. Telling some of the same lies. Inventing new ones to spice things up and fill in the backstory. This feels like it has become our destiny. A country whose misfortune is to hold the same referendum over membership of the EU every decade. Always to the same background noises of betrayal.

And that’s just from the winners. A referendum that settles nothing much, apart from the next one. Make no mistake, if a second referendum is the defining policy of the next election, a third referendum is nailed on three or four governments down the line. Each government crushed by its own divisions and economic stasis. And so it will go on until all the main protagonists have died. Even then, you wouldn’t put it past there being a delusional younger generation determined to maintain the tradition. It’s enough to make you think the campaigners for assisted dying had a point.

You just can’t escape the feeling of deja vu. Not just from the same faces rehearsing the same dud arguments. But also the endless splinter groups. Those wanting to stay out of the EU can’t even agree on why they want to stay out of the EU. The Bad Boys feat One Girl are the hardliner fundamentalists. They are the ones who hate everything to do with the EU. Meeting too many French people makes them projectile vomit. They have coalesced under the moniker Keep Britain Out. This is the group for leavers who like their campaigns riven with grievance.

Then there is Stay Out, a group led by Michael Gove. They like to think they are the acceptable face of leave. People who quite like Europeans as long as they are kept at a distance. Needless to say, Keep Britain Out hate Stay Out far more than they hate remainers. And vice versa. Nige and Arron believe Stay Out is for dripping wet Tories who have always been not-so-closet remainers. They also reckon that the Govester probably hedged his bets and voted remain in 2016. They may have a point. No one looked more horrified to discover leave had won the referendum than Michael.

Somewhere among all this is Kemi Badenoch’s Chicken Nuggets wing. So called because Kemi has had it confirmed that “chicken nuggets” is gangsta patois for “in out, in out”. The idiot’s idiolect for the halfwit who doesn’t know what she’s doing. What she would most want is for everyone to stop talking about rejoining the EU. Because it gives her PTSD as she remembers that it was the Tories who did so much to fuck everything up. She longs to be able to forgive herself but in the quietness of her own home she is plagued with guilt. The country is not in the mood to forgive or forget.

Mid-afternoon and Nige, Arron and Catherine take the places behind a table in a room in Westminster. Let battle commence. “I don’t really want to be doing this,” Arron begins. An outright lie. He’s loving every nanosecond. He’s missed the attention. The feeling of his ego rushing on its run. Everything has been building up to this moment when that feeling of gaping need will be filled once more. Brexit has been a huge success, he says. So once again the lies and the half-truths are reincarnated. Arron has been slagging off the Tory Brexit deal for years.

Then it was Catherine’s turn. Her proposition was quite simple. What you had to understand was that every other economist had been wrong about everything. Forget the Office for Budget Responsibility. Forget Nobel prize winners. They knew nothing. They were all part of an establishment conspiracy to prop up a ruling global elite. Only Catherine could be trusted to have done the right analysis. A lone voice howling at the moon until Arron rescued her from the bonfire of failure and obscurity. She had just the one message. Everything that Andy Burnham said was wrong. The end. That was her theory. The theory that was hers.

Finally, we got to Nigel, back in his familiar shadow world where truth could be whatever he chose it to be. Brexit had been betrayed by Tories wanting to join the single market. Much as Nige himself had once said. Though that was then, this was now. The UK had blossomed on the world stage since Brexit. We were now a superpower, the equal of the US and China. We had taken the lead on Ukraine. Well, some of us had. We rather remember Nige as having originally sided with Russia. And so it went on. Just one fact bent after another. For Nige, one lie is too many, a thousand never enough. He was the status quo. He was the moral compass. All directions lead back to Nige.

As for questions from the media, they were more an ego trip for Arron and Nige. A chance to mispronounce people’s names – probably foreigners, so fair game – and to be generally unpleasant. No, Arron wouldn’t say how much money he was shelling out on this latest vanity project. Though he was happy to sacrifice other people’s economic livelihoods on the altar of his failure.

And who cared if it was just another front for Reform? Certainly not Nige. He sounded as if he was half-minded to rename it back to the Brexit party. Just need to check out the legalities. “Thanks for the useful question,” Arron sneered. Not bothering to hide his contempt. This was his show. He could do what he liked.

“I can’t bear the thought of all this agony and division,” Nige said, loving every bit of it. Kemi was dismissed as just an angry woman, Andy as lightweight. Only Arron, Nige and – sometimes – Catherine were blessed with perfect vision. No one should trust the polls that suggest two-thirds of the country think Brexit has been a mistake. The people were wrong and Nige would teach them the error of their ways. He would kill them with kindness. And if that didn’t work he would kill them with hatred. Either way, they would die.

Here we were again. Two old-time politicians past their sell-by date offering a broken journey back to the past. Lucky us.

EU nationals will pay higher tuition fees than UK students, Burnham indicates

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:19:19 GMT

Asked by Kemi Badenoch to rule out equal rate for UK and EU students, PM says proposal ‘will not be put on the table’

European students will have to pay higher fees than their domestic equivalents at UK universities under a still-to-be-finalised part of the new deal with the EU, Andy Burnham has indicated.

The issue of fees paid by EU nationals studying at British universities is the main element of the arrangement hailed by Burnham in Brussels on Friday that has not been agreed, with both sides giving an extra six months to reach a solution.

Since Brexit, EU students – aside from Irish nationals and those with settled status in the UK – are treated as overseas entrants, so pay tuition fees which can exceed £30,000 a year, rather than a home student rate capped at £9,790.

The EU has been pushing for a lower rate, as part of the reset deal agreed at Friday’s summit in Brussels, which also included plans for looser checks on food and drink, emissions trading and a mutual exchange scheme for young people.

There have also been reports that Brussels has pushed for EU students to pay the domestic rate, while an annual charge of about £12,000 was suggested as a possible compromise.

Asked by Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions to rule out an equal rate between UK and EU students, Burnham indicated that this was requested by the EU but it would not be granted.

“In relation to the deal, the right honourable lady is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position,” he told her. “That has not been put on the table, and it will not be put on the table.”

Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “Both sides have agreed to negotiate a reciprocal agreement, and any deal would have to be in our national interest.”

Higher overseas fees are an important source of income for most UK universities, and dropping them significantly for EU students could cost the sector hundreds of millions of pounds a year.

Burnham said the deal on tuition fees with the EU was “not done” when asked by the leader of the opposition if the government would compensate universities.

He reiterated the UK’s position that the implementation of the deals agreed on Friday would not be dependent on an agreement about tuition fees, something EU officials took a different view of on Friday.

Burnham said Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, referred to the tuition fees talks as being “a separate piece of paper” to the main deal at the summit, meaning they were not linked.

He also said the Conservative party had to be clear on whether it opposed the plans: “Will it stand against a deal that will remove mountains of paperwork from British businesses and British exporters? A deal that the vast majority of Britain’s major supermarkets support because, they say, it can bring down pressure on the weekly shop? The Conservatives were once the party that opposed the imposition of red tape; they are now the red tape Tories.”

Gukesh and Sindarov draw Game 2 of world chess championship in just 20 moves

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:16:22 GMT

Game 2 ends by threefold repetition in 1hr 57min

World champion opens with the London System

Sindarov plays with white in Game 3 on Thursday

All your Gukesh v Sindarov questions, answered

India’s Gukesh Dommaraju and Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov drew the second game of their world chess championship match in only 20 moves and 1hr 57min on Wednesday, leaving the score level at 1–all at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs.

The quiet encounter was one of the shortest classical world title games since the sport’s rival championships were reunified in 2006 and the first to finish in under two hours since Ding Liren and Ian Nepomniachtchi drew their 11th game in just over 100 minutes in Astana in 2023.

The reigning world champion from Chennai, playing with the favored white pieces for the first time in the match, opted for the London System and made his first seven moves in under two minutes. Sindarov brought his queen out early to attack the b2 pawn (7 … Qb6), prompting Gukesh to pause for more than six minutes before moving a rook to protect it. Sindarov then traded off the knight Gukesh had planted in the center and castled on the 10th move.

The players

India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is defending his world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov in the youngest world title match in chess history. The best-of-14-games contest is set to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, overlooking Lake Geneva, with both players aged 20 when the first move is played.

Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history when he defeated China’s Ding Liren in December 2024, aged 18, shattering the previous record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in 1985. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai-born grandmaster has struggled badly for form since winning the title, plummeting to No 26 in the world rankings from a career-high No 3 after an extended string of underwhelming performances, raising doubts over his chances of retaining the crown in his first title defense.

Sindarov, roughly six months older than Gukesh, stunned the chess establishment with a commanding performance at this year’s eight-man Candidates tournament in Cyprus, finishing unbeaten with six wins and eight draws against a stacked field that included Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri. Known for his cool-headed precision and ability to mine advantages from seemingly quiet positions, the Tashkent-born grandmaster has climbed into the world’s top five after a breakthrough year that included winning the 2025 Fide World Cup in Goa. He is the first player from Uzbekistan to challenge for the world championship.

The format

The match consists of 14 classical games, with one point awarded for a win and a half-point for a draw. The first player to reach 7½ points wins the title. Each player has 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting at move 41. Players cannot agree to a draw before black’s 40th move.

If the match is tied 7-7 after 14 games, a series of faster tiebreaks will decide the champion: first four rapid games (15 minutes plus 10 seconds per move), then two rapid games (10 minutes plus five seconds), followed if necessary by two blitz games (three minutes plus two seconds). If still tied, single blitz games will be played, alternating colors, until one player wins.

The schedule

Sun 22 Nov Media day and opening ceremonyMon 23 Nov Media day and technical meetingTue 24 Nov Game 1 (Sindarov–Gukesh, ½-½)Wed 25 Nov Game 2 (Gukesh-Sindarov, ½-½)Thu 26 Nov Game 3 (Sindarov–Gukesh)Fri 27 Nov Rest daySat 28 Nov Game 4 (Gukesh-Sindarov)Sun 29 Nov Game 5 (Sindarov–Gukesh)Mon 30 Nov Game 6 (Gukesh-Sindarov)Tue 1 Dec Rest dayWed 2 Dec Game 7 (Sindarov–Gukesh)Thu 3 Dec Game 8 (Gukesh-Sindarov)Fri 4 Dec Game 9 (Sindarov–Gukesh, if necessary)Sat 5 Dec Rest daySun 6 Dec Game 10 (Gukesh-Sindarov, if necessary)Mon 7 Dec Game 11 (Sindarov–Gukesh, if necessary)Tue 8 Dec Game 12 (Gukesh-Sindarov, if necessary)Wed 9 Dec Rest dayThu 10 Dec Game 13 (Sindarov–Gukesh, if necessary)Fri 11 Dec Game 14 (Gukesh-Sindarov, if necessary)Sat 12 Dec Tiebreaks (if necessary) and closing ceremony

All games start at 3pm local time, 2pm GMT, 9am on the US east coast and 7.30pm in India.

Why isn't Magnus Carlsen playing?

Norway's Magnus Carlsen holds the top position in Fide’s world rankings with a classical rating of 2823. The 35-year-old has been at No 1 for more than 16 years uninterrupted. He was considered the best player on the planet even before removing all doubt against India’s Viswanathan Anand in their 2013 world title clash.

Carlsen bolstered his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021 when he crushed Russia’s Ian Nepomniachtchi in his fourth defense by a margin of four wins and no defeats, the most lopsided result in a world championship match since José Raúl Capablanca’s dismantling of Emanuel Lasker exactly 100 years prior. But he decided against defending it for a fifth time before the 2023 cycle, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long slog of preparation that world title matches demand. The abdication marked only the second time in history that a holder voluntarily declined to defend his title after Bobby Fischer controversially forfeited the crown ahead of his scheduled 1975 match with Karpov in Manila.

Instead, Ding outlasted Nepomniachtchi for the vacant title, even if critics including Kasparov branded it an “amputated” event without the world’s best player involved. Ding’s reign lasted only 593 days before Gukesh unseated him in Singapore in 2024, winning 7½–6½ to become the first teenager to win the sport’s biggest prize.

Carlsen remains active at the highest level, though he’s increasingly shifted his focus away from classical chess toward alternative formats. In February, he defeated Caruana 2½–1½ in Germany to win the Fide freestyle world championship, his 21st world title across classical, rapid, blitz and freestyle disciplines. Also known as Fischer Random or Chess960, the variation randomizes the starting positions of the pieces on the back rank, placing a premium on creativity over rote opening preparation.

The prize money

The overall prize fund is $2.5m (£1.9m), unchanged from 2024. Each player will receive $200,000 for each game won, including games won by forfeit. What’s left will be split equally between them. If the winner is decided on tiebreakers, the champion receives $1.3m with the runner-up taking home $1.2m. The same split applies if the match finishes 7½–6½ with 13 decisive games or 8–6 with 14 decisive games.

How to follow

The Guardian will provide live move-by-move commentary, expert analysis and reaction of select games throughout the three-week match. Fans can also watch every game live on Fide’s official YouTube and Twitch channels.

Gukesh described the London as a “nostalgic opening” he had played quite a bit as a teenager during the pandemic lockdown. He thought it might come as a surprise so early in the match, but Sindarov had studied the line closely and said the early queen move was part of his preparation.

“Sometimes it just happens that your opponent has his prep and you get nothing with white,” Gukesh said afterward. He called that “a very normal outcome at the top”, especially in the early stages of a world championship match after months of intense study.

Both players had castled by move 12 and the early pace gave way to longer spells of thought. Gukesh spent nearly half an hour on his 16th move (16 f3), advancing a pawn to support a possible push in the center. That left him with less than 50 minutes on his clock, while Sindarov still had nearly an hour and a half.

But the center stayed closed. Gukesh shuttled his bishop between two squares and Sindarov did the same with his knight. The position appeared for a third time on move 20, ending the game with 42 minutes left on Gukesh’s clock and 1hr 21min on the challenger’s.

Gukesh said he had looked at another pawn advance (c4) that might have kept the game going, but couldn’t see how to make it work. “I just found it very hard to see a way where I could pose some serious problems for my opponent,” he said. “You hope for your opponent to go wrong at some point, but also it’s equally likely that you’ll get into trouble.” The peaceful result was the second in as many days. Gukesh was left scrambling to make the time control in Tuesday’s opener before holding off Sindarov in a 38-move draw with black.

Few world championship games have ended as quickly as Wednesday’s, which came in two minutes shorter than The Devil Wears Prada 2. The first two games of Magnus Carlsen’s 2013 match against Viswanathan Anand ended in draws after 90 and 70 minutes, respectively. Carlsen and Sergey Karjakin needed only 35 minutes and 30 moves to draw the final classical game of their 2016 match in New York, seemingly content to play for tiebreakers, an outcome that disappointed fans and chess experts alike. “If the 12th game were a restaurant dish, I would send it back to the chef,” the British grandmaster Nigel Short tweeted.

Both Gukesh and Sindarov are 20 years old, making this the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title. Sindarov will turn 21 on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12.

Their careers have traced sharply divergent trajectories since Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world champion in December 2024. The Indian has struggled badly since defeating Ding to shatter the age record previously held by Garry Kasparov, plummeting from a career-high No 3 ranking to No 26 after a prolonged run of disappointing results. That makes him the lowest-ranked reigning world champion since Elo ratings were introduced in 1971.

Sindarov, meanwhile, has surged from No 25 a year ago to a career-best No 4 after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup in Goa last November and going unbeaten at this year’s Candidates tournament in Cyprus, where he became the first player from Uzbekistan to earn a world title shot.

The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified 20 years ago. Sindarov entered the match as a prohibitive favorite despite being the challenger, having won twice and drawn once in their three classical meetings before the match.

Gukesh was asked whether he would have liked at least one of the games to go his way given the undercurrent of doubt about his chances. “I’d prefer both results to go my way,” he said with a laugh.

The $2.5m showdown in Switzerland resumes on Thursday with Sindarov playing behind white in Game 3 before the first scheduled rest day on Friday. The players get one point for a win and half a point for a draw. The first to reach 7½ points will be crowned champion, with rapid and blitz tiebreaks scheduled if the score remains level after 14 games. Three of the past five world championship matches have required tiebreaks: in 2016, 2018 and 2023.

UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:14:27 GMT

Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged

A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

The nine workers had their contracts terminated in January 2024 “in the interests of the agency” and were told in termination letters that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”. The dismissals were confirmed after a UN investigation found they might have been involved in the 7 October attacks.

The decision, which was taken by former Unrwa commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini after consultation with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, was apparently made in the hope that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work to continue in Gaza.

Critics warned at the time that the decision, on the basis of allegations rather than evidence, compromised the UN’s integrity and had the opposite effect, giving credence to unproven allegations.

The dismissals failed to prevent the Biden administration ordering a pause in funding, a measure that was echoed temporarily by other backers, leading to a financial shortfall of $450m (£340m).

“I have always said on the record that the Israeli allegations against Unrwa were the mother of all lies,” said Chris Gunness, a former Unrwa spokesperson. “Sacking the workers without any evidence confirmed their guilt unfairly in the minds of journalists, led 16 top donors to abandon Unrwa and produced the worst financial crisis in the agency’s history, from which it may never recover.”

The Unrwa dispute tribunal that ruled in favour of one of its sacked workers, Abu Awad, described the Israeli allegations as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability”.

The tribunal also found that an internal UN investigation had not interviewed the 19 staff members initially accused by Israel of involvement in the 7 October attacks because of “safety and security” concerns.

“The allegations against the applicant and the other staff members, it seems, are therefore based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession,” the tribunal said.

It cast doubt on intercepted mobile phone conversations and messages offered by Israel as evidence, noting that one case had involved mistaken identity based on a cloned sim card, a common phenomenon in Gaza.

It also said that voice recognition claims made by Israel were dubious and some transcripts of conversations were found by UN investigators not to support claims that they proved links to Hamas or the 7 October attacks.

The allegation against Awad was that he was a “platoon commander” in Hamas’s military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, a claim he rejected. He was not alleged to have physically taken part in the 7 October attack and witness statements to the tribunal said he was on an Unrwa staff bus as normal.

The specific allegation against Awad was that he “had been instructed in a telephone call intercepted by Israeli intelligence to monitor the events of 7 October 2023, while simultaneously receiving Hamas intelligence updates related to the attacks”.

The tribunal said the Israeli security services had failed to clarify who was alleged to have made the call to Awad and in what way the mobile phone that received the call was associated with him.

Unrwa did not respond to a request for comment. Asked by the tribunal to provide evidence underpinning the dismissal of the workers, the agency cited the Israeli government as well as a report in the Times of Israel and another on the website UN Watch, a pro-Israel pressure group that has campaigned against Unrwa.

In its ruling, the tribunal said Unrwa’s claim that the cited sources had informed the decision to dismiss the workers was “open to some doubt” because all the supporting documents it had submitted were produced after the disputed decision was made on 26 January 2024.

Lazzarini, a Swiss humanitarian expert who left the commissioner general post in March, did not respond to a request for comment. In February 2024, he admitted his decision to sack the workers represented “reverse due process” in that the investigation followed the dismissal.

“My judgment, based on this going public, true or untrue, was I need to take the swiftest and boldest decision to show that as an agency we take this allegation seriously,” he said, adding that “the ability of the entire agency to continue to operate and deliver critical humanitarian assistance was at stake”.

The tribunal said it could not decide on the allegations against Awad but ruled that Unrwa had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to sack him. It awarded him a year’s pay and $5,000 for “moral damages”.

In the wake of its allegations against the sacked workers, Israel claimed that Unrwa was heavily infiltrated by Hamas and its parliament voted in 2024 to ban the agency from operating in Israel or in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The international court of justice stated in October 2025, however, that “Israel has not substantiated its allegations that a significant part of Unrwa’s employees are members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions”.

Cop31 collapse must be a catalyst for genuine climate action

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:08:06 GMT

Readers on the failure of the climate talks in Turkey and the lessons we can learn

The failure of Cop31, as commented on by Bill McGuire (A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption.

The disjunction between peril and necessary action is explained by the impossibility of taming appetites that are insatiable. It is convenient to blame fossil fuel producers, and while they are obviously guilty parties, the ultimate problem is the continuing demand for their products.

In any contest between material wealth and the health of the natural world, there is never any competition, as your report (23 November) on the proposed scrapping of the Environment Agency and Natural England demonstrates, because maintaining and extending our material demands is, it seems, absolutely imperative.

It is also a mistake to blame politicians, who are a symptom of our value system, not its cause. They know very well that when the rhetoric of easy solutions comes up against the reality of actions, people everywhere will not tolerate the necessary decline in material consumption that will be the inevitable consequence of the changes that might have a chance of averting catastrophe.

It is no coincidence that despite the massive expansion of renewable energy across the world, the only recent years when the world’s carbon emissions did not grow were 2008-09 and 2020, associated with an involuntary decline in global output caused by the financial crisis and the Covid pandemic. Pessimism is rational, because the evidence is so stark that our civilisation cannot change its compulsive ways even to save itself. Stephen Smith Glasgow

Bill McGuire’s article makes for alarming reading, especially for someone who taught about climate risks 40 years ago and fears for his grandchildren. Cop is dead, revealed in all its glory for what it is: a fig leaf and a pretence of action – a classic stalling mechanism.

I am so pleased that it has exploded. Goodbye Cop, and good riddance! Effective action often results from failure. Let’s use this moment to raise a storm of protest and demand that this abject failure produces new leadership and real action. John Crossman Sherborne, Dorset

The failed Cop31 talks are the final signal to governments and societies that we need clear conversations about the future – globally, nationally and around community hearths. It’s now clear that vested interests will not separate their own profiteering from everyone’s survival – both humanity and the biosphere. Either we all accept that and embrace dystopia, or we start the conversations that matter about the future. Our relationships with money cannot eclipse our relationships with nature, the past and the future.

If governments fail to take the lead here, each one of us can start these conversations and push for change. This is civilisation-shift stuff. And now’s the moment. Prof Phoebe Barnard Wallingford, Oxfordshire

Was there any point in holding the Cop meeting when, at the same time, three self-appointed “world leaders” agreed to maximise oil production for their own financial benefit (China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars, 19 November)? Michael Peel London

Cop31’s stark failure leaves us with critical questions: can we limit warming to below 2C with only technical fixes like renewables, efficiency and electrification? Or must we confront the capitalist system that treats ecosystems as infinite resources, prioritises profit over sustainability and measures success in growth and extraction?

Can we continue organising production without democratic planning, public policy and participatory decision-making? Or will we remain trapped in a model where competition and individualism dictate our future? How do we shift from a system that rewards exploitation to one rooted in solidarity, equity and justice?

The answer lies in redefining wealth to include the rights of communities and nature, abandoning false solutions like carbon capture, and embracing a low-carbon economy guided by collective wellbeing.

For the global south, urgent action is needed: debt cancellation, grants, technology transfer, and support for resilience – not conditional aid, but true cooperation. Peace, dignity and prosperity cannot be achieved through charity, but through structural change. The tools for transformation exist. What’s missing is the political courage to use them. The time for half measures is over. Hakan Oygur Muratpaşa, Antalya, Turkey

The collapse of Cop must be one of the darkest days for multilateralism and for the imperative of sustainable development, which was conceived more than 50 years ago. In truth, and in retrospect, it represents the inevitable denouement of a process that all along was one of deception, dishonesty and pusillanimity on the part of the powerful.

As the learned people that you quote say, this is not an end and it will not stop the inexorable evolution away from fossil fuels. But it epitomises the criminal hypocrisy of those countries and organisations, public and private, that are masquerading as willing partners, but in reality zealously profiting from the destruction of the planet’s life support systems.

This betrayal must lead to a sustained collaborative effort by those who represent the true interest of humanity to inject an utterly irresistible momentum into creating a global movement for climate and social justice. The postwar settlement is utterly unfit for purpose and must be transcended in the interests of humanity. Neil Blackshaw Alnwick, Northumberland

The Labour party has lost the plot on net zero

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:07:55 GMT

Raymond T Pierrehumbert and Dr Lynne Jones respond to an article by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh

Watching Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, forced to defend the government’s retreat from net zero (Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep, 17 November) was painfully reminiscent of the way in which Colin Powell, a former US secretary of state and an honourable man, was forced to defend George W Bush’s claims justifying the disastrous Iraq war.

Fahnbulleh states that people need to see the benefits of net zero on their doorstep – meaning jobs, cost of living and warm homes. But in fact the policies of this government mark a retreat of all of these “doorstep” benefits. Andy Burnham has slashed heat pump subsidies, which means more vulnerability of homes to heating price shocks from international affairs spiking fossil gas prices; it also means fewer warm homes and jobs in the heat pump manufacturing and installation industry.

The impending rollback of the electric vehicle mandate means more costs for drivers, who will continue to pay high prices for petrol, and an ultimate collapse of jobs in the UK auto industry, which will be unable to compete with the inexorable shift to electric vehicles. And Fahnbulleh turned down the Botley West project, which would have been the UK’s biggest solar farm and would have done more for the country’s energy security (and jobs) than the contributions of Jackdaw gas or Rosebank oil (destined in any case for export).

Labour has lost the plot on net zero. Even if one neglects the toll of climate disruption, progress toward net zero is part and parcel of UK prosperity and addressing the cost of living crisis. The only alternative at this point is to ditch Labour and vote Green. Raymond T Pierrehumbert Professor of planetary climate, University of Oxford

Good to know that Miatta Fahnbulleh thinks “the climate crisis is now a national security issue and we must prepare for future threats”. I hope this means that she will push for the full, unredacted release of the national security report that was produced by the joint intelligence committee a year ago. I assume she will also now join the 187 MPs calling for the government to organise a live emergency briefing on the climate and nature crises. I was surprised she did not mention taking these actions in her article. She does acknowledge that “the first duty of government is to protect people: cutting emissions”, so I assume that means “no” to developing the Rosebank oilfield. What people want from their government is complete honesty, transparency and effective and meaningful action to address the climate and nature emergencies. Dr Lynne Jones Mousehole, Cornwall

The British Library is wrong to repurpose its reading rooms

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:07:50 GMT

To distort what was actually a reduction in supply into a reduction in demand and then use it as ‘evidence’ is unworthy of our world-class research institution, says Marcia Saunders

After a cyber-attack in 2023, which Ciaran Martin, a former CEO of the National Cyber Security Centre, described as “one of the worst cyber incidents in British history”, use of the British Library’s reading rooms fell dramatically (British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces, 20 November).

Throughout 2024-25, services were heavily affected, including archives, manuscripts, books and online journal articles. All readers’ tickets were suspended and initially were reissued for limited periods of time. It should surprise no one that use of the reading rooms fell off. Only last month was access to the UK web archive (partially) restored.

To distort what was actually a reduction in supply into a reduction in demand and then use it as “evidence” is unworthy of our world-class research institution. In addition, the hiving off of an essential part of the library team – the security staff – is plain stupid.

Regular users have seen our numbers steadily returning. Having said that, if sophisticated remote resources fulfil their promise, there could remain some underused space. And here is an opportunity staring the library in the face: the corridors and landings outside the reading rooms are packed every single day with large numbers of students sitting four to a table, and even on the floor, poring over their laptops. Nearly silent and impressively focused, they are the overspill from London’s universities, whose libraries have not grown apace with student numbers through lack of resources.

It has always seemed sad to me that these young people are not using the reading rooms and their resources. Students? Books? Research facilities? Rubbing shoulders with academics? Surely there’s a win-win here. Why don’t the British Library and leaders of London’s universities get together and have a chat? Marcia Saunders London

Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album review – even GTA sceptics will warm to this zeitgeisty, star-packed soundtrack

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:50:18 GMT

(Atlantic)Justice bring some 80s nostalgia but this compilation of new material from music’s A-list – from Dua Lipa to Travis Scott and a host of Latin talent – stays at the cutting edge

It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish.

Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. This style is synonymous with Grand Theft Auto VI’s setting, a fictionalised version of Florida last seen in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was beloved for its inclusion of 80s hits.

Yet this time around the concerns are more modern, and global. Appropriately, given its mock-Florida geography, there are plenty of A-list rap acts including Cardi B, Playboi Carti and Gunna, while songs from Rauw Alejandro, Jhayco and more give a substantial Latin flavour. Even if it’s not quite as region-specific as GTA V’s soundtrack of hip-hop, punk and psychedelia was to southern California, you can still imagine plenty of this material wafting around real-life Miami.

The brand new songs collected on the soundtrack album are only a small fraction of the music heard in Grand Theft Auto VI. Within the game are 22 radio stations, each with a playlist of at least two dozen songs each with its own genre focus, from country to blues to global music and pop hits new and old alike. There are 700 songs spanning nine decades licensed here, reflecting the spirit of exploration the game is meant to inspire.

That breadth makes the game feel fresh and exciting every time you play, and there are moments of gleeful serendipity when a playlist delivers the perfect accompaniment for a clean getaway (Mojabi Ghost by Bad Bunny and Tainy) or a moment of viral cheer (a romantic jetski romp set to Carly Rae Jepsen’s Run Away With Me) or a jaw-dropping surprise (Kamikazi, a funky previously unreleased song from the neo-soul legend D’Angelo.)

Despite the endless variety, Rockstar’s shifting aesthetic sensibilities stand out. With rap not quite as pop-culturally central as it once was, Grand Theft Auto VI looks to the nightclub, heralded by Justice’s score and a clear focus on dance-pop artists: Arca, former Blackpink star Jennie, Fcukers and Rina Sawayama. Rockstar’s bet seems to be that this decade of unrest will keep us searching for escapism on the dancefloor, as well as in their own virtual worlds.

What is certain is the extraordinary cultural clout Grand Theft Auto has amassed, securing true megastars such as Travis Scott, Dua Lipa and Morgan Wallen to record new tracks. That starriness gives a celebratory bent to the album; almost every act seems to sense the scale of the occasion, and strongly delivers. There are a few misfires – regional Mexican music revivalists Fuerza Regida settle for a run-of-the-mill urbano jam – and there aren’t many moments to slow down, though when you need a break from boosting cars and high-stakes stickups, the dreamy, heartbreaking Largate, by Helado Negro and Kali Uchis, is a standout.

Grand Theft Auto is notoriously fond of taking the piss. In-game adverts lambast US gun culture and rightwing politicians; podcasters and TV programmes are routinely mocked. Music, however, is the one place where the games are deadly serious. Last time we were in Vice City, Rockstar seemed content to use music as a mere signifier of the era. Today, it may be the most important non-algorithmic curator of music in the world. It’s heartening that their taste in music is this good – criminally so, you might say.

Anselm Kiefer review – Holocaust-haunted forests and a glimpse into a gigantic grave

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:37:39 GMT

White Cube Bermondsey, LondonKiefer asks what art means after the Holocaust – but even the vast scale of his powerfully seductive paintings can’t do justice to the gravity of his themes

When the world is falling apart, the artist retreats to the studio. It’s an old story, and Anselm Kiefer has always loved the old stories, drawing for his monumental and reliably blockbuster paintings on narrative traditions ranging from Norse mythology to German Romantic poetry. So it makes sense that an artist who has dedicated his life to the question of what art means after the end of European civilisation – which is to say, after the Holocaust – should now seek out the solitude of the studio to make sense of what’s coming. Kiefer’s exhibition at the same gallery a decade ago had the title Walhalla, after the beer hall in the sky in which dead Vikings drink away the afterlife. Now comes the more modest (you would think) subject of the artist’s studio, depicted here in a suite of lustrous landscapes and a simple wooden cabin in the forest. Rendered in flat gold leaf, the sky in these paintings gleams like a tarnished halo in an old altarpiece, while the verdigris grass pushes roughly off the canvas. Here is the place where heaven meets the earth and is transmuted – by the alchemy of this painter’s touch – into quietly numinous paintings containing elements of both.

If you can put aside the fact that Kiefer’s own studio is a vast warehouse complex on the outskirts of Paris, these paintings present a very German vision of communion with nature. They also evoke the most famous hut in modern philosophy: the Black Forest hideaway where Martin Heidegger formulated his argument that “authentic” culture must be rooted in the native landscape. The flipside of this idea, that nature is not just a scenic backdrop to human history but a living participant in it, would have, let’s just say, consequences for German painting after 1945. Here is the challenge that Kiefer has spent his career meeting: how to paint the landscape as an unspoilt refuge from society when it is littered with mass graves?

Given that his forests are haunted by these horrors, it is inevitable that a series of paintings of hunters’ lookouts, displayed back to back on trolley wheels, should call to mind camp watchtowers, their high windows like unblinking eyes. And that an eight-metre-tall canvas of a building’s interior collapsing into a bonfire of real charcoal planks (affixed to the canvas and painted with brilliant licks of flame) should imply more than the destruction of an artist’s inventory. Here is a world of fire and ash, burning so that it might be reborn. The dark glamour, the virtuoso handling of the paint and the sheer scale are seductive.

Yet the power of the studio paintings derives more from their marvellous combination of colours and textures than their symbolism. For a hermetic artist, who magpies from esoteric theories as scattered as alchemy, string theory and Kabbalah in a search for hidden correspondences that can sometimes manifest as a generalised profundity, this focus on a subject qualifies as restraint. I was wondering whether this might even herald a new and (relatively) pared-back late style when I came to a painting of a naked man resembling the artist lying in a blasted landscape, learning from the handout that it was titled (in Latin, no less) On the Third Day He Rose Again, and thought: aha. Faint hope.

It is not surprising that an octogenarian artist’s thoughts should turn to mortality, and everyone must make their own private sense of that approaching horizon. It’s your funeral, as they say. But the enormous paintings that end this show – featuring solitary men staring morosely into pits, lying in open graves, and being miraculously resurrected – link the archetypal figure of the artist to the martyrdom of Christ and the genocides of the 20th century. Even for someone as indifferent to appearing pretentious as Kiefer, this is heady stuff.

In fairness, the idea that the death of the artist might redeem humanity is – I think – intended as bleakly ironic: one man gazing blankly into what could be a mass grave is identified as Narcissus. But at worst, it seems crass. Two paintings in the same room are dedicated to the poets Paul Celan and Ezra Pound. Here it is important to know that Celan, who was Jewish, wrote the line that is quoted in Kiefer’s painting while he was imprisoned in a forced labour camp and his parents were being murdered. Pound, at this time, was living in Italy and broadcasting violently antisemitic propaganda on behalf of the fascists. It is not enough to place them together without context, as if their incorporation into Kiefer’s intricately networked but generally obscure artistic universe constitutes some magical resolution of these tensions.

Kiefer has stated his commitment to “ambivalence”, which I understand to mean that his role as an artist is to memorialise the horrors rather than unravel the contradictions that produced them. But when art reproduces the past rather than processes it, we are bound to get stuck in a loop – and we are now living through another conspiratorial age in which the profusion of myths and alternative belief systems serves to obscure clear truths.

These last paintings seem to me realised on such a vast scale not just because the artist wants to overwhelm the viewer, but because the subjects he has taken on are, in the end, too big for him to manage. Anselm Kiefer: Des Malers Atelier is at White Cube Bermondsey, London, until 24 January
