Woman did not believe husband had drugged her for rape by strangers, Manchester trial told

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:36:42 GMT

Wife said to detectives: ‘I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can’t believe it’s true’

A woman who was allegedly raped and sexually assaulted by men her husband invited to their home after he drugged her told police she could not believe it happened.

In a video interview played to a jury at Minshull Street crown court in Manchester, she told detectives: “I had no knowledge of what you told me had happened and I still can’t believe it’s true, and I think you have made a mistake.”

The woman asked: “Is this my fault that he has done this?” while telling police she had not knowingly had sexual intercourse with her husband for several years. The interview was filmed a fortnight after the arrest last October of her husband, who has not been named in order to protect her identity.

He has pleaded guilty to more than 60 offences, spanning a period of more than 20 years.

Nine men are on trial accused of either visiting the couple’s home in Stockport to rape or sexually assault the woman, or of encouraging the abuse online as they “hid behind a screen”.

Two police video interviews were played to the court in which the woman said she did not recognise any of the men on trial and had never consented to sexual intercourse while she was asleep or unconscious.

She said it was a long time since she had had sex with her husband – “more than five years, probably more like nine if I’m honest”.

She described her marriage to her husband as “just a normal relationship”, adding: “A loving couple, we did things together, went out with other people. We’ve always had quite a lot of friends and a good social circle, and done things.”

She said that back in around 2006, the couple would have sex a “couple of times a week”, which she said was “normal, vanilla”.

This stopped in around 2016 and they “got out of the habit”, she said. “I was menopausal at the time and I was really hot and sweaty, and I just didn’t like to be touched by anybody because it was uncomfortable. He never pressured me or asked or anything.”

“We did hug and cuddle and kiss,” she added, before asking officers: “Is this my fault that he has done this?”

Appearing in the witness box, the woman faced the jury and said she had been unaware that her husband had been drugging her.

She dismissed all claims that she had been a willing participant, only “play-acting” at being asleep, occasionally shaking her head and telling the jury: “That’s a load of rubbish, is what I say.”

In her police interviews, the woman said she was put on medication for blood pressure and cholesterol problems in the summer of 2024.

“I went to the doctors because I’d woken up and felt really ill and couldn’t remember what had happened and my heart was, I felt my heart was racing,” she said. “I woke up really late for me. Probably either late morning or early afternoon, which is late.”

She said she “felt a bit weird” and “like I was drunk, but I wasn’t” and her “legs felt wobbly”.

Among those on trial are taxi driver Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport; building supplies worker Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester; and Jonathan Kirk, 43, a senior paramedic, also from Stockport.

Wild’s lawyer, Pierce Power, asked the woman whether she had answered the door or spoken to Wild, who is charged with sexual assault, attempted rape, assault by penetration and conspiracy to rape. She replied: “No.”

When he suggested she had consented to Wild touching her sexually, she replied: “That’s not true.”

Appearing on behalf of Wallace, who is charged with rape and attempted rape, Rachel White indicated she was not suggesting the woman was lying – and all three defence lawyers said it was their job to put the defence case to her.

White said: “Can I make it clear from the outset that I’m not suggesting that you have told lies, or are telling lies.”

When asked whether she was sitting up in bed on the night Wallace visited and had offered him a drink, the woman said: “It didn’t happen.”

She told the court she had “never taken part in role-play” and, when asked by the judge whether she had “this fetish”, replied: “No.”

Appearing on behalf of Kirk, who is charged with rape, conspiracy to rape and conspiracy to assault by penetration, Katy Thorne KC asked the woman whether she had spoken to Kirk and “responded with a nod and a yes”. She replied: “That’s not true. I’ve got no memory of Mr Kirk being in my house.”

The men on trial all deny the charges against them. The trial continues.

Is Vanity Fair’s takedown of Taylor Swift illuminating – or just a lot of hot air?

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:10:03 GMT

A war correspondent interviewed 100 sources about the pop star, but what does the 4,500-word story reveal?

If you are extremely online you will have known for a while that a big takedown was coming. An exposé of a well-known blond billionaire, a powerful figure that people are terrified to criticise, was in the works at a large publication. A former war correspondent had been assigned the story! A hundred sources had been interviewed! The reporting had taken a year! The truth would finally out!

For everyone else, let me explain in plain English. On Monday Vanity Fair published an eagerly anticipated, 4,500-word piece, about Taylor Swift called The Mastermind. While it was labelled as “commentary”, it was framed as a deeply sourced piece written by May Jeong, a journalism professor at Princeton who has won awards for her reporting from Afghanistan.

So what did we learn about the world’s richest female pop star? Not much, I’m afraid. While Jeong may have spoken to 100 sources, only a handful were quoted by name, and their anecdotes were underwhelming.

Arielle Peppers, for example, who transferred to Swift’s school from a nearby city “after her neighbor was stabbed in the neck”, remembers the pop star owning multiple pairs of Uggs. “She had the brown one, the black one, the blue one,” she reveals.

Sharon Luyben, a music teacher at one of Swift’s schools, pushed back on Swift’s claim that kids didn’t want to sit next to the pop star at lunch. “We had assigned seating in junior high,” she says. The Wyomissing area school district, meanwhile, did not respond to Vanity Fair’s questions about this very important matter.

Chanice Skinner, who sat next to Swift in music class, also contradicts Swift’s claims that she had no friends when she was younger, asserting that, actually, she was “always part of the popular crowd”. Skinner recalls watching a Target commercial where Swift says she was bullied at school. “I was like, You were part of that. What are you talking about? If anything, you were one of the bullies.”

I’m not sure you really needed to interview 100 people or request a statement from the Wyomissing area school district to learn that a skinny, white, blonde girl with rich parents and a conventionally attractive face was not unpopular at school. I say this with the full authority of having once been a teenage girl.

Anyway, you get the gist of it. Apart from a few new details about Swift’s teenage Ugg collection everything else in the article – the lengths that Swift’s parents took to make her famous, the fact that Swift does not take criticism well – is already well established.

Still, while there is not much substance to the Vanity Fair piece, there is plenty of style. The piece is written in an alternating A side/B side format. Each A side presents the version of Taylor’s life that has been carefully constructed and sold to the press: the unassuming little girl who grew up on a Christmas tree farm and had no friends. The B side is the reality as Jeong heard it from the 100 sources: the rich kid who grew up in a house once visitor called a “six-star hotel”, who became a ruthless businesswoman. Various random letters are capitalized and bolded throughout, in a nod to the Easter eggs that Swift leaves her fans in her music videos and liner notes. (Spoiler alert: they spell out “LOOK WHAT YOU MADE ME DO”.)

It is a clever conceit, but I personally found it quite grating to read. Also irritating was the fact that only a few people in the story are named and everyone else gets nicknames like The Machine or The Manager or The Protégé or The Person Familiar. (Travis Kelce, Swift’s husband, is called Redwood.) Swift herself is called The Star. It is, as others have remarked, reminiscent of American Canto by Olivia Nuzzi, which was pretentious filler marketed as hot gossip about the writer’s affair with Robert F Kennedy Jr. If you already know a lot about Swift’s life then you may enjoy deciphering the puzzles in the piece. If you know nothing about Swift it will be like trying to read Finnegans Wake in ancient Greek.

None of this is meant as criticism towards Jeong. She is a very talented writer who is probably spending Thanksgiving in a bunker, hiding from irate Swifties. But even the rarest reporting talent will have trouble making something out of nothing.

That said, “the nothing” is a large part of the story. Jeong writes that people close to Swift “do not dare speak ill of her – dare not speak of her at all”. Jeong adds: “When these mortals did speak of The Star in public … it was softly, using initials. A Washington Post reporter who recently wrote a book about The Star has noted that countless sources refused to go on the record even to say nice things about her.” The dearth of juicy anecdotes, it is strongly suggested, is because people are terrified of The Star and the powerful PR machinery around her.

While it is certainly true that a lot of people are scared to criticise Swift, I don’t think this is the only reason Jeong couldn’t dig up interesting anecdotes. Have you read any profiles about the early lives of Stephen and Katie Miller? Those are chockful of named sources detailing how the pair were basically deranged bigots from a very young age. While Swift is scary, she isn’t the president’s henchman and she has never been responsible for a mass deportation campaign. (Although, as the Vanity Fair piece notes, she did invite an ICE contractor to the midtown Manhattan networking convention that masqueraded as her wedding.)

The real reason there is nothing of substance in the Vanity Fair piece, I would wager, is because there is nothing of substance to Swift. She is nicknamed Blandie, after all. Her parents turned her into a product from a very young age and she’s been aggressively marketed to the masses ever since.

That marketing machine, predictably, has gone into overdrive since the Vanity Fair piece came out. “Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism?” Chris Willman at Variety asked. I dunno, Variety? Is writing endless puff pieces about Swift journalism? Meanwhile a source close to Swift told Page Six that the pop star herself is not bothered by Jeong’s hatchet job. Swifties, however, are so furious that Page Six reports the Committee to Protect Journalists has been in touch with Jeong to ensure her safety.

While many of Swift’s fans may be rushing to her defence, some are slowly starting to question their idol. Last week CNN put out a piece about a Swift superfan, known as The Swiftologist explaining that he had finally been able to “deprogram” his brain and allow himself to critique his idol. Swift has always been able to adapt. But, as a billionaire in a world where people are increasingly angry about inequality, she may find it harder to capture the zeitgeist. Her ostentatious wedding was seen as out of touch and she has become a glaring symbol of a world in which the creative industries are dominated by nepo babies and the uber-wealthy. “We all had promise,” Skinner, one of Swift’s former classmates told Vanity Fair. “It’s just that she had money.” It may not have revealed anything new, but the fact that this Vanity Fair piece was even published seems to suggest the megastar is entering a new era: one where she is seen as less untouchable than before.

Alejandro Garnacho and the curious case of Aston Villa’s outcast loanees

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:00:31 GMT

Unai Emery wanted the winger but, like Harvey Elliott last season, he has been left out in the cold despite Villa’s attacking struggles

It is three years this week since Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring for Manchester United in a 3-3 draw at Galatasaray in the Champions League, on a typically boisterous night in Istanbul when Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, now his teammates at Aston Villa, were also among the starters. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award.

He went on to score twice at Old Trafford on Boxing Day, in a 3-2 victory against Villa, and a couple of months later his double at home to West Ham was the catalyst for that iconic celebration photo of Garnacho, Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund sitting on the advertising hoardings at the Stretford End, beaming smiles all round. All three were at the heart of United’s plans for a bright future, beacons of hope. At the end of that season, Garnacho signed off in style, he and Mainoo scoring against Manchester City at Wembley to win the FA Cup.

This week at Galatasaray’s Rams Park, however, Garnacho, who in the summer signed on loan for Villa after a season at Chelsea, was nowhere to be seen. Villa, per competition rules, were permitted to name a dozen substitutes but Unai Emery named only 11. Garnacho did not travel and was again conspicuous by his absence, left out of the matchday squad for the third successive game. He has played only 95 minutes across seven games in all competitions, 34 across four league outings. He is yet to start for Villa and his last appearance was a three-minute cameo against Fulham at the end of last month. Welcome to The Curious Case of Alejandro Garnacho.

It is happening again, isn’t it? Last season it was Harvey Elliott who was left out in the cold for the season after signing on loan from Liverpool and now it is Garnacho on the periphery. On Wednesday it emerged Garnacho has wiped all trace of Villa from his Instagram account, the latest nadir for a talented player once the recipient of gushing compliments, and the ultimate telltale sign of a deteriorating relationship. Will Garnacho still be at Villa post-January? Villa halted Elliott’s game time to avoid triggering a permanent transfer and it appears they are doing similar with Garnacho, whom they have a conditional obligation to buy for about £43m. It is thought the buy option relates to appearances but, unlike the Elliott deal, the details remain a secret.

At this point it is important to remember the power structure at Villa. In short: Emery has the run of the place, great autonomy, and further control is pending with the Basque expected to sign a new long-term contract. Emery decides which players come in the door and he pushed for Garnacho’s signing. The president of football operations and de facto sporting director, Roberto Olabe, helps make Emery’s wishes come true. When Garnacho joined Villa in July, Emery expressed delight: “He is so talented … we are really happy.” So, what has changed?

The picture has shifted since the start of October. Emery and his staff felt there were green shoots during the extended international break, in which Garnacho scored in friendlies against Southampton and Sevilla. As one of the players not on international duty, he had the chance to get up to speed during Villa’s warm-weather camp in Spain. “He is getting better and for him the two weeks we worked were very important,” was Emery’s take. “He is working well and progressing.”

Or at least that was the thought. He has been omitted from four of Villa’s past five league squads. Garnacho is believed to have been training professionally but after Saturday’s stalemate with Sunderland, Emery suggested the 22-year-old was a long way from featuring. “I am trying to select the players I think that are ready to play,” Villa’s manager said to a question about the absences of Tammy Abraham, Lamare Bogarde and Garnacho. It was damning, then, that Abraham and Bogarde were on the bench for Tuesday’s defeat. When asked whether Garnacho was fit, Emery did not dress things up. “I think the players here are the best players to be with us,” he replied.

It is all the more perplexing given the chances – and goals – have dried up. Villa have failed to score in four of their past six matches – their four goals at Manchester United, whom the table tells us are the second-worst team in the division, represent an anomaly on this run – and Emery acknowledges they are not producing enough offensively. How low is Garnacho in the pecking order if he cannot make the bench? Johan Manzambi, Alysson, Emiliano Buendía, John McGinn, Ibrahim Mbaye and George Hemmings are in front of him.

Sign up to Football Daily

after newsletter promotion

A campaign that got off to a bad start for Garnacho – he missed the Super Cup in August owing to a concussion sustained in a friendly in Thailand – has never got off the ground. It is hard to believe a player bought by Chelsea for £40m has nothing to offer and easy to forget Garnacho made 43 appearances last season, 24 in the top flight, including 14 starts. By this point last year, he had started five Premier League games, two in the Champions League and another in the Carabao Cup. It is a year to the day since he began Chelsea’s 3-0 win over Barcelona. At the same time Garnacho was not a regular and Chelsea, who did summer deals with Villa to buy Morgan Rogers and Emiliano Martínez and sell Nicolas Jackson, were happy for him to depart.

A slow start under Emery would be nothing new – just ask Youri Tielemans who became undroppable – but none of the noises generate belief that the winger could yet prove a slow-burning success. Four months in, is this the beginning of the end? The former Villa striker Gabriel Agbonlahor raised a series of legitimate questions on TalkSport amid a backdrop of ticket-price hikes for the fifth straight year and the battle to meet financial regulations. “What are you wasting on wages? What are you wasting on loan fees?” he asked. Perhaps the most pertinent question talked to the bigger picture. “What player is going to want to come on loan to Aston Villa?”

Influencers Behaving Badly at No 10? Burnham’s problems could be worse

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:37:59 GMT

For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one

These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape.

To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett, was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”.

If you can absorb any of these details without laughing like a drain, you are a more serious person than me. But in any case, it isn’t the content so much as what the influencers represent that has launched Burnham’s opponents into orbit. I’m not familiar with the line “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, but for those of us with young children, it is instantly recognisable as the latest contribution to the “skibidi toilet” meme tradition of conjoining rude words a 10-year-old would find funny and putting them on endless repeat. This would be more embarrassing for Burnham were it not for one fact: between them, Balegde and Hamnett have more than six million followers across Instagram and TikTok, substantially more than the Daily Telegraph. We can be confident the average age of those followers is not 61.

Data as provoking as this obviously calls for a full-throated overreaction, and Kemi Badenoch didn’t disappoint. On Tuesday, the Tory leader requested an apology from the prime minister for turning No 10 into “his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks”. All right, grandma! She went on to point out that, assuming Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping had watched these videos, enemies of the UK would “see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country”. I have to say this was my favourite part of the whole saga, evoking as it did the tail lights of a ship that sailed decades ago when we elected a former head of communications at Carlton TV, David Cameron, followed by fake model-bus enthusiast Boris Johnson and highly perishable Liz Truss to the top job in this very serious nation. Good one, Kemi!

Meanwhile, Burnham himself had to put a certain amount of damage limitation into place. While it stopped short of an apology, it did involve a spokesperson calling the Balegde video “clearly not acceptable” and it being removed from the influencer’s account. And just when you thought it couldn’t get any better, up popped Nigel Farage with what read to me like a very ambivalent condemnation, indicating that he too – and it pains me to say this, since it plays in his favour – had found the whole thing hilarious. “I wouldn’t let them behave quite the way that it happened,” he said when asked if, were he prime minister, he’d invite influencers to Downing Street. “It showed a slight lack of respect for the place and for the office and was really very inappropriate indeed.” Lot of qualifiers in that statement, Nigel; we can hear you laughing from here.

For the rest of us, I suspect Influencergate has provided a brief, luminous break from real news. If it has a vibe of Michael Crawford on runaway skates flying down a hill – to cite a reference followers of Hamnett and Balegde probably won’t get – there is also a serious part: it’s entirely sensible for Burnham to court influencers in an effort to engage young people in politics. As a cautionary tale, we might look to the US and the disastrous decision made by Kamala Harris during the last presidential election not to appear on Joe Rogan’s podcast and talk to parts of the country old media can’t reach.

In Burnham’s case, the charge isn’t that he sucked up to political enemies, but rather that he engaged in a puff piece at the expense of more robust political interviews. (Hamnett opened the encounter with the remark: “I’m so proud you’re prime minister”, and it got friendlier from there.) And yet there’s no indication the prime minister will stop talking to higher-end hacks and, for my money, he has come out on top – partly for the sheer entertainment value of watching the Tories try to grab the moral high ground and partly because of a quality in Burnham himself.

At the top of Hamnett’s interview, with a bloody great neon sign advertising his podcast jammed into the Downing Street fireplace and the influencer sitting there in slacks, (Prada!) trainers and a daffy look, you can see something happening in Burnham’s expression. It advances, slowly, from affable, to sheepish, to what looks to me like an “oh, God” moment when he understands there’s a good chance all this nonsense will go south. Ironically, it’s the thing politicians dream of; an instant in which the audience, with a smile, thinks we can all relate to that.

They belong to Jerusalem’s past and present: meet the African Palestinians

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:28:29 GMT

Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited

Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure.

There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem.

A member of the community walked me through the Old City, telling me about their rituals and food. Every Friday, he said, they would gather in a courtyard under the shade of an ancient tree and have a group meal. I was surprised to hear the names of exactly the same dishes that would be gathered around after prayer in Sudan. Aseeda and weika, a thick dough and okra stew, scarcely exist anywhere outside Saharan Africa. But, as is the case with all African diasporans, culture survives.

Under occupation

The pilgrims became guards, groundskeepers and arborists at the mosque, and were leased two compounds close to the mosque, in which many remain today. As Jerusalem and all of Mandatory Palestine fell under occupation and annexation by what later became the Israeli state in the mid-20th century, African Palestinians became involved in the decades of violence and resistance across the region. My companion led me to the locations of the small historic homes of activists now long passed yet still remembered, through alleys and courtyards that snaked through the Old City.

A double marginalisation

This community describes itself as African Palestinian rather than “Black” Palestinian. They emphasise origin rather than race. They are strongly connected to their ancestors’ route from Africa into Palestine, driven by a particular cultural and religious pull. Their historical presence reflects a vast Islamic civilisation long defined not by nation states and capitals, but by religious and cultural hubs.

But there have been challenges. African Palestinians have reckoned with racism and marginalisation from Arab Palestinians. Those I spoke to described this as resulting from “ignorance”, and something that has receded over time. This small community has cemented itself as an enduring population in the city, its members are well known in its neighbourhoods, and their role within the broader Palestinian resistance is recognised.

Like all Palestinians, the African community is labouring under the pressures of occupation, economic suffocation, heavy-handed policing, and bureaucratic chicanery. Most are effectively stateless, occupying a liminal space as the descendants of peoples who came to Jerusalem at a time when passports and citizenship as such did not exist. They were classed as “foreign” during Jordan’s rule of Jerusalem between 1948 and 1967. Now, like all Palestinians from Jerusalem, harsh policies mean that permanent residency in the Old City can be revoked if they legally reside in or become citizens of another country (affecting those who may otherwise want to obtain citizenship in African countries). They face the same risks if they leave the city for an extended period of time.

Sign up to The Long Wave

Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world

after newsletter promotion

An unbroken chain of heritage

As I walked and chatted with my companion on the streets of the Old City, I realised that, to the observer, we resembled a father and daughter. We looked so similar in that particular Sudanese and central African mien. But we were joined by something more than our genealogical extraction: the reason we were on those streets. That sense of Jerusalem, and al-Aqsa, as places that, despite occupation, annexation, and militarisation, remain an integral part of our religion, culture and history. A repository of heritage and ancestry, and a site that will keep calling to our descendants in an unbroken chain – eternally claimed, eternally unrelinquished.

The bathroom’s wrecked, I’m soaked – but at long last the dog is clean

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 16:27:56 GMT

‘It’s the washing he doesn’t like,’ said the dog groomer sagely. Talk about an understatement

He knew what was coming. I don’t hold with the idea of dogs being super-clever. All the bum-sniffing, squirrel-chasing and obsession with balls and sticks suggest otherwise. But on this occasion my dog was on the money. I know this, because he disappeared.

We’d got in, mid-afternoon, and I’d put the bath on. The dog groomer was coming later, you see – though with my dog it’s more about shearing than grooming. What the job really demands is a bare-chested Aussie sheep-shearing champion, but there are none advertised in my area.

I struck a deal with a young woman who used to deal with him but left the grooming business behind. She comes out of retirement to do the business at our place, but only if it’s me who washes him first. “It’s the washing he doesn’t like,” she said, with feeling. True, that. “And especially the drying,” she added. True, that, too. Or too true, that. Whatever, I just take the afternoon off to wash him and let him air dry. So it was for him that the bath ran, and he knew it.

Carefully, I had prepared myself and the bathroom for battle. Beach towels got a winter outing, spread all over the floor. I stripped to the waist and put on Crocs, as they’re non-slip and I enjoy the slight vibe of a clinical environment, as if we were in an operating theatre. I say “we” but for the moment it was just me. The dog had vanished, having developed a sudden talent for hide and seek.

Impressive in its own way, but I’m no mug in the hide-and-seek department myself, so I soon found him tucked away behind the bed in the spare room. He looked at me unapologetically but without defiance. Miserably, with heartbreaking resignation, he made his way to the bathroom and balefully beheld the half-filled tub. “In!” I commanded. And in he went.

Instantly, the water turned black. He’s quite big and very hairy. I suppose it’s the downside of having a dog who doesn’t shed – if the dog doesn’t shed, then logically the coat just keeps on growing. And as it grows it hoovers up ever more dirt, especially at this time of year. The colour of the water put me in mind of the time our university football team had to follow the rugby players into the team bath at the sports ground. A memory I’d rather not revisit.

The weight of the filth in his coat seemed to act rather like a water repellant, with the shower and the shampoo initially struggling to find purchase. But I worked away, going to places no man should have to venture. He just took it, submissive, literally hangdog, his head drooping so low that his black nose was almost touching the black water. Every so often, ignoring my entreaties not to give himself a shake, he gave himself a shake, spattering dark water droplets far and wide.

We got there in the end, and, as he reached the point of sufficient soapiness, I praised him for his cooperation. My hangdog dog ignored me, remaining stock still. Then, as I reached for a jug to commence the rinse, he made a break for freedom.

If he’d waited for this moment of peak soapiness to make his move, the tactic worked. He wriggled free of my desperate grasp without difficulty. As he made for the door, I lunged to catch him but slipped on a towel. Away he went, haring around the place exacting his terrible revenge, rolling and rubbing his filthy soapy wetness on carpets all over the house.

Darkly comic scenes ensued, featuring a fierce bollocking from me and some barking from him, before he was recaptured, rinsed and rigorously towelled down. The bathroom looked like the aftermath of a mud wrestling contest.

As for the formerly hairy dog, he’s now all but hairless. I suppose he might feel the cold for a couple of days, but my sympathy is limited. And don’t worry: it’ll all have grown back by Christmas.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

The world’s coolest street? Is Heol Maengwyn in Machynlleth finally getting the recognition it deserves?

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:50:11 GMT

A Michelin-listed restaurant, designer boutiques, art spaces: this little corner of Powys has it all, according to Time Out

Name: Heol Maengwyn.

Age: The earliest written reference dates to 1291.

Appearance: The coolest street in the world.

I’m pretty sure I would have heard of the world’s coolest street. OK, it’s one of the 28 coolest streets as chosen by Time Out, alongside Corniche des Almadies in Dakar, Karl-Heine-Strasse in Leipzig and East Passyunk Avenue in Philadelphia.

I take it back: I’ve never heard of any of those cool streets. You’re not cool, but you’re not alone.

Where is this chic thoroughfare? Oslo? Helsinki? Buenos Aires? It’s in Wales.

Maybe you could be a little more specific? The country is literally the size of Wales. Heol Maengwyn (meaning White Stone Road) is the main street running through the ancient market town of Machynlleth in Powys.

I’ve heard of Powys. According to Time Out, Heol Maengwyn “takes the region’s rep for innovation and debonair dining and displays it liberally along two rows of eccentric Georgian facades”.

Debonair dining? In a tiny market town? Where have you been? Ynyshir, Gareth Ward’s world-renowned two-star-Michelin restaurant, is only about five miles away. And its Michelin-listed sister restaurant, Gwen, is right here at 21 Heol Maengwyn.

Perhaps I’ll drop in next time I find myself in Machynlleth. Gwen’s exclusive dining experience accommodates just eight guests a night, so it gets a little booked up.

In that case, what else is there to do? Heol Maengwyn is where “antiques stores rub shoulders with creative cafes and centuries-old pubs,” says Time Out.

Again, can you be more specific? There’s Waggys Records and Hermit Crab Coffee, plus bars, vintage shops, designer boutiques and arts spaces.

It sounds as if it might be too cool for me. The place also retains its traditions. The street has hosted a market every Wednesday since the late 13th century. And there’s the Victorian clock tower that gives Machynlleth its nickname.

Which is what? “The town with the clock.”

They might want to work on that. Machynlleth will take no lessons from you in how to market itself.

Any other points of interest? The Owain Glyndŵr Centre is dedicated to the military commander who established the first Welsh parliament on this spot in 1404, making Machynlleth the ancient capital of Wales.

How is the weather at this time of year? I’ll be honest – it’s not looking good for the weekend.

Do say: “I love Powys in the springtime.”

Don’t say: “There’s nine of us, mate. But don’t worry: we can pull up another chair.”

PIF seeking investment to fund infrastructure projects

JP Morgan appointed to handle the sale

Newcastle United’s owner, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), is looking to sell up to 25% of the club by issuing new shares.

The New York-based bank JP Morgan, whose most recent involvement in a major football deal was Fifa’s aborted attempt to sell off 20% of its commercial rights last summer, has been appointed to handle the sale, as first reported by the Athletic.

PIF is seeking investment partners to help fund major infrastructure projects, such as building a new stadium or redeveloping St James’ Park, and would dilute its shareholding rather than profiting from the proceeds of the share issue.

The state-owned fund owns 84% of Newcastle after the departure of the minority shareholder Amanda Staveley two years ago, with the remaining 16% owned by the London-based Reuben brothers.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Newcastle are the second Premier League club to formally seek investment this season, after Everton’s owners appointed the US bank Moelis & Company to handle their sale process last month. Last summer Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, sold 38% of the club to a consortium which includes the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

PIF sources insist it retains a long-term commitment to Newcastle, whose value has soared since it bought the club from Mike Ashley for £305m five years ago in a deal that has not proved as transformative for their fortunes as many expected.

Newcastle qualified for the Champions League twice under Eddie Howe, who also led the club to their first domestic trophy for 70 years by winning the Carabao Cup in 2025, but the Premier League’s spending rules have prevented the owners from investing as heavily as the competition’s other state-owned club, Manchester City.

PIF has also cut back its spending on sport generally, with the Newcastle share issue coming months after the fund withdrew its support for LIV Golf, which filed for bankruptcy this month.

PIF has also sold a stake in the Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal, is open to selling other clubs, and has withdrawn from a three-year deal to host the Women’s Tennis Association finals 12 months early.

Newcastle have been wrestling for several years with the issue of whether to expand St James’ Park or build a new stadium on an adjacent site, but have made clear a project on that scale would require external funding.

The club declined to comment.

Stick or switch? UK billpayers weigh up how to beat January energy jump

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:23:59 GMT

Despite dozens of fixed deals lower than next Ofgem price cap, many customers argue savings do not justify the risk

Energy bills in Great Britain to rise 26% in January

“I’m looking at the off-peak rate more than doubling, peak increasing considerably as well as the standing charge,” says Andy, who lives on Scotland’s west coast.

“I have an electric vehicle and an air-source heat pump and use a lot of off-peak energy. I’d like to stay with Octopus Energy … but there are better-looking deals out there.”

The retired woodworker is among the millions facing a jump in energy bills when the price cap in Great Britain rises by 26% in January. He says he “got lucky” last time with a “very good” 12-month deal, but it ends next month.

The new cap, set by the regulator Ofgem, works out at £2,166 for a typical annual gas and electricity bill – up £443 on the October to December equivalent. Yet, even though there are dozens of deals available to fix for less, two-thirds of households remain on the default tariff that tracks the cap.

So what is stopping people from switching? We asked for people’s views on why they plan to change provider or stick with a variable account.

For Andy, a big concern is locking in at the top of the market. He has switched numerous times to save money but with variable tracker rates “eye-wateringly high”, he says he worries “that if I fix now at an increased rate, prices could start to come down”.

The cheapest current fix is Fuse Energy’s 18-month deal at £1,754, according to the price comparison service Uswitch. That is £412 a year below the new cap, while the 10 cheapest deals are all at least £317 below it, according to Sabrina Hoque of Uswitch. Its data shows 41 deals are priced below the Ofgem rate.

Opting for a fixed deal is a “way to take control”, Hoque argues. “With only a 1% fall [in the cap] forecast for April, waiting is unlikely to bring much relief, and a fix also protects you from any further rise.”

However, if you are already on a fixed tariff contract with 50 or more days left until it ends you may have to pay an exit fee if you want to switch. The size of this charge varies by supplier and length of deal. They can be as much as £100 per fuel - so if you’re on a gas and electricity deal, it could cost you £200 to leave early.

Hailey, who is a London-based university administrator, has trawled price comparison sites but found that “all the notably cheaper tariffs came from providers I’d never heard of with terrible customer satisfaction ratings”.

“Ultimately, the savings on offer weren’t enough to justify the risk,” says the 36-year-old, who also has an account with Octopus, the UK’s largest supplier with more than 8 million customers. “My provider is reliable, and energy is too important to chase a great offer that might turn out to be too good to be true.

“The prices are getting all but impossible to manage, especially as someone living and paying for bills alone. But I really don’t see what I can do except cut back in other areas, because you’ve got to have light, heat, and electricity for appliances.”

Steve from Merseyside feels there is little point shopping around for a different deal because there “really isn’t much competition any more. They pretty much all charge whatever the cap is.”

The father of two, who works in education, says: “I don’t see that the government has customers’ needs first and foremost with these price increases. They are looking after the energy giants’ profits.”

There are certainly fewer energy providers – and deals – to choose from than a couple of years ago. The rise in global gas prices caused about 30 small energy suppliers to go bust during late 2021 and early 2022, including Bulb. The number of suppliers in the domestic gas and electricity retail market has fallen from about 70 before the crisis to just 17 today.

Annette, who is in her 40s and lives in Edinburgh, is “stuck” on a variable tariff. “I can’t switch because I’m in a precarious job where I can’t commit to a two-year contract as is usually required. I will likely have to move.”

She says that “paying sky-high rent” is crippling her ability to save: “I already don’t turn the heating on – in Edinburgh. It’s a miserable way to live.”

To help households cope with their energy bills this winter, the government will make a one-off payment of £100 in January to 20m households in council tax bands A to D. The 5% VAT levy has also been taken off electricity bills until July next year.

Rich from Gloucestershire thinks this is not enough. He says: “I remain hugely disappointed that the regulator seems not to be working on behalf of consumers, and that the government is tweaking rather than making the changes necessary to decouple electricity prices from gas, and challenge the profits of the suppliers.”

Rather than fix at a time when wholesale costs are high, Plymouth-based Nick plans to stay on his “no frills” variable tariff with Home Energy, having switched from Octopus.

“We’re planning on riding out the increase in January,” says the 52-year-old telecoms product manager who describes himself as “ultra cautious and tight-fisted by nature”.

“Octopus has a far more attractive user experience and the usage stats are handy, but ultimately it’s all about the tariff rate,” he adds.

“We’ll be OK. We’ll try to be even more energy conscious, but overall we’re counting ourselves to be fortunate enough to be able to absorb the increase.”

Is grandma asking rude questions at the dinner table again? This Instagram account can help

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 15:21:38 GMT

Life100 features the wisdom of two women in their 80s and has gone viral by exploring important life lessons

It is, unfortunately, a familiar scene. At the dinner table, a woman berates her granddaughter with invasive, personal questions – why are you still single? When are you going to have kids? – punctuated by unnerving thrusts of her steak knife. The granddaughter is clearly uncomfortable, but her grandmother pays no attention.

Anyone who has been in this situation likely knows what comes next. The granddaughter may try to deflect, only to invite further questioning, or call out her grandmother’s rudeness, which risks escalation.

But last month, in a popular video, the cycle was interrupted. “Stop! What’s wrong with this picture?” asks another woman, seemingly descended from heaven.

She admonishes Grandma: being close to someone does not mean you can demand such personal information from them! The grandmother apologizes, saying her granddaughter doesn’t have to answer any of those questions.

Oh, to live inside an episode of Life100, a web series in which emotional life lessons are served warmly but with a hint of irreverent humor, like Sesame Street for people who have to pay rent.

Since its launch in May, Life100 has racked up hundreds of thousands of followers and millions of views. Its two protagonists, Susan and Sondra, archly explore the frustrations of adulthood, and how to navigate it without being an asshole. Lessons include what to do if you’re catastrophizing, the importance of collaboration and how to ask for help.

In our age of isolation and weaponized therapy-speak, a careful, gentle and funny look at human relationships from two women in their 80s is exactly what we need.

The stars of Life100 are Susan Thau and Sondra Goldstein, both PhDs and licensed clinical psychologists in Los Angeles. Both in their 80s, Thau and Goldstein met more than 20 years ago, working at healthcare consortium Kaiser Permanente. Both specialized in attachment theory, which focuses on how humans connect with each other and the barriers to that connection. They have written a book, The Roller Coaster of Emotion in Couples Therapy, and created a film, Living Love at Last.

But though they were no strangers to presenting their ideas in public, they had mostly spent their careers speaking to other professionals.

“We began to feel that we were missing something because we were not part of the internet,” says Goldstein. They tried starting their own Instagram page, but it didn’t take off. For once, they didn’t know how to connect.

Conversely, Thau’s grandson, Weston Goodman, knows just what to do online. “Every one of my friends is on social media – it’s their primary form of media consumption. And yet there’s a shame around it, like it’s a waste of time or a distraction,” he says.

Goodman and his friend Mason Collins founded B6 Studios to work with the internet-based creators they found exciting. To them, social media was a new broadcast medium and they wanted to “create television shows for the feed”, says Goodman. They started with a surreal comedy fiction series called Forever Zone, created by Gaspar Cello.

At the same time, Goodman was trying to help Thau and Goldstein with their social media presence. (Conveniently, Goodman lives with Thau.) “Susan and Sondra come to relationships with a very different framework than my generation does. They’re very connected to their community and their friends, and I think they know what it is to have lifelong relationships, and the skills that it takes to maintain those,” he says.

Goodman conceptualized Life100 as a kind of internet home economics for a generation whose schools defunded the program, and thus never learned some key life and relationship skills. Goodman writes and edits the episodes based on topics Thau and Goldstein want to cover. Ariadna Thau, Goodman’s cousin, produces the series and sometimes shows up on-screen (she plays the granddaughter being interrogated at the dinner table).

Originally, the first few episodes didn’t get more than a few thousand views, but then came Empathy. In it, Susan’s friend, Carol, has just canceled on dinner plans, saying she’s overwhelmed. Susan is furious – she’s spent all day cooking a beef stew. She’s offended – her time and effort haven’t been respected!

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

“It’s a pretty universal situation,” says Goodman, but also one that’s easy to argue about.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Some viewers saw themselves in Carol, overcommitted and needing some me time. But others knew the pain of being flaked on, and began debating the limits of empathy for someone who never shows up. People began to comment and share the post. “Carol is dead to me,” wrote one, while others mused whether or not Susan should freeze the stew for the next time Carol came over. The video, per Goodman, got about 3m views.

There’s been a growing awareness of mental health as an issue worthy of attention. But as ever in the US, access to even basic mental healthcare (or physical, for that matter) remains tied to employment or out of reach. So it’s no surprise that, according to the Pew Research Center, half of US adults under the age of 50 say they get health and wellness information from social media and podcasts. However, about 38% of those health and wellness influencers are selling some product or subscription. And even if they’re not, many content creators scaremonger and employ therapy-speak to amp up engagement and followers.

Life100 is searching for engagement, but not for engagement’s sake, the team say. “We want to help build community, help people connect and confront the uncomfortable so they can become better humans, friends, children, parents and partners,” says Ariadna Thau.

And just a few months after launch, the community is there. Both Thau and Goldstein have been stopped in public and recognized for their work. Fans have parroted Goldstein’s catchphrase – “Stop! What’s wrong with this picture?” – to her. “It’s beyond my life experience to have somebody know me from something that’s not my personal life,” she says.

Life100 has covered what it feels like to not be listened to and why you should apologize to your friends. Though some of the videos deal with intergenerational communication, they never come off as scolding younger generations. Mostly, it sounds like advice to fellow older adults, reminding them it’s not just the kids who need to mind their manners.

In a recent video, Susan says she’s going to learn how to kickflip, then admits to that she doesn’t know how to skateboard. “Aren’t goals supposed to be ambitious?” she asks. Sondra explains that there’s a difference between a challenging goal and one that skips all the steps where you’re actually learning.

I thought of all my failed attempts to start a new hobby, where I figuratively and perhaps literally jumped into the deep end of a professional project, or tried a DIY project at home, only to wind up mad at myself when I couldn’t do it. It was so obvious that an octogenarian newbie should not try an advanced skateboarding maneuver at the top of the stairs. And, if I was being honest with myself, there were times when I also had gone too far, too fast.

The language of therapy has become second nature for the terminally online. We are constantly hearing about holding space, trauma dumping, toxic asks and being triggered. Sometimes this language is misused to excuse poor behavior or accuse someone.

“Humor makes all of this digestible. People would not take this in if it were serious,” says Thau. It’s also probably why the message is resonating. The lessons in Life100 are not new to many people; most of us can probably guess at the value of knowing, say, how to compromise. But watching Susan crash out over a jigsaw puzzle resonates because you too have probably totally lost it over something completely innocuous. And even if the emotions are real, you can see it’s also a bit silly to be mad that your friend has achieved more than you have.

“When you add humor, when you add action to it … that’s what stays in people’s minds,” says Goldstein. Your guard is lowered, which lets the message in. That connection is really what Thau and Goldstein have been looking to create in their entire careers. They were just waiting for the internet to catch up to them.

Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:59:44 GMT

Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

In February, the supreme court ruled Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs illegal. The court issued a narrow decision saying the administration had improperly used a specific emergency powers law to implement the tariffs, but did not broadly curb the president’s power to introduce new tariffs.

The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the new rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations.

Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January.

This is the second major batch of section 301 tariffs, after the White House announced a broad slate of tariffs on more than 80 countries in July, including the UK, Mexico and Canada, saying the countries had failed to enforce bans on forced labor. A lawsuit fighting those tariffs is currently awaiting a decision in the court of international trade.

“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said in a statement on Wednesday.

“President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”

Tariffs have proven unpopular with US voters, who handed Democrats a decisive victory in the midterm elections that will give the party control of Congress. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs currently in effect have added an additional $900 annually in costs for each US household.

The rising cost of living was the number one issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a Harris Poll survey for the Guardian. An earlier Harris poll found seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices.

Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, the Bureau of Economic Analysis announced on Wednesday, the highest rate since May and well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% annual target.

World has six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels for first time

Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue

For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned.

This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating.

The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days.

“This is an exceptional global temperature anomaly,” said Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the Copernicus Climate Change Service. “We have seen record global temperatures persist for several months now. While individual days fluctuate, temperatures at this level are a striking indication of how much the climate has heated.”

There have only been two other periods when daily temperatures climbed over 2C, in November 2023 and February 2024, but they did not last as long or climb as high as this latest spell.

“Another day, another global temperature record,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, , adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been “smashed”.

The temperature spikes are driven by long-term global heating caused by humans burning fossil fuels, and by an unusually large El Niño, which is approaching its peak.

The last El Niño on this scale was in the 1870s, when it led to a mass famine that killed 50 million people, Burgess said. Scientists expect the current El Niño to peak between now and January, though its full impact will not be felt until several months afterwards.

The extra heat in the global system is already creating feedbacks that worsen the climate crisis, such as drought and fire in the tropical rainforests of Indonesia and in the Amazon.

The UK Met Office predicts a very large rise in atmospheric CO2 in the coming months, largely because tropical ecosystems are growing less vigorously due to droughts, which diminishes their capacity to remove carbon from the atmosphere.

“This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning,” said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. “The CO2 increase from this year to next will be about 3.5 parts per million, a third faster than in recent years and nearly twice as fast as what it should have been limited to if we’d been on track to limit global warming to 1.5C.”

after newsletter promotion

At the UN climate summit in Paris in 2015, almost 200 countries signed a landmark agreement to “pursue efforts” to limit global temperature rises to 1.5C, and to keep them “well below” 2C above those recorded in preindustrial times. After the failure of this month’s Cop31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, the UN secretary general, António Guterres, warned of an acceleration of global heating.

This heating is making weather disasters more extreme and deadly. This year’s record summer heat killed more than 50,000 people in the EU and 5,000 in the UK.

Against the backdrop of the growing health impacts of extreme heat, Burgess said governments faced a dual challenge: preparing societies for higher temperatures while accelerating reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

“Our infrastructure is maladapted for our current climate. We’re already struggling and we saw that this summer – the roads were melting, the train lines were buckling, the schools were closed, the hospitals were completely overwhelmed, and we will only see more of that. There’s a lot more heat coming down the pipeline,” she said.

Betts shared similar concerns. “The immediate impacts of droughts in places like the Amazon can be severe, leading to forest fires with severe human health impacts through smoke pollution, and also damaging the ecosystems,” he said. “More widely, there may be risks to food and water supplies. In the longer term, the rapid CO2 rise is a reminder that we’re on track for ever more severe impacts of climate change until we stop putting carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.”

Steal a chopper listening to Liszt! I love how Grand Theft Auto VI went crazy for classical

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:16:09 GMT

Rob a bank to the sound of Sibelius, mow down an alligator to the music of Mahler … piano sensation Yuja Wang is one of the surprises of GTA VI – and her thrilling musical choices made me crash into a G-Wagen

I blame Yuja Wang for crashing my car. You know how it is, you’re cruising as fast you can on the freeway, listening to Symphony FM. And then DJ Yuja says: “It’s afternoon here in Vice City: for the worst of you, the day is just starting. Maybe the next piece will inspire you to turn your life around.” And then she played Tchaikovsky – the finale of the Fifth Symphony – and I just lost it to the music. The energy and tempest of the finale turned me into a driving maniac, and I ended up crashing into a G-Wagen down a one-way street as the minor-key maelstrom took over. Thanks Yuja. I’ll send you the repair bill.

Such are the hazards of discovering that among the 24 stations you can listen to in Grand Theft Auto VI – and not only in your car – is Symphony FM, hosted by the in-game Yuja, who really is the real-life piano superstar Yuja Wang. And in choosing her “favourite pieces and curating a playlist for players to discover”, she’s put together a set of 16 pieces that only she could have come up with.

She’s included herself on the list – and why not, in showstopping performances of Ravel’s La Valse and the finale of Prokofiev’s Second Piano Concerto – but gamers can also romance Jason and Lucia, GTA VI’s central couple, to the final movement of Janáček’s Sinfonietta; they can fly stolen helicopters with Liszt’s Les Préludes, rob banks to the elemental soundtrack of the last movement of Sibelius’s fifth symphony, or cruise the clubs with the first movement of Lutosławski’s Concerto for Orchestra, music that in-game Yuja says “would be the national anthem in a perfect world”. Most impressively, in one of the longest music cues in any video game ever, the whole of the first movement of Mahler’s Sixth Symphony – 24 minutes of it in the recording they’ve chosen, from Antoni Wit and the Polish National Radio Symphony – can be your choice of accompaniment to scenes in which you blow up your rivals, mow down some blameless alligators, or indulge in the many legal – and illegal – activities that GTA inspires.

Yuja’s hosting for Symphony FM is both very funny and scurrilously insightful. “Classical music has a reputation for being complicated and therefore better than pop music … It really depends on how drunk you are,” or “some people find classical music boring. Personally every time I press a piano key, my heart rate doubles. Doctors say this is not ideal.” And there’s this: “If you stumbled on this station, but want some heavy metal: classical music can be hardcore. You can head-bang to Stravinsky. I mean everyone head-bangs to Stravinsky.” That’s before she plays Handel’s “I know that my Redeemer liveth” from Messiah – and admittedly there’s no Stravinsky on the playlist – but it’s a good point.

This is the longest classical station that GTA has had in its history. (The operatic Double Clef was in GTA III, and there was Sinowav FM in some versions of Chinatown Wars.) We all might have different choices – couldn’t The Rite of Spring have been there; or Lili Boulanger’s Du fond de l’abîme, to hear the emotional consequences of all the mindless violence in the game? – but really that’s just me being persnickety (Apart from the fact that Yuja announces the Nuages movement from Debussy’s Nocturnes and then we hear Fêtes. We’ve all been there, Yuja …) Symphony FM is giving a massive potential listenership, in the biggest single entertainment phenomenon there is right now, the chance to immerse themselves in musical worlds that are as multi-dimensional as GTA VI’s seemingly infinite sandbox of immoral opportunity. It’s a brilliant use of Yuja Wang’s reach, and it opens up whole new worlds of meaning for classical music and gaming.

And those worlds are just beginning to be discovered: the comments underneath this YouTube video on how you might use Yuja’s classical playlist to accompany GTA VI’s story of guns’n’romance story are fabulous: “... a video targeting the most terrifying demographic of all: classical gamers” – guilty as charged – “why not? I use games to help me learn long pieces. Can’t stand Sorabji’s 8-hr bullshit? Try it with an equally long-ass game!” The commenter is obviously a fan of musical extremes: they mean the music of Kaikhosru Sorabji, whose works – most for solo piano – are epically long. He is in fact one of the few composers to write pieces as long as video games.

So yes: how about for GTA VI’s follow-up, Symphony FM broadcasts the nearly five hours of Sorabji’s Opus Clavicembalisticum or – even better – the eight hours 23 minutes of the pianist Jonathan Powell’s astounding recording of Sorabji’s Sequentia Cyclica? Yuja, over to you.

This week Tom has been listening to: as well as music in a game, I’ve been listening this week to music for gaming: one of the Nintendo DS’s last brilliant RPGs (and better in the original than the 3DS remake, IMHO) is Radiant Historia, a world of time-travelling myth and sublime grid-based battling. The world really comes alive thanks to Yoko Shimomura’s stellar soundtrack, which gives the story a melancholic grandeur in every encounter, making every decision feel momentous.

‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 12:00:56 GMT

The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali

Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states.

Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role.

The play also attracted a famous fan: the boxer Muhammad Ali. He came to watch it several times, says Alexander. “He said, ‘This is my story, all except that white chick,’ Alexander remembers. “And in many respects it was.”

The previous year, after refusing to be drafted to fight in the Vietnam war, Ali had been stripped of his world heavyweight boxing title and banned from boxing. The few times Alexander saw him, Ali seemed “hurt and angry – rightly so”. She remembers watching him once, unseen by Ali, after the show. Everyone else had left, except the stage doorman, and Ali wandered out on to the stage. He reprised the end of the second act, in which Johnson thunders “in a Hungarian train station thousands of miles from home, ‘You want me? You come and get me. Here I is. Here I is. Here I is.’ And that’s what Muhammad Ali did. ‘Here I is, here I is, here I is!’ to an empty house.” He walked off the stage but Alexander hadn’t “moved an inch. I was left stunned how much it meant to him. Beautiful.”

In 1970 a film adaptation of the play was released. The following year Alexander’s performance earned her an Oscar nomination and, although she lost to Glenda Jackson, her career was set.

The next 60-odd years saw a wealth of film roles: All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer, Testament. Interesting modern TV roles: last year, she had a guest role in Apple TV’s dystopian thriller Severance. And a lot of theatre, still her passion. “I love being in a room with musicians or actors, the collective experience,” she says.

Now 87, Alexander is speaking via video from her home in Canada, where she has lived for nearly 30 years. She also spends half her time in an experimental retirement complex on a college campus in New York, where the residents can take courses and mentor students. “I’m the only actress, but there’s plenty of lawyers, doctors,” she says. It’s working so well, with “so many cognitive and physical experiences going on”. “Hardly anybody’s died in three years,” she adds. “We have people going into their late 90s and 100s. We’ve filled up all the places, and nobody new’s coming in.”

When she’s in Canada, she is mostly outdoors. She walks her dog, sees friends. Birdwatching is her great love. “I’m out every single day birding,” she says. One of her current projects is working to prevent bird collisions, most of which are from striking windows and glass buildings. Such strikes may kill more than 1 billion birds in the US alone each year. But, she says, “it’s pretty exciting because it’s all human-made, and so we can fix this problem”.

Alexander has many good stories and is writing a memoir. But some of the best ones predate her. Her grandfather, Daniel Quigley, was a doctor whose patients included William Cody, the wild west showman known as Buffalo Bill. Quigley was interested in the use of radium to treat cancer, and established one of the first radium hospitals in the US. He obtained two chunks of the element from Marie Curie in Paris. “My grandmother had half of her brain removed in her late 40s – I think because they kept the radium in the icebox in the kitchen.” Quigley lost a finger to it.

When he died, Alexander inherited his unused radium. What did she do with it? “I buried it. I didn’t know what to do with it. I probably should have given it to the Soviet … Smithsonian,” she says, course-correcting her Freudian slip to refer to the US museum and research organisation rather than the Soviet Union.

We’d just been talking about Testament, the 1983 film in which she plays a mother dealing with the aftermath of a nuclear attack on the US. It was made at a time of prolonged cold war anxieties. More than 40 years on, the “Doomsday Clock”, set by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, is set at closer to catastrophe than at any other time in its history, due not just to the nuclear risk; it also includes the huge threats of the climate crisis and AI. “I just know that the proliferation of [nuclear weapons] around the world isn’t a good thing,” says Alexander. “Somebody’s going to use it some time.”

Alexander was born as the second world war started, and grew up in a Boston suburb in a medical family. When her father, a surgeon who had been away treating wounded British soldiers, came back, he took her to the ballet. “I just sat there, gobsmacked, out of my mind. I didn’t even dare speak because it was all so new to me, and I said to myself, ‘I want to be there. I want to be up on that stage.’” It was the colour, the movement, she thinks. “We had nothing during the war. We didn’t go to the theatre. We made our own little things up, but it was nothing professional, and high professional art is something that gives me chills still to this day.”

By her 20s, Alexander was forging a steady stage career, until The Great White Hope sent it rocketing. Her next film was a western, A Gunfight, starring Johnny Cash. “My gosh, what a man!” says Alexander. She became close to Cash’s wife, June Carter, who would bring their baby son to the set.

Carter once asked Alexander to accompany them to one of Cash’s famous prison concerts. “She said as ‘eye candy’.” Carter “was nursing the baby and was wearing long dresses. She wanted me to wear a miniskirt that was in style for younger women, and at that time, we did not wear bras. Believe it or not, this was part of the feminist movement. Be liberated, take your bra off. What was that about? All it did was attract the guys more.” She laughs. Carter introduced Alexander on stage to 4,000 maximum security prisoners. “There was an incredible roar. I couldn’t wait to get off the stage,” she says. “Then out [Cash] came, and there was huge applause, cheers.”

It must have been tricky to be an actor in the 70s and 80s, when sexual harassment was blatant. Alexander was aware of it, but says she didn’t feel threatened. When she was about 12, she says, her father taught her how to knee men in the balls if they came on to her. Alexander only had to do it once, with someone backstage at a theatre. “It worked like gangbusters,” she says. But the “casting couch” was a fairly overt part of the industry. “I said no thanks. A couple of times, I just laughed at them. But other actresses had problems.” She says some made the decision to use what they had to “to get their career going, and that was OK with me too. For many of them it worked. For those who are more vulnerable, I understand it does not work, and I’m glad the #MeToo movement happened. It had to come out in the open.”

In 1993, Alexander became chair of the US’s National Endowment for the Arts, the organisation that provides federal arts funding, after being nominated by President Bill Clinton. This was a time when there was immense pressure from conservatives to shut the body down, amid controversy about what art its funds were supporting. “It was a very difficult time,” she says. A few years earlier, there had been protests against grants for exhibitions featuring work by the controversial photographer and artist Andres Serrano, and particularly his photograph Piss Christ, which appeared to show Jesus on a crucifix submerged in urine. Then there was controversy around an exhibition of work by photographer Robert Mapplethorpe: “homoerotic, for the most part, pictures”, says Alexander.

She was, she says, “inheriting a volatile situation. I wanted to reach the American people, so I went on the road.” In just over a year, she visited 200 towns and cities in all 50 states, reminding people that art was for them, not only for the elites, and “in their backyard”. The organisation was set up, she points out, “to create expansion of the arts away from the big urban centres. It was so that every place in the United States of America could have art, or exposure to art.”

Public arts funding is always under threat – certainly in the US, where in Trump’s first term he proposed cutting all funding. Since last year, executive orders have restricted the use of federal funding for art that promotes diversity, equity and inclusion. Losing money, says Alexander, means “we lose a lot of people able to be exposed to art, and do their art”.

Individual artists, she says, “can’t be kept down. They will find a way to do art.” But the big arts companies, the symphony orchestras, “the more complex art, the individual art that needs help, those will be very tough to bring back. They should be part of a civil society everywhere in the world. But of course they’re not.” The arts will become only accessible to the wealthy. “That’s exactly what’s happened. Look at the price of things, the price of theatre tickets.” She gives the example of Broadway theatre: “It’s profit-making and tickets have gone absolutely bananas.”

No long, rich life is without grief, and Alexander has survived some crises. She and her husband, the director Ed Sherin, were married for more than 40 years and had four sons between them, until his death in 2017. In the early 90s, they were embezzled out of most of their money by their accountant. Then to lose Ed after decades together was, she says, “very, very hard. But he’s still very much right here. We talk about him almost every day in my family.” He was, she says, “a huge, generous soul,” and she misses him all the time. “But you just get on with life. Everybody tried to set me up with other people, but you can’t follow an act like that. I will be single the rest of my life.”

In 2015, her son Jace Alexander was arrested for possessing images of child sexual abuse; he was convicted the following year. The family got through it – including his wife Maddie Corman, an actor, who created a one-woman play about surviving betrayal and shame – by prioritising “support, and love”. Alexander took the view that her son was “sick”. She adds: “I’m not for one minute condoning it.”

This year, Alexander played the leads in two films – as a former CIA agent who spies on her neighbours in the comedy drama Lillian, Next Door, and in a Canadian film, Clara and Vanessa, as a woman married to a retired concert pianist who has dementia. “I loved it because it is so beautifully written,” she says. It was a change from most of the roles she started being offered once she turned 60. “You play judges, you play Alzheimer’s victims,” she says.

Alexander has no plans to retire, but she regrets that work cuts into her birdwatching. “There are two things that are incontrovertible to my mind: one is art, the other is nature,” she says. Both need our protection. “Those two things we can collectively praise and adore, and ask for in our lives. All people, everywhere.”

This article was amended on 25 November 2026. In an earlier version, a picture from All the President’s Men was said to feature Jane Alexander. In fact it featured Penny Fuller, who also starred in the film.
