Still racist, misogynistic and homophobic. I’m putting Britain’s biggest police force on notice – we won’t tolerate this

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 11:53:47 GMT

Another day and, despite all the promises, another damning report on the Met. There will be a reset: the public won’t be brushed off any more and neither will I

In March 2023, Baroness Louise Casey published her damning review into the Metropolitan police. The review – which I commissioned after a series of appalling scandals – called for systemic reform to a failing organisation unable to tackle the profound problems it faced. But yesterday’s independent follow-up report by Dr Gillian Fairfield shows that, while the Met has made some important improvements, nowhere near enough has been done. I agree.

Fairfield’s report concludes that the Met remains institutionally racist, sexist and homophobic. This will be acutely concerning for communities across the capital. So, too, will evidence of the Met’s failure to treat many victims of crime with care and compassion at the very moments they need it most.

Londoners expect change – and so do many of the hardworking officers and staff who, faced with organisational failures, find themselves unable to do the job they joined the force to do. There must be no cherrypicking or spin with this report – and the commissioner and his team must respond with humility and reflection, not hubris. The fact is, it is simply not possible to change the culture of the Met if the existence of institutional racism, sexism and homophobia continues to be denied, underplayed or tiptoed around.

The commissioner and his team must move much further and faster to proactively embed a positive new culture that recognises and promotes the highest standards, prevents misconduct and prioritises inclusivity and wellbeing, enabling them to attract and retain the very best officers and staff. The drive for reform must also reach the sealed-off spaces where change has been resisted and prejudice has too often been left to fester in the past – from toxic group chats to specialist teams working away from the public eye. There can be nowhere to hide for officers who fail to meet the standards expected of them – and top-to-bottom cultural change must include every custody suite and corner of the organisation.

The Met must also change its attitude towards scrutiny. We have already taken some significant steps to improve accountability, including the creation of the London policing board and the appointment of the capital’s first independent victims commissioner. But too often we have been met with defensiveness where there should have been openness. The Met must recognise that operational independence is not the same as independence from constructive challenge, and I am looking at how public oversight can be strengthened further.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

I now expect thecommissioner and his team to reset their relationship with those of us tasked with holding the Met to account. Recommendations made by successive independent victims commissioners, which have too often been ignored by the Met, must also be urgently looked at again and actioned.

The history of law enforcement in Britain is long and complex, but there is one idea which threads through it all: “policing by consent”. The authority of our police officers does not derive from sheer force. Instead, it stems from their ability to gain and retain the trust of the public.

When it comes to cutting crime, we have made impressive progress. In 2025, London’s per capita homicide rate fell to its lowest level on record. Neighbourhood crime is falling across the capital and mobile phone theft is down significantly year-on-year. The Met’s V100 programme has seen the conviction of more than 200 of London’s worst perpetrators of violence against women and girls, and in the two years to October, the force reports that it has doubled its positive outcomes – including arrests and charges – for rape. But the fact remains that successful policing depends on public confidence.

The Met must prove to all the capital’s communities, particularly those who it has failed in the past, and is still failing, that it has their best interests at heart. And it must prove it will treat people equally no matter their race, gender or sexuality, and protect them at the moments when it matters most. We deserve action, accountability and institutional change from the Met.

Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London

Raheem Sterling avoids jail over reckless driving while using nitrous oxide

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 11:34:10 GMT

He gets 12-month sentence suspended for 18 months

Former England forward must do community service

Raheem Sterling has avoided being sent to jail after he received a suspended sentence of 12 months for pleading guilty to a prolonged period of reckless driving while impaired by the drug nitrous oxide.

The former England international, who five years ago was leading the Three Lions’ charge to a European Championship final, stood expressionless in the dock as the sentence was read out by district judge Kirsty Allman at Basingstoke magistrates court.

Sterling was sentenced to 18 months in prison, reduced to 12 months, for dangerous driving on the morning of 28 May this year. He was awarded a sentence of two months for a failure to provide a specimen of blood for analysis, which is to run concurrently. He received no punishment for possession of a class C drug. Canisters in Sterling’s possession were seized and destroyed.

In sentencing, Allman found the first two offences to be of the highest levels of culpability but argued that Sterling’s charitable work, and his award of an MBE in 2021, acted as “significant and substantial” mitigation. Sterling was also commended for having voluntary submitted to addiction treatment, spending 12 days at the Banbury Lodge addiction treatment centre in June. Under the sentencing act of 2026, there is a presumption that any custodial sentence of 12 months or less be suspended.

Sterling must complete 100 hours of community service and has been banned from driving for 24 months.

Sterling was first observed behaving erratically at 1.30am on 28 May, when he was spotted inhaling from a large pink balloon while behind the wheel of his black Lamborghini Urus outside McDonald’s in Hayes. After a night without sleep, Sterling got behind the wheel again at 7.45am. Four police forces received reports concerning Sterling’s driving along the M25, M40 and M3, with one witness describing it as “absolutely horrendous”. Forced to overtake, the witness saw Sterling inhaling from a large white balloon.

On leaving the M3, the Lamborghini veered off the carriageway on the A327, crashing into the central reservation and causing “substantial damage” to the vehicle which “was no longer drivable”, according to Allman’s sentencing remarks.

Sterling complied with initial roadside breath and saliva tests, which proved negative for alcohol, cannabis and cocaine. At Basingstoke police station Sterling admitted he “had a problem with nitrous oxide” and went on to fail a preliminary impairment test. He was also asked to judge 30 seconds with his eyes closed but recorded 52. Sterling then refused to give a blood sample for further testing until he was accompanied by a lawyer.

Allman said the nature of the offences were such that she had considered the possibility of passing sentencing on to a crown court. “These offences are so serious that neither a fine nor a community order can be justified,” she said. “The custodial threshold is clearly crossed, and custody is unavoidable.”

Custody was avoided, however, after Allman took into consideration Sterling’s receipt of an MBE for services to racial equality in sport in 2021 and his ongoing commitment both to the Raheem Sterling foundation and the RS7 football academy. “I attach substantial weight to your personal mitigation,” she said.

“I further accept that nitrous oxide became a maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period in your career,” Allman went on. At the time of his arrest, Sterling had just completed an unsuccessful period at Feyenoord, having spent the previous six months training alone, excluded from Chelsea’s first team.

Speaking for the defence, Jason Bartfeld KC, described the incident as “extremely sad” and said for Sterling it was “a matter of his own intense personal regret” which had “tarnished his personal reputation”. Sterling left the court without making comment.

We’re in a flaking epidemic. No wonder no one wants to host gatherings

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 11:00:47 GMT

We point to self-care as we skip out on activities – but routinely staying home poses its own risk to our mental health

You might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely, especially if they’re young.

The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing. (For reference, chronic loneliness has a comparable impact on long-term health to smoking.)

And if you’re looking for a culprit, there are many to blame: the dissolution of third spaces and encroachment of car culture, the declining participation in social networks such as churches and unions, and the harsh economic conditions that have people working longer hours for less money with each passing year.

And data shows that sheer disposable income is not as strongly correlated with social life as one might think: we are often completely eschewing the budget-friendly forms of contact that used to be standard in favor of being alone and scrolling on our phones.

But, as someone who literally wrote the book on getting together, and doing so across all income and age brackets, I would like to posit another reason why the American social fabric has so rapidly dissolved.

It’s not just that phones make it more appealing to scroll aimlessly than to have a conversation – it’s that they’ve made us more selfish, less community-minded people. Nearly every time I post a video about hosting, for example, my comments are filled with the same refrain: What’s the point of spending all this time and effort if no one actually shows up?

And the concern that you might go through all the trouble of planning a party just to sit in an empty room surrounded by food and decorations is not irrational.

When I posted this recent video about the psychic damage inflicted on a host by no-showing on an RSVP, it quickly racked up thousands of commenters sharing their experiences with the phenomenon. I am tagged daily in videos of people who did what I firmly believe we all should do: they took the risk of trying to get people together in real life, and they were left feeling humiliated by the realization that their party was simply an inconvenience that could be tossed overboard at the last minute.

And with social media and party apps making it easier than ever to invite anyone you’ve ever met, and to perpetually “maybe” your entire calendar so you can make a game-time call as to what invitation you deem worthy (as this excellent Substack explores), we have entered a dual crisis. Fewer people than ever are willing to host, and when they do, it’s a massive gamble: who will actually show up?

While there are, very occasionally, legitimate reasons to bail on a gathering at the last minute, we’ve also gotten very good at leveraging the language of mental health to lean into our most selfish impulses.

We speak in terms of boundaries and self-care about actions that don’t just devastate the person on the other side of our unreliability, but also sap at our own mental health, as community is arguably more important to it than our own immediate comfort.

The truth is, whether it’s exercising, spending time outside, showing up to a social commitment, or opting for more nutritious food over some quick takeout, it is often in doing the less immediately comfortable or enjoyable thing that we are truly caring for ourselves and those around us.

And when it comes to gathering, the social isolation factor is very real: making and keeping platonic bonds is a skill, and the longer you are out of practice, the harder and more scary it becomes to start again. People are losing friends, and the process can accelerate until the entire concept of socializing feels like a threat.

It has never been easier in those moments to get under a blanket, make up a thin excuse for not showing up to a commitment, and reassure yourself that you have engaged in a powerful, therapeutic exercise by choosing to watch a screen again instead of literally anything else.

We increasingly speak of gathering in terms of self-sacrifice and effort, but, as this meme deftly satirizes, the thing we’re talking about – making friends and then hanging out with them – is supposed to be the fun part. It’s supposed to be the reward for all the work we do, both professionally and in our daily lives.

Instead, the act has slipped so far from our cultural routines in just two generations that we no longer understand it as a leisure activity. (The performance of ultra-perfect hosting and homemaking on social media doesn’t help, but that’s a subject for another day.)

Simply put, we have so radically devalued not just what it means to spend time with people we love, but to show respect for the people who facilitate it, that we have enabled a full-blown flake epidemic. And while I’m not willing to say that being a chronic flaker makes you a bad person, I am willing to say that it should not be acceptable – to you, or to anyone else.

There are so many problems to fully address our hosting and loneliness crises, but none are more immediately solvable on a personal level than holding ourselves accountable. If we say we are going to do something, it is our responsibility to actually show up.

No, it doesn’t matter that you don’t really feel like it, or that it’s raining outside: grab an umbrella, put on a smile (and maybe pick up a nice little hostess gift on the way), and go be a part of the community we all desperately need to rebuild.

Chelsea Fagan is an author and the co-founder of The Financial Diet

‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 10:00:11 GMT

Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’

The other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day.

The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it.

If you’ve ever fallen into a similar retail trance only to experience buyer’s remorse, chances are that you, too, have been ambushed by “consumption noise”. Since the rise in popularity of weight-loss drugs we’ve heard quite the cacophony about “food noise”, with users celebrating the welcome absence of cravings. In a similar vein, consumption noise can best be described as the low-level but relentless triggering of a hunger to buy stuff just for the sake of it.

“Consumption noise is everywhere. It’s online, it’s outdoors. If you look at the amount of advertising we constantly receive, when we’re on public transport, on the streets, especially in big cities, it’s a lot,” says Emilie Bellet, a former private equity analyst and the founder of the financial education platform Vestpod. This constant exposure is best summed up, she says, by the phrase “‘visual pollution’, a term invented by Marine Tanguy, the author of The Visual Detox. Then, of course, there’s online pollution as well. You buy from a brand one time and you’re on their mailing list, bombarding you with offers, which creates more temptation.”

I like to think that I’m good with money. I’m a thrifty Scot who agonises over whether to buy the posh butter or the Aldi dupe. And yet when it comes to marketing tricks, I’m pretty gullible. When I see a tempting offer online flagged with “only two left in stock”, I can feel my heart-rate speed up. Recently, this drove me to buy the world’s most useless slow cooker – it doesn’t have a timer. “I mean, even if it is true that the stock is about to run out, don’t worry. Chances are good that the item will come back,” says Bellet. “For me, the feeling of just putting an item in the basket makes me happy. I get a little hit of dopamine. And then after two days, I realise actually, I don’t really want it, or I’m busy with something else and decide not to buy.”

Bellet goes as far as using a Brick blocking device to remove social media from her phone in the early morning and in the evening. The gadget contains a Near Field Communication chip and works with a companion mobile phone app. You choose which apps and websites to block and tap your phone against the Brick to activate. The device is magnetic, the idea being that you stick it on the fridge so you can’t turn your apps back on until you return to the kitchen to tap it. “It creates more clarity, more space for something other than always looking at people trying to sell you stuff,” says Bellet. Another option is to pay £3.99 a month to go ad-free on, say, Instagram. “It sounds like a lot to pay but it’s a gamechanger,” reports a colleague. “Weirdly, now I’m free from falling down rabbit holes into fashion brands I can’t afford, I am drawn to look at the app a lot less.”

But the special-occasion buzz around Black Friday and its manufactured sense of urgency can destabilise the best of intentions. “We’re bombarded with these time-limited discounts; perhaps there’s even a countdown timer or warnings about how many other customers are viewing the same item,” says Aarron Atkinson-Toal, the author of a new book, Influenced: The Science of Why We Buy. “Suddenly not buying something can feel like missing out on an opportunity rather than choosing not to spend our money. It’s easy to feel overwhelmed by all that information, all the different offers, and so we start to respond to these quick prompts to ‘buy it now’ instead of carefully considering what we actually need.”

Atkinson-Toal identifies an interesting paradox. “Humans are generally risk-averse. We don’t like missing out on something. So with Black Friday-style offers we are forced to decide which is worse for us as an individual – the pain of missing out on the deal or the pain of buying something that you later realise you don’t need. More often than not, we make the purchase.”

This explains why even the most mindful among us can sometimes make unwise impulse buys. When I asked around for examples of crazy splurges, the responses were reassuringly plentiful. “I spent a fortune on an Alexander McQueen tartan mini kilt, inspired by Claudia Winkleman on Traitors,” says Ros. “I left it too late to return, and in truth I look ridiculous in it.” Buying for an imaginary version of yourself is not uncommon.

Social media marketing is particularly hazardous. “I bought a floor cushion sofa I saw on Pinterest,” says Jane. “Basically a load of big grey cushions masquerading as an L-shaped sofa. Stupidly expensive. When it arrived the boxes filled up my small living room – I didn’t take measurements. It looked silly and was incredibly uncomfortable.”

And then there’s that sense of needing retail therapy. “I’ve had a really stressful time at work lately,” says Dave. “Well, that’s my excuse for buying, in the past month, a Gibson Les Paul guitar, a pair of leather trousers and a mid-century modern sideboard.”

Situational spending – temporarily suspending budgetary rules according to where you are – can be especially hazardous. Airports seem to dial up the consumption noise by making us feel as though we’re not spending real currency: overpriced tins of biscuits, truffle butter and luxury brand eyeshadow palettes, as totally hypothetical examples.

The marketing language used around small purchases can be particularly seductive. “Brands have started using the concept of ‘little treat culture’ to convince people that buying yourself something nice will make you feel better. And if we don’t have the budget to buy big designer items offered by luxury brands, the smaller options they’re selling can give us a boost,” says Atkinson-Toal. “We’re rewarding ourselves with small purchases to make everyday life feel a little better because we’re being bombarded with all this doomsday news. So perhaps we buy a coffee on the way to work, or a fancy pastry. Maybe a small bottle of perfume or a piece of jewellery. Each purchase might be relatively small. But we’re essentially using shopping as a way of managing how we feel.”

His top tip for overcoming consumption noise is to stop shopping on autopilot. “The truth is that 95% of our buying decisions are subconscious. We all rely on mental shortcuts to make expedient choices. We might be guided by our emotions or recall familiar experiences. Or we might look to what other people are doing, like friends, family, celebrities or even strangers online. And marketers understand this incredibly well.”

He advises getting savvy with marketing tricks, and to pay close attention to selectively good reviews. “Happy customer testimonials or claims about 99% effectiveness are directing your attention away from negative reviews elsewhere. Pay attention as well to ‘priming’ – language such as ‘artisan’ or ‘handmade’ designed to make you spend more.”

At this time of year, as collective spending peaks, another factor comes into play and that is the influence of other people. “Consumption tends to be a substitute for social connection,” says Olaya Moldes Andres, a senior lecturer in marketing and strategy at Cardiff University. “Feeling part of a collective social experience like Black Friday gives us a sense of feeling connected to others, even strangers online. We are all highly influenced by what others do.”

Her research analyses advertising content to identify the most common hooks brands use to influence us, which we can be alert to. “There are five key things – first status and the idea that we can create an ideal version of ourselves. Another one is making life effortless. Third a sense of belonging, selling us a product that will help us to strengthen and develop social connections. Then there’s the idea of a product that will make us more capable. And finally, escapism and excitement, the idea that we need to have amazing experiences with intense emotions to take us away from our everyday lives.” It’s not so much a question of what we buy as why we buy, she says. “Brands are not so much selling us products as elaborate narratives about the lives we aspire to have.”

Moldes Andres suggests, before getting sucked into a buying frenzy, asking yourself if you are being triggered because you’re feeling low, “hangry” or another negative emotion that you believe shopping will fix. “Ask yourself if it might be possible to improve your mood or feel less lonely or anxious by another means than shopping,” she says. “It’s about trying to understand that consumption is only one available option to obtain the feelings you think your shopping basket will give you. The problem is that we have learned a core mechanism to seek happiness through purchasing.”

Instead of spending money, you could choose to do other things to feel satisfaction – for example, going to the gym, walking in nature or spending time with loved ones. “And if you can’t think of anything, it’s maybe time to start thinking about more sustainable alternatives instead of shopping.”

Listening to music is another way to change the channel, suggests Moldes Andres. Last year she ran a public engagement session at the Green Man festival where she launched a 21-day “buy less” challenge. “My favourite strategy to step away from consumption noise was to get participants to choose a song whenever they felt the urge to shop. The idea is that a song can lift your mood and it will give you two to three minutes to think about whether or not you really need to buy the item. It’s to stop the impulsivity and give you a dopamine boost.”

What if you are maybe a bit shallow and want to buy great new sunglasses to show off to other people? “My research has shown that if you are buying to fulfil extrinsic motivations such as to impress others or receive social gratification and admiration from the things we buy, we tend to get less positive emotions from the experience.”

Technology has made shopping way too easy, so one way to arm ourselves against consumption noise is to make impulse buys harder. “A great first step would be to remove all your stored card details from frequently visited sites,” suggests Bellet. “That introduces some friction because sometimes you don’t even have time to think, you’ve already bought it. Another thing I recommend, if you’ve been browsing for ages, is to change the environment. Go out, do something else, meet a friend. Try to stop this cycle of looking at things online.”

Bellet also recommends taking inventory of what you already own. “Say you’re tempted to buy a beautiful new jumper. If you know you already own 20 other jumpers, ask yourself what this purchase will give you. OK, you will look fantastic when you’re out at dinner. But then it will just join all the others. It’s also good to ask yourself if you need the new thing. I saw a Black Friday offer on a new electric toothbrush. They were 60% off. I said, ‘Wow!’ But then I reminded myself my old one still works fine. I decided to save the £100 or maybe to allocate it for my Christmas shopping. I also keep a list of items that I want on my phone and remove things I’ve lost interest in.”

An awareness of how much consumers are being manipulated is also useful. “Influence is more effective when the individual doesn’t know that they are being influenced,” says Atkinson-Toal. “Make a plan, before you leave home or go online, for what you need and what you are willing to spend. Question the bargain. Don’t focus on how much you are supposedly saving but ask yourself whether you’d still want the product if it wasn’t on offer. Because a 50% discount isn’t much of a bargain if you had no intention of buying it in the first place.”

However, he does acknowledge that having said all that, it’s not so easy to entirely avoid the hype. “I’d love to say that writing a book about consumer psychology has made me completely immune to marketing. But I’m still really looking forward to Black Friday.”

Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 08:01:09 GMT

In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions

Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human.

Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband.

Since it is ultimately about the video fragments in our minds, Blade Runner has, from the start, presented its conception of the future as more of a mood than a story. One of the many things Blade Runner 2099 creator/writer Silka Luisa gets right is keeping that allusive wooziness, prioritising images over details and vibes over the desire to build a complete, logically functioning world. It’s important to, uh, remember that before diving in.

But what images, and what vibes! Switch off all the lights and get drunk on Blade Runner 2099’s rich neons and fathomless, paranoid shadows, its abandoned spaces and urban centres that teem like an unfamiliar capital city too packed for you to find your bearings. Retro cathode-ray screens flicker; dangling wires and botched concrete hang haphazardly from ceilings; to a soundtrack that mixes shimmering synths with insistently soulful saxophone. Anyone unlucky enough to be alive in 2099, human or not, determinedly copes as well as they can with everything being broken, while dreaming of something better.

Our protagonists are Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a veteran blade runner nearing the end of her lifespan, and Cora (Hunter Schafer), a human posing as a replicant who infiltrates the blade-running operation and becomes Olwen’s sidekick. For different reasons that may not need to make perfect sense, both of them have the same quest: to track down Olwen’s former colleague/lover Marek (Johnny Harris) – who, along with a group of replicants, appears to have gone rogue.

Blade Runner 2099 is a fear-of-discovery thriller, with Cora constantly required to react to situations in an authentically replicant way on pain of death, and an Andor-style political allegory, as a fragile network of rebellious humans plot their resistance, swapping intel in rainy alleyways and backstreet bars. Like Andor, it likes to throw in a British actor when it needs a bit of extra irony or intrigue: as well as Harris there’s Tom Burke, Daniel Rigby and, as an inscrutable administrator who enjoys being unhelpful from within a scratched glass booth, Tim Key.

The striking visuals are indelibly vivid, from the backstreet pleasure parlour where replicants cosplay as humans, hiring skin suits with puckered flesh and distended pregnancy bellies, to the way humans placed under arrest have their heads smothered by sacks with built-in intubation tubes. Death scenes include a forced hanging after a crunching hand-to-hand fight, and an eerily pretty immolation. Every scene has something gorgeously unsettling.

As Olwen and Cora’s shared mission progresses, it becomes clear – not very clear, but as near to it as Blade Runner has ever felt the need to be – that their quest is an emotional one, since they are both chasing elusive memories. The franchise tradition for grandly philosophical dialogue, perched just on the edge of absurdity, is kept up: “You’re so alone you’re not a person any more,” Cora is told as she’s sent under cover, while Olwen’s summary of her own insignificance is a smart twist on the immortal “tears in rain” monologue delivered by Rutger Hauer’s dying replicant in the first movie. “I’ve been to the stars,” she says, wearily. “I know how small I am. Even the sun dies.”

So it’s not a laugh a minute, and perhaps Blade Runner 2099 could have done slightly more to conform to an episodic structure without losing its elliptical end-times cool. But its beautiful doomsday visions are unforgettable.

Blade Runner 2099 is on Prime Video now.

What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one

The Guardian Wed, 25 Nov 2026 07:00:09 GMT

Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health

Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel, sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above.

Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead. Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure”, and downgraded its sustainability ratings. How on earth did that happen? Beats me.

The society now gives bluefin tuna caught in the UK a green rating, which means the “most sustainable seafood option”: let the killing continue. Yet, as the government told me last year, “there are no estimates of the number of bluefin tuna in UK waters”. As a leading marine conservation charity notes, “it’s not yet clear if populations have reached sustainable levels that can withstand increases in commercial fishing pressure”. Which charity? Ah yes, the Marine Conservation Society. We also know that very large animals are especially vulnerable to population collapse and extinction. How did a “conservation” charity end up advising us to eat marine megafauna? What next? Eco-friendly whale meat?

Another group, the Marine Stewardship Council, slaps its happy fish logo on your packet of fish fingers, and you feel like a good person, which doubtless you’re trying to be. A little while later, you discover that your fish-friendly fish turns out, astonishingly, to be unfriendly to fish. Who knew?

Earlier this month, the council recertified Antarctic krill as sustainable, despite the fact that, once again, we know far too little about the likely impact of the industry, while the major fishers refuse to make fundamental concessions to lessen that impact. Krill underpin the entire Southern Ocean ecosystem, feeding the great whales whose numbers had at last begun to recover, as well as seals, penguins and other seabirds. The giant fishing ships operate among the major whale pods, and compete directly with them for prey. A fishery that could take down everything gets the blue tick of approval.

Macmillan Cancer Support doesn’t certify lung-friendly cigarette smoking. Age UK doesn’t advocate slaughtering elderly people. Why do our conservation and animal welfare groups (the RSPCA with its “assured” labels on slaughtered livestock is another astonishing example) so often side with the killers against the creatures they were founded to defend?

In the 19th century, the fishing industry claimed that ploughing the seabed made it more productive. Now we know that the seabed in many places was once as rich and complex and multi-storied as a rainforest, and that dragging trawl nets or scallop dredges across it, as has happened almost everywhere, smashes this delicate system, which can take centuries to recover.

But it’s as if the old myth persists. Perhaps this is why bottom trawlers are still allowed into marine protected areas, and why Greenpeace is left to do the job of the government, by dropping boulders on the seabed to try to stop them. But guess what? Fish caught in these “protected” places get the same sustainability rankings as fish caught outside them.

There are plenty of organisations trying to reconcile marine protection with the demands of the fishing industry. But where are the major groups campaigning for an end to commercial fishing? It’s never going to be good for the ecosystem, however it’s done, just as tobacco is never going to be good for your health. And surely, whatever we’re seeking to achieve, we should bargain high?

Instead, we must make do with calls to tweak the killing industry. Of these, the new report by Oceana is a useful guide to just how bad things have got. What it shows, broadly speaking, is that the bigger the boat, the bigger the problem. Inspections at sea of fishing vessels over 12 metres long found them breaking the rules 66% of the time, while smaller boats, under 10 metres, did so just 10% of the time.

The infractions are devastating. Oceana’s report shows that in 2025, an estimated 100,000 tonnes of fish from UK quota stocks, much of it saleable, were dumped dead or dying overboard. Why? Because once you’ve caught your quota of one species, you have to stop fishing. So if you’re targeting a more valuable one, you dump the first fish and carry on. The truth goes overboard. At least 80% of the plaice caught between 2023 and 2025 in the Irish Sea were dumped, which could be why their population is now classified as “critically low”.

This practice could be stopped almost immediately if governments insisted that every boat carries remote monitoring equipment, which is extremely cheap and makes enforcement very easy. But despite conservation groups demanding this for many years, all the UK governments still mostly side with the law-breakers against more responsible fishers. Why?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Oceana discovered that in the 2024-25 financial year, only 1.5% of the infringements discovered by inspections at sea resulted in a financial penalty. The total value of the fines imposed was £28,000: probably less than a single large boat makes just once by breaking the rules. Most law-breakers got “verbal advice”. That’ll learn ‘em.

Worse still, we’re paying for it. The biggest boats – which are the most likely to break the rules – also get the biggest fuel tax subsidies. Between 2012 and 2022, Oceana shows, an average of 27 fishing ships over 40 metres long harvested £230m in these subsidies, or £8.5m per vessel. The more damaging they are, the bigger the benefit: bottom trawlers use the most fuel, so they get the biggest subsidy. Owners of the large boats tend to be extremely hard to identify, as they often hide behind a network of shell companies. But they’re likely to be very rich. Last year the five companies with the biggest fishing quotas made combined profits of £125m. Why are we helping them to plunder our seas?

None of this seems to land, partly because we’re simultaneously being assured that by continuing to eat fish – including fish caught by subsidised, rule-breaking trawlers smashing up protected areas – we’re doing the world a favour. Why do some “nature defenders” seem to prioritise the fishing industry over the recovery of broken ecosystems? They too have become lost at sea.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

I’m a Therapist. I Wish These Patients Would Not Cut Off Their Family Members.

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Jonathan Alpert

Mr. Alpert is a psychotherapist and the author of “Therapy Nation.”

A patient sitting across from me was trying to understand why his son had cut him off and wouldn’t let him see his grandchildren. He hadn’t abused, threatened or abandoned his son. By his account, they’d been close for most of his son’s life. Now the son wouldn’t speak to him.

The reason? The father had voted for Donald Trump. I’m seeing more families like his in my psychotherapy practice. Parents aren’t just losing arguments with their children. They’re losing relationships they spent decades building.

The result of this month’s midterms might have been a blue wave, but America remains a deeply divided place. Many of the races touched on the toughest subjects out there — religion, immigration, transgender rights — and parents and children stopped speaking to one another over these issues. Some of my patients have worried about the approaching holidays, wondering whether to spend Thanksgiving, Hanukkah or Christmas with relatives whose politics they can’t stand. A study published in PNAS Nexus found that 37 percent of Americans surveyed in April 2025 reported experiencing a “political breakup.” Among those who had, 40 percent reported one involving a family member.

To some, a relative’s vote isn’t simply a political preference. It’s a rejection of fundamental values. A progressive daughter in Michigan may see her mother’s vote for Mike Rogers as evidence that the woman who taught her tolerance is prejudiced against Muslims. A conservative father in Texas may wonder how he raised a son who voted for James Talarico, whose abortion views clash with his own. Political choices have real consequences. But I’ve become deeply concerned about what happens when a political choice becomes the organizing principle for understanding an entire relationship.

A judgment about something a person did can easily turn into a judgment about who that person is. In cognitive behavioral therapy, we call one version of this “labeling.” “My father voted for Trump” becomes “My father is hateful.” Once the label becomes the person, contradictory evidence becomes harder to accept. A once-happy holiday becomes evidence of a family that avoided difficult conversations. Years of love, generosity and sacrifice may be dismissed as exceptions rather than evidence of character.

Political disagreements sometimes expose problems that were already there. A parent may have spent years belittling a child’s beliefs, dismissing concerns about discrimination or treating disagreement as disloyalty. In those cases, a vote may be the final confirmation of a longstanding problem rather than the cause of the estrangement.

But a ballot is a remarkably poor substitute for knowing someone. It doesn’t tell you which issues mattered most to a voter, what compromises he made, what he disliked about his candidate or how he treats the people closest to him.

Cutting someone off can become easier the longer an estrangement continues: The arguments stop. The anxiety before family gatherings disappears. You no longer have to listen to opinions that infuriate you.

In psychotherapy, we recognize that avoidance can be reinforced by the immediate relief it provides. That relief can be mistaken for evidence that estrangement was the right decision. But feeling better after avoiding someone doesn’t necessarily mean you’re better off without that person. Sometimes it simply means you’ve removed a source of discomfort.

I worked with a man who had stopped speaking to his father after an argument over the 2024 election. His father tried calling several times, but the son ignored him, assuming they’d eventually work things out. Then his father died. My patient was left thinking about those unanswered calls and the fact that their last conversation had been a fight over politics.

Some mental health professionals are making matters worse. After the 2024 election, the psychiatrist Amanda Calhoun appeared on MSNBC and said it was fine to avoid relatives who “voted in ways that are against you.” I’ve had patients tell me that previous therapists encouraged them to cut ties with family members over politics. This is where the therapeutic language of “boundaries” can obscure more than it clarifies. Boundaries are often most useful when they address behavior. Don’t insult me. Don’t use racial slurs around my children. We’re not discussing politics at Thanksgiving. If you start screaming, I’m leaving. Those are concrete limits. Refusing to see your father because of how he voted is a different kind of decision. It’s a judgment about whether the relationship itself should continue. That judgment may be justified, but calling it a boundary doesn’t settle the question of whether ending the relationship is necessary or healthy.

I’ve experienced political estrangement in my own extended family. I learned that a relative no longer wanted to associate with me because of my appearances on conservative television and my perceived political views. I often use those appearances to argue that relationships should transcend politics.

In my practice, I try to bring patients back to the actual relationship. What has this person done to you? How does he treat you? What happens when you disagree? Is he cruel, contemptuous or threatening? Or are you holding him responsible for everything you associate with his politics? Then comes a more difficult question: If his political beliefs never changed, could you still have a relationship with him?

Sometimes the answer is no. Some relationships are abusive or destructive, and ending them is necessary. But I try to remind my patients that it is possible to reject someone’s political views without rejecting the person. Cutting off a family member may feel principled, but it won’t change the outcome of an election and is unlikely to change how that person votes.

I think about the father who sat across from me, trying to understand why his son had cut him off. He could accept that his son disagreed with his vote, but he couldn’t understand how that vote had apparently changed the way his son saw him as a father. He remembered a loving relationship. He no longer knew whether his son did.

Jonathan Alpert is the author of “Therapy Nation: How America Got Hooked on Therapy and Why It’s Left Us More Anxious and Divided.”

I find this quote to be telling: "In my practice, I try to bring patients back to the actual relationship. What has this person done to you? How does he treat you?"That is the problem -- my morals extend beyond myself. I care how you treat everyone, not just me.

I'm all for trying to salvage relationships if possible. But too often that only justifies someone's views that are cruel and corrupt. My dad was a John Bircher and I spent a lot of time trying to understand his views. But he didn't reciprocate the effort and it was a thorn we never were able to overcome, although I still loved him from afar. As coach Bill Parcells famously said, " You are what your record says you are."

The error in this article is pretending that political polarization under Trump is in any way comparable to political disagreements in the past. His zero-sum-game, destroy your enemies approach, demonization of women and immigrants and refusing to admit error at any level is not comparable to any president in living memory. While I wouldn’t cut off a family member (completely) over Trump support, I’d completely support anyone who did. The sides aren’t remotely equivalent at this point. Anyone who supported Trump should be judged and held responsible for his actions.

Judges in Israel Suggest Dropping Key Corruption Case Against Netanyahu

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in a long-running trial that has divided the country. He denies all wrongdoing.

By Isabel Kershner

Reporting from Jerusalem

The judges presiding over the long-running corruption trial of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said on Wednesday that the attorney general should consider dropping one of three cases against him, in which he was charged with bribery.

The judges, who will ultimately decide Mr. Netanyahu’s fate, also questioned whether any offense had been committed in another of the cases. The move dealt a blow to state prosecutors and bolstered Mr. Netanyahu’s position in a trial that has dragged on for six years and divided the country.

The country’s attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, was summoned to attend the hearing at the Jerusalem District court on Wednesday and is the only one with the authority to make decisions on whether or not cases should proceed.

Ms. Baharav-Miara told the court that she and her team would take the judges’ suggestions under consideration and was open to all options, based on the evidence, according to a transcript provided by a Justice Ministry spokeswoman.

Mr. Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but interlocking cases. They center on claims that he granted regulatory favors and diplomatic support to business tycoons in exchange for gifts and sympathetic media coverage for him and his family.

Israel’s longest serving prime minister, Mr. Netanyahu, a conservative, has denied any wrongdoing, claiming to be the victim of a witch hunt by a liberal deep state. He and his supporters have long insisted that the cases would collapse in court.

“Today, the trial has fallen,” Mr. Netanyahu said in a televised statement hours after the hearing on Wednesday, adding that it “must end immediately.”

“It took 10 years for that truth to be revealed to all,” he said, referring to the beginning of the investigation into his conduct a decade ago. He described the judges’ remarks on Wednesday as “a ray of truth and justice.”

The judges’ comments come at a fraught political moment for Israel. National elections last month left Mr. Netanyahu battling for his political future after he and his allies failed to win a majority of seats in the Parliament. His chief political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and centrist, has been granted the first chance to try to form a new government by Israel’s president.

Mr. Netanyahu’s indictment and trial set off years of political instability as most mainstream parties refused to sit in governing coalitions with him, saying he was unfit for office.

Mr. Netanyahu finished testifying in his trial in June, leading the judges to take stock of where the proceedings stood, they said.

The judges emphasized that their remarks were based on their impressions of the cases and did not constitute a verdict. If the cases proceed, these judges would render an official decision, unless there’s a plea deal.

They said it would be difficult to prove the charges of bribery and conflict of interest in the case known as ‘4000’ involving a telecommunications mogul. He is accused of allowing Mr. Netanyahu and his associates to shape coverage on a news website he owned in the hope that Mr. Netanyahu would help him with various business interests.

The chances of conviction in that case were low, the judges said.

In another case, involving an alleged backroom deal between Mr. Netanyahu and the owner of a popular daily newspaper, which never came to fruition, the judges said they had serious doubts from the evidence presented that any offense had been committed.

The judges said it was possible to move toward conclusion in a third case, in which Mr. Netanyahu is accused of fraud and breach of trust.

Prosecutors said he had accepted nearly $300,000 in illicit gifts, including cigars and Champagne, between 2007 and 2016 from Arnon Milchan, a film producer, and James Packer, an Australian billionaire. The prosecutors said that, in return, Mr. Netanyahu tried to help extend a tax exemption for Mr. Milchan and to use his influence to help Mr. Milchan renew his American visa.

The attorney general, Ms. Baharav-Miara, said that the options in that case were either a verdict or a plea deal.

A year ago, Mr. Netanyahu formally requested a pardon from Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, with the backing of President Trump. Mr. Herzog instead offered to initiate a mediation process to reach a plea deal.

The attorney general expressed readiness for talks. Mr. Netanyahu’s representatives did not respond to Mr. Herzog’s offer, the president has said.

Isabel Kershner, a senior correspondent for The Times in Jerusalem, has been reporting on Israeli and Palestinian affairs since 1990.

A Thanksgiving Storm Approaches the East Coast

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Advertisement

The storm, developing offshore, is expected to move inland over North Carolina and grind northeast through Thanksgiving Day.

By Nazaneen Ghaffar

Nazaneen Ghaffar is a reporter on The Times’s weather team.

A powerful coastal storm is expected to batter swaths of the East Coast through Thanksgiving, bringing heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding, forecasters said on Wednesday.

The storm was developing off the Southeast on Wednesday and will track north before turning inland into North Carolina, said David Roth, a meteorologist at the Weather Prediction Center. It is then forecast to head northeast toward the Mid-Atlantic and New England over Thanksgiving Day.

While this is the time of year when nor’easters typically develop along the East Coast, Mr. Roth said, this storm does not fit that definition. Nor’easters generally remain offshore, with winds predominately from the northeast.

This storm is nevertheless expected to bring the winds, rain and flood risk typically associated with powerful East Coast storms.

Forecasters said that power outages and tree damage were possible from the strong winds, and issued high wind watches for parts of Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina.

High wind warnings, more urgent than watches, were issued for parts of New Jersey, Maryland, Delaware and eastern Pennsylvania, where some of the storm’s strongest winds are expected on Thanksgiving. Mr. Roth said that gusts could reach 60 miles per hour or more, including inland along the Interstate 95 corridor and into the Central Appalachians.

New Jersey’s governor, Mikie Sherrill, declared a state of emergency beginning at 6 p. m. Wednesday. “While this declaration does not restrict travel, I strongly encourage New Jerseyans with holiday travel plans to reach their destination today to avoid the worst of the storm tomorrow,” she said on social media.

Gusts of up to 60 m. p. h. are also possible in New York City, where the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is scheduled to take place on Thursday morning, said Dave Radell, a meteorologist at the New York office of the National Weather Service.

As of Wednesday, the strongest winds in the city were forecast for Thursday afternoon. Forecasters will be watching for any changes that could move the most intense winds earlier and overlap with the parade and its giant balloons.

City regulations say the parade’s big balloons cannot fly if sustained winds are above 23 m. p. h. or gusts exceed 34 m. p. h.

Mr. Radell said, “We will have one of our meteorologists on site working with New York City Emergency Management to help make those decisions about when or if any of those balloons can fly.”

On Wednesday morning, the New York office of the Weather Service upgraded its high wind and storm watches to warnings. While Thursday afternoon is when the strongest winds are predicted, the office stated that there was uncertainty in the timing, giving a window of “roughly 10 a. m. through the overnight,” on Thursday.

Soaking rain is also expected, with the heaviest downpours forecast from the Southeast coast through to southern New England.

Along the coastal Carolinas, especially Wednesday night, rainfall rates as the storm passes could reach up to 1.5 inches an hour, totaling between three and six inches of rain, the Weather Prediction Center said. The highest totals were expected near Newport, N. C., and Morehead City, N. C.

The heaviest rain is forecast then to shift north, into the Mid-Atlantic, on Thanksgiving Day, with widespread totals of 1.5 to three inches from around Delaware to eastern Massachusetts. The heaviest amounts, the Weather Prediction Center said, were forecast for east of Interstate 95. Rainfall rates could approach one inch an hour for several hours, especially from Long Island and points south during the day on Thursday. Farther inland, toward the Central Appalachians, totals of up to two inches were expected.

Tidal and river flooding

Moderate flooding could lead to inundation of structures and roads, causing some evacuations. Major flooding could lead to extensive inundation of structures and roads, causing significant evacuations. Source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Bea Malsky/The New York Times

Coastal flooding will be another major concern, driven by strong onshore winds, high surf and king tides. The threat will extend from Georgia to the Northeast on Wednesday and Thursday, with the greatest potential for flooding forecast along the Mid-Atlantic coast from the Outer Banks of North Carolina to New Jersey, according to the Weather Prediction Center.

Along the North Carolina coast, the combination of the storm and unusually high tides could produce significant coastal flooding, with up to four feet of inundation possible in some low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways, the Weather Service said. The worst impacts are expected to arrive with Thursday morning’s high tide.

Farther north, the Mount Holly, N. J., office of the Weather Service was warning of significant coastal flooding on Thursday, with one to three feet of inundation possible near shorelines and tidal waterways, along with the potential for major tidal flooding and beach erosion.

Coastal flood warnings are also in effect for parts of the Delaware coast, New Jersey and New York from Wednesday into Thursday, with additional watches and advisories extending into Friday.

The storm is expected to pull away from the Northeast on Friday, clearing New England by Saturday morning, Mr. Roth said. Winds will then ease across much of the East Coast, allowing for a calmer day on Sunday, he added.

Nazaneen Ghaffar is a Times reporter on the Weather team.

Lukoil to Sell Foreign Assets, but Not to Kushner and Witkoff Associates

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Valuable properties belonging to the Russian energy giant will be sold to an American-led consortium. But Middle Eastern business contacts of the two Trump envoys pulled out because of political winds.

By Eric Lipton and Anton Troianovski

Eric Lipton and Anton Troianovski have been reporting on the business deals that are being discussed with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia as part of peace negotiations over the war in Ukraine.

An American-led investor group has signed a $10 billion agreement to buy the international assets of one of Russia’s largest oil companies, a piece of the deal-making plan that the Trump administration has pushed as part of its peace talks with the Kremlin.

But the tentative deal announced on Wednesday, in a nod to the changed political environment in Washington, excludes business partners of the families of Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s two main envoys to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. The involvement of the two envoys in talks regarding Lukoil, even as their families’ business partners stood to benefit from the deal, drew bipartisan criticism.

The partnership announced on Wednesday is led by the billionaire investor Todd Boehly, a major donor to President Trump’s political causes, and his Eldridge holding company, along with Catena Investment Holding, a United Arab Emirates-based energy investor; and Xtellus Partners, a Miami-based energy trading company. The U. S. International Development Finance Corporation, a federal agency, is also a partner in the deal.

But the announcement on Wednesday excluded any mention of the Syrian-born, Qatari-based brothers Moutaz Al-Khayyat and Ramez Al-Khayyat, who are business partners with Ivanka Trump and Mr. Kushner on a planned luxury resort project in Albania. Participants last month had told The New York Times that the brothers were a part of the partnership.

The final partnership announcement also no longer includes International Holding Company, an Abu Dhabi-based investment consortium led by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the national security leader of the United Arab Emirates. Sheikh Tahnoon controls other funds that invested in a cryptocurrency firm, World Liberty Financial, started by the Witkoff and Trump families in 2024.

One person close to the negotiations, who had not been authorized to speak publicly about the deal, said on Wednesday that conflict-of-interest questions — whether they were justified or not — played a role in the change in the makeup of the investment group and that the Khayyat brothers and the Tahnoon-led investment firm are now out of the partnership.

When Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff met with Mr. Putin at the Kremlin in September, he asked them to get the Lukoil deal done as a way of showing Russians they can do business with the United States, The Times reported. The Trump administration has long argued that discussing business deals with Mr. Putin could help persuade him to mend ties with the West and end his war on Ukraine.

In the weeks after the Times article, people close to the Lukoil negotiations said that questions about the appearance of a conflict of interest — the deal could bring billions of dollars worth of profits to the buyers — created a cloud around the transaction.

Democrats in Congress also called to investigate the deal, among others involving the Trump and Witkoff families, once the change in power takes place in January.

The Treasury Department in October 2025 imposed sanctions on Lukoil in an effort to try to force Mr. Putin to end the war in Ukraine. The company’s international division operates in 11 countries and produces approximately 350,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day.

“Given President Putin’s refusal to end this senseless war, Treasury is sanctioning Russia’s two largest oil companies that fund the Kremlin’s war machine,” the department said at the time.

Lukoil’s most important international assets include three refineries, Burgas in Bulgaria, the largest refinery in the Balkans; Zeeland in the Netherlands; and Petrotel in Romania. It also owns hundreds of gas stations in New York, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

The deal must still be approved by U. S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. It is structured so that at least for now no cash payments go directly to the Russian owners of Lukoil or to the Russian government, a requirement set by the Treasury. Instead, the Boehly group has mostly bought up stock in Lukoil and other Russian companies owned by non-Russian parties to take control of certain pieces of the company’s international assets.

Benefits from the deal that could reach Russia would be held in restricted accounts for five years or until sanctions are lifted, according to the participants.

The involvement of the Khayyat brothers and Sheikh Tahnoon had become a major target for Democrats in Congress, including Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who repeatedly highlighted the proposed Lukoil deal in his campaign, citing reporting by The Times.

“Amidst a global energy crisis, the president’s son-in-law and the president’s business partner are brokering the sale of Russian oil fields to the first family’s friends,” Mr. Ossoff said at an October rally in Georgia. “The same friends who have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Trump family businesses.”

Representatives for International Holding and the Khayyat brothers did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday. Mr. Kushner also did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Boehly is a co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers and donated $1 million to MAGA Inc., the Trump-aligned political committee, in December 2025. He gave another $1 million through his investment firm, Eldridge Industries, to Mr. Trump’s inauguration.

Xtellus Partners is led by Paul Swigart, who for nearly a decade until 2018 ran the U. S. operations of Russia’s state-backed VTB Capital. He and other business partners then moved to buy out VTB operations in the United States, after the initial Russian incursion in Ukraine in 2014. The new company, called Xtellus, now does energy deals worldwide, including in Uzbekistan and Venezuela.

There is little public information about the other named partner in the new deal, Catena, but deal participants say it is based in the Emirates.

The U. S. International Development Finance Corporation would also hold an equity stake in the deal, meaning the U. S. government stands to profit from the transaction.

Federal officials, in discussing the deal in October, said the government was not planning to immediately put up capital to help finance the purchase. But its participation will help the deal win approval and reflects a series of recent moves by the White House to take equity stakes on business transactions, from nuclear power to computer chips.

The purchase of the Lukoil international assets could generate large profits once it is approved, since the assets would no longer be under U. S. sanctions as a result of the change in ownership. The oil refineries, oil production and gas station network has faced intense challenges and a lack of investment since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the Trump administration’s sanctions in 2025.

The fate of Lukoil became a topic of discussions among Mr. Putin and Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner during their Sept. 5 trip to the Kremlin. It was one of several potential energy deals that have been proposed — including using Russian technology to help export natural gas from the North Slope of Alaska and reopening a natural gas pipeline through Ukraine — that have been examined as part of the peace talks, although this is the first to move ahead.

The exit of the Khayyats and the investment group tied to Sheikh Tahnoon reflects a growing sensitivity among business partners with ties to the Trump family and their circle now that Democrats are promising to issue subpoenas to investigate these financial ties.

These kinds of deals over the last two years have brought enormous revenues to the Trump family from these business operations, including from World Liberty.

The Trump administration itself most likely wanted to curb concerns about those potential conflicts, said Thomas Glynn Hanley, the deputy director of the Europe, Russia and Eurasia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

“From the government standpoint, they want to be able to bring the most credible case they can to the U. S. Congress that they are taking these assets out of Russian hands and putting them in clean hands,” he said. “Despite that, Congress is going to have significant questions about this transaction starting with why Lukoil gets paid in five years even if sanctions are still in place.”

Eric Lipton is a Times investigative reporter, who digs into a broad range of topics from Pentagon spending to toxic chemicals.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Border Barrier Cannot be Removed for Decades, Texas Republicans and D. O. J. Agree

The New York Times November 25, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Just before Democrats take over the state government, Trump administration and outgoing Republican officials in Texas ink legal settlement barring removal of wire for 30 years.

By Zach Montague

Reporting from Washington

For three years, the federal government has been locked in a lawsuit with the State of Texas over whether federal agents can legally remove razor wire the state erected along a section of the southern border to discourage border crossings.

The lawsuit began under the Biden administration, when Republican state officials sued, claiming that border patrol agents were routinely cutting through concertina wire that the state had strung along a section of the border near Eagle Pass, Tex.

On Wednesday, the two sides alerted a federal judge that they wished to dismiss the case, after they reached an unusual legal settlement to end the dispute. The Trump administration has agreed with Texas’ outgoing state Republican leaders that both sides will be barred from removing razor wire along the Del Rio sector of the border — between Laredo and Big Bend, Tex. — for the next 30 years.

The extraordinary arrangement comes less than two months before Texas’ Republican governor, Greg Abbott, and attorney general, Ken Paxton, will be replaced by Democrats who won the November election.

It was the latest example of a legal tactic that the Trump administration has used repeatedly, in which the administration has reached settlements with friendly adversaries, with both sides agreeing to limit the government’s powers far beyond their time in office, locking in shared political goals.

Democrats decisively swept into nearly every statewide office in Texas during the midterm elections. But the settlement, signed on Nov. 19, would bar “all successors” to the officials named in the document from removing concertina-wire barriers, except in narrow circumstances.

That would include future senior officials in the Justice Department and the Homeland Security Department no matter who wins the presidency in future elections, as well as Gina Hinojosa, Texas’ incoming Democratic governor, and Nathan Johnson, who will become attorney general. It also applied to subcontractors and “all those in active concert and participation” with the government.

Spokesmen for Ms. Hinojosa and Mr. Johnson declined to comment this week. But Tom Jawetz, a former deputy general counsel at the Homeland Security Department, said Mr. Abbott and Mr. Paxton “simply gave away the state’s ability to decide what to do with all of this concertina wire that it owns.”

Mr. Jawetz, who served under President Joseph R. Biden, said he worried the agreement would make it harder for Border Patrol agents to save people drowning in the river.

“There is no reasonable justification for tying Texas’ hands to mitigate those dangers or to otherwise decide to remove its own razor wire,” he said.

The Justice Department, Mr. Abbott and Mr. Paxton did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Paxton’s office sued the federal government in 2023, claiming that border patrol agents under former Mr. Biden had unlawfully cut Texas’ concertina wire. The state alleged that immigration agents were working “to encourage and assist thousands of aliens to illegally cross the Rio Grande and enter Texas” by destroying the barriers.

The lawsuit followed a power struggle between the state and the federal government amid a wave of immigration, in which thousands of people crossed the Rio Grande and arrived in Eagle Pass over the span of several days. The Homeland Security Department argued that agents handling the surge needed the authority to cut the wire to gain access to the riverbank, particularly to process crowds and respond to emergencies.

A number of migrants drowned while crossing in the weeks before the lawsuit was filed, and border patrol agents rescued dozens of people as the surge grew.

Judge Alia Moses, a Federal District Court judge in the Western District of Texas, sided with the Biden administration. While she harshly criticized the Biden administration’s immigration policy as chaotic, and “dysfunctional and flawed” she nonetheless found that immigration officials handling border enforcement had not broken the law by cutting through the state’s concertina wire.

The decision was initially reversed by the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in December 2023, largely barring the federal government from removing the wire. But the next month, the Supreme Court sided with the Biden administration on an emergency basis, agreeing in a 5-4 vote that the federal government could keep cutting the wire as litigation over the issue proceeded.

The federal government has been barred from removing the wire since November 2024, after a three-judge panel of the Fifth Circuit again sided with Texas by a 2-1 vote.

In the joint filing on Wednesday, the Justice Department and attorneys for Mr. Paxton and Mr. Abbott asked Judge Moses to dismiss the case, in light of the settlement agreement.

Under the agreement, both sides agreed the wire could still be cut or removed in some limited circumstances, including to “administer emergency aid” to help someone facing “imminent death.” But it will otherwise bar not only the federal government but also all future state officials from cutting, removing or interfering with dozens of miles of concertina wire the state laid during Mr. Abbott’s tenure.

The only apparent exception under the agreement would be if Texas officials removed existing wire with the “prior written consent” of the Homeland Security Department.

Judge Moses, an appointee of former President George W. Bush, now has 60 days to decide whether to accept the settlement and dismiss the case. If she does, the court would be assigned to enforce the settlement. If Judge Moses declines to dismiss the case or to maintain jurisdiction, the agreement would be void.

The settlement was signed on the Trump administration’s side by Stanley Woodward Jr., the third most senior official at the Justice Department. It came after months of legal jockeying by Mr. Abbott and Mr. Paxton over which of them should sign on behalf of the state.

In a filing in August, lawyers for Mr. Abbott moved to intervene in the case, arguing that only the governor could “bind Texas in agreements with the United States.” Mr. Paxton’s office resisted the change, indicating that the attorney general’s office had the power to ink the deal.

“The only reason that this settlement has not been finally memorialized and the case resolved has been the efforts of the general counsel of the governor to involve himself in a case in which the governor is not party,” Mr. Paxton’s office wrote in a filing in September.

Ultimately attorneys for both men signed on to the final document.

The agreement mirrored several others in which the Trump administration signed binding settlements with ideological allies in Texas and Florida. While some legal experts have criticized the arrangements as collusive, Republican-appointed judges have approved such agreements and agreed they could be enforced by the courts, if either the federal government or the state strays from the terms of the settlement in the future.

In February, the Trump administration entered into a consent decree with Florida, in which the Department of Homeland Security gave up one of its authorities to admit immigrants for 15 years.

Last year, Mr. Paxton also settled with the Trump administration to invalidate a Texas law that allowed undocumented migrants to pay in-state tuition at public universities. The settlement meant the law, which had been adopted on a bipartisan basis, was dissolved, even though the Texas legislature had tried and failed to repeal it.

Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.
