The Ensemble Cast of a New York Sitcom Is Suddenly Running the Country

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Kurt Andersen

Mr. Andersen is the author of the novel “The Breakup” and a longtime New Yorker.

Saul Steinberg’s New Yorker cover showing the detailed contours of Manhattan’s West Side in the foreground and across the Hudson River a compressed, denuded, inconsequential America remains the perfect depiction of New Yorkers’ parochial self-satisfaction, our collective certainty that we live at the epicenter of everything and everyone important. Since the illustration’s debut in 1976, the city’s miraculous reduction in crime and return to prosperity have only reinforced its inhabitants’ sense of primacy in finance, media, fashion, publishing, visual art, the performing arts, food, coolness.

Suddenly and improbably, however, New York finds itself at the center of a realm in which it is usually marginal: national politics and governing. The enormous incoming Democratic majority in the House of Representatives voted last week to nominate the Brooklynite Hakeem Jeffries as speaker. His fellow Brooklynite Charles Schumer hasn’t yet been elected Senate majority leader but is heavily favored to win that vote next week. As mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani has emerged as a national power broker who engineered the election of three of the city’s new House members and became a model for several victorious candidates in other cities. His fellow leader of the American left Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of Queens and the Bronx is a serious contender for the Democratic presidential nomination.

Mr. Jeffries will be the first speaker of the House from New York City. As for a quadfecta like this, there’s almost nothing to compare it to in U. S. history. And, of course, for the next two years they’ll all be arrayed against the son of Queens in the White House.

It’s not simply a cute I ❤️ NY coincidence; it’s politically consequential. These leaders’ overlapping constituencies and deep mutual familiarity add to their potential collective power.

Half of Mr. Jeffries’s House district was the heart of Mr. Schumer’s district when he was a House member; the two men, both Democratic centrists, have known and worked with each other for two decades. An aspirational model for the two of them could be the supersuccessful Texas Democrat tag team of Lyndon Johnson (Senate majority leader) and Sam Rayburn (speaker of the House) before Johnson became vice president in 1961.

And then there’s the 80-year-old right-wing president’s curious crush on the 35-year-old left-wing mayor, a case of New York rizz recognizing New York rizz that Mr. Mamdani exploits whenever he can. On a visit to the Oval Office in February, he got the president excited about a 12,000-unit affordable housing project in Queens for which he wants $21 billion in federal funding — and also got a Columbia undergraduate sprung from ICE detention. Two weeks ago, the mayor had a real policy win, bipartisan to boot, persuading President Trump to delay the enforcement of a nationwide bodega rule, which requires small grocery stores that accept food stamps to carry lots more fresh, healthy food.

In our attention-economy age, putting on a good show is more essential than ever to political success. Having this New York City Gang of Four will make for a more compelling national narrative, a political advantage at this moment of Democratic ascendancy.

As the capital of American news media and the repository of a surfeit of main character energy, New York is a natural platform for national stardom. Mr. Trump, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez and Mr. Mamdani, in addition to having all lived in or represented Queens, were anti-establishment populist outsiders with uncanny performance skills who astonished the world by winning impossible elections.

Moreover, they’re all where they are now because they’re New Yorkers. Mr. Trump’s unshakable New Yorkness — and his history as a high-living, insatiably self-promoting Manhattan real estate developer — launched him to TV stardom, without which he’d never have become president. If Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had beaten an incumbent Democratic House member in Miami or Seattle, it might have taken her longer to become a household name. And if Mr. Mamdani had been elected mayor of a city like Austin or Columbus? Fuggedaboudit.

Devoid of charisma and connection to the zeitgeist, Mr. Schumer and Mr. Jeffries are products of the unglamorous side of Gotham. They are stock characters in every New York ensemble production: the older Jewish guy who’s got an answer for everything and the competent, middle-aged Black guy who’s just trying to do his job. Their two sexy, young upstart co-stars — South Asian hip-hop nerd! Latina bartender! — and the narcissistic, self-deluding old billionaire round out the production perfectly.

Central casting, as the president likes to say. Audiences will be on the edge of their seats for the end of Act I to see if Ms. Ocasio-Cortez elbows Mr. Schumer out of the Senate seat he’ll have held for more than 28 years.

All five politicians have in common a distinctly New York appetite for hardball pragmatism. Mr. Jeffries’s and Mr. Schumer’s lack of any shake-it-up anti-establishment instinct is what led them to become congressional leaders. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez arrived in Washington as an insurgent, joining a leftist sit-in in then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office, but she fairly quickly turned into a canny team player. She ended up voting for Ms. Pelosi for speaker and this time around seems to have acquiesced to Mr. Jeffries’s candidacy early on, despite the objections of some fellow progressives.

As a candidate, Mr. Mamdani wisely disavowed the problematic “defund the police” stance he once espoused. Since taking office, he’s hired plenty of establishment Democrats to work in his administration, and on Fox News the other day, he blithely disavowed several far-left positions.

Exhibiting a different strain of pragmatism, like most Democratic leaders of his generation, Mr. Schumer has been extremely friendly to Wall Street and the very rich. And who was one of the biggest donors to Democratic candidates in this election cycle? Michael Bloomberg, New York City’s former mayor, a former Republican and an unapologetic billionaire.

The New York style doesn’t always play in the heartland — a fact relevant for Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s possible presidential candidacy. But for now, in Congress, it’s just what Democrats need to break through the stalemate and bring a little star power to a pettifogging institution. Indeed, in their New Yorky way, the city’s national political players embody the new big-tent approach that allowed the Democratic Party to achieve its huge new congressional majorities.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez and Mr. Mamdani are devoted supporters of the Palestinian cause, whereas Mr. Schumer and Mr. Jeffries have been reliable supporters of Israel. That’s New York City, a place where lack of conformity is the whole point and diversity is the status quo.

Like America, the city is too big, too much a hodgepodge to fit any narrow political stereotype. Of the 13 House members who’ll represent New Yorkers in the new Congress, one is a Republican, three are moderates, half are various shades of mainstream liberal, and three are members of the Democratic Socialists of America. As for the mold-breaking mayor, he’s governing like an old-fashioned progressive of the Franklin Delano Roosevelt type.

Speaking of Roosevelt, the last time a comparable convergence of New York City and Washington politics occurred was in the 1930s, another great inflection-point moment in history. The president had a team of fellow New Yorkers as his key New Deal architects — Frances Perkins, Harry Hopkins and Henry Morgenthau in the administration; Robert Wagner in the Senate; and Mr. Mamdani’s favorite mayor, Fiorello La Guardia, leading the city but speaking to the nation.

Today, in place of the Great Depression, we have crisis-level economic inequality, insecurity and unaffordability. Instead of electrification, telecommunications and nuclear fission that were transforming the nation in the 1930s and ’40s, we have the digital revolution and its artificial intelligence apotheosis. And then as now, we have a disturbing new world disorder. Here’s hoping New York’s new Gang of Four can steer us to a New Deal equivalent without a third world war.

I don't much care where our leaders come from—if they actually lead. Reform health care. Raise the minimum wage. Make affordable housing worth building. Underwrite renewable energy. (Yes, that's a platform, not a slogan.)I have no use for vibes or rizz. I want to pay my bills, and I want my grandchildren to prosper, to vote, and to take part in a democracy that still works for the rest of us. That isn't too much to ask of people we pay to govern. Perhaps it's time they remembered who the "public" in public servant is.

Dems will need Schumer's knowledge to fight Trump's attempts to bypass Congress. Sadly Chris Van Hollen doesn't have that. Schumer should lave in 2028.

Schumer and Jeffries may have New York-y-ness but where’s the plan? They’re talking about picking new leadership and raising the minimum wage. Even with their N. Y. state of mind and unique brand of moxie they’re still taking the victory lap from the midterms. If they’re hustlers let’s see it. This country needs major reform and there is a massive legislative punch list after Trump’s dismantling of democratic institution, political oversight, and blatant corruption. No time like the present.

"The New York style doesn’t always play in the heartland."Here, let me fix it for you: The New York style rarely plays in the heartland, and if we could change the Democratic leadership, we would.

Kurt Andersen is the author of the novel “The Breakup.”

Mamdani Wins Against Landlords in Rent Freeze Lawsuit

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

A Manhattan judge handed a victory to Mayor Zohran Mamdani by dismissing a lawsuit filed by landlords over a rent freeze for rent-stabilized apartments.

By Mihir Zaveri

Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s successful push to freeze rents on nearly one million rent-stabilized apartments in New York City survived a legal challenge Wednesday, when a judge sided with the mayor over landlords who had sought to undo one of his signature programs.

The judge, Brendan T. Lantry of State Supreme Court in Manhattan, dismissed the lawsuit in a 20-page decision that was published on Wednesday.

The decision was yet another legal victory for the mayor, who earlier this month prevailed in an appeals court in a case challenging a contentious tax on second homes in New York City.

Mr. Mamdani said in a statement on Wednesday that the decision was a “victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in.”

“Because housing is not a luxury,” Mr. Mamdani said. “It is a basic necessity.”

Justice Lantry acknowledged that his review was not focused on whether the rent freeze was “wise or if it may cause negative collateral consequences to the overall real estate market.” He also wrote that Mr. Mamdani’s promises during the mayoral campaign to “freeze the rent” were “reckless and irresponsible.” But he said those campaign statements were “inconsequential” to the legal case, which focused on the legality of the freeze.

Mr. Mamdani’s campaign promise became a rallying cry for his supporters, representing his focus on affordability as many New Yorkers struggle to keep up with the rising costs of housing and other essentials.

But it drew the ire of landlords and some housing experts, who said the slogan played down the serious economic challenges facing the owners of many rent-stabilized buildings. They argued that given the increasing financial burden of insurance, building upkeep, taxes and other costs, a rent freeze would hurt landlords’ ability to properly maintain their properties.

In February, Mr. Mamdani appointed six members to the Rent Guidelines Board, the nine-person panel that decides annually whether to increase rents in rent-stabilized homes and by how much.

At the end of June, the board voted in favor of the freeze, halting rent increases on both one- and two-year leases for the first time in its nearly 60-year history. (The board has frozen rents just on one-year leases a few times before, including in 2015, 2016, 2020 and the first half of 2021.) The freeze applies to leases that started on or after Oct. 1.

Pro-landlord groups immediately denounced the vote. Critics have said the board is too willing to do the current mayor’s bidding and is not living up to its mandate to be independent.

On July 22, several landlords sued, saying the board had ignored landlords’ financial challenges and had relied on limited and sometimes outdated data. One of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs is Randy Mastro, a former first deputy mayor under Eric Adams and a critic of Mr. Mamdani.

Mr. Mastro did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It was not clear whether the landlords would appeal.

The Legal Aid Society and Legal Services New York City, two nonprofit groups that were involved in the case and supported the freeze, said in a joint statement on Wednesday that they were “gratified” by the result.

“Today’s ruling is a victory for millions of rent-stabilized tenants across New York City,” they said. “After shouldering multiple consecutive years of rent increases, these tenants — the majority of whom are low-income or working-class New Yorkers — will finally be provided with the long overdue relief they need and deserve."

Rent stabilization is a mid-20th-century program that is meant to keep rents from spiking sharply. Nearly one million New York City apartments, or about 40 percent of all rentals, are rent-stabilized. They typically are cheaper than market-rate units.

Most of the city’s stabilized apartments were built before 1974, but a growing number of newly constructed buildings contain some stabilized units because of separate agreements between their developers and the city.

These apartments are the source of major political tension. Landlords claim that financial pressures are driving them to hold units off the market. The City Council is pushing a bill to analyze why so many units are vacant.

Mihir Zaveri covers housing in the New York City region for The Times.

Stocks Slump Again as Investors Fret About A. I., Tariffs and Inflation

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Advertisement

Nvidia and other tech companies fell as investors weighed developments in global trade and the path of interest rates.

By Jason Karaian and Joe Rennison

The steady sell-off in U. S. stocks resumed on Wednesday, pointing to investors’ lingering worries about the artificial intelligence boom despite Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia earlier in the week.

The S&P 500 dropped as much as 3.2 percent on Wednesday morning before rallying to a more modest 0.2 percent fall. The Nasdaq Composite, which tracks the biggest tech companies, fell as much as 4.6 percent before rebounding to a loss of less than 1 percent.

Investors have faced daunting volatility recently, with stocks recording both their biggest daily rise and fall in more than a year. The swings in price on Wednesday were more typical for the holiday-shortened week, with many analysts noting patchy volumes ahead of Thursday, when markets are closed for Thanksgiving.

But while the sell-off on Wednesday may not reflect any significant change in sentiment among investors, it pointed to a return to the caution and concern that was on display last week when the S&P 500 entered a correction, reflecting a 10 percent drop from the index’s most recent peak and a symbol of the souring mood among investors.

On Monday, when Nvidia’s shares surged more than 30 percent after the reinstatement of its former chief executive, it appeared that investors’ deep concerns about that chipmaker’s ability to continue fueling the A. I. boom had been largely allayed. But Nvidia has since given up a lot of those gains: It fell another 5 percent on Wednesday, in early, volatile trading.

Beyond the A. I. trade, investors are awaiting clarity on the Trump administration’s proposed tariffs on imports from dozens of countries, announced Wednesday.

Investors also parsed a report on inflation issued on Wednesday that could influence the path of interest rates, with consumer prices running well above the Federal Reserve’s target. Fed officials are widely expected to raise rates at their meeting next month, which could add even more pressure to already heightened borrowing costs for companies using debt to fund the build-out of data centers and other A. I. infrastructure.

Anthropic, the A. I. giant that broke records in its initial public offering last week, fell as much as 10 percent on Wednesday before rallying to a gain of over 3 percent.

“We see the retreat as a broadening, sentiment-driven correction rather than a deterioration in fundamentals or a popping of the A. I. bubble,” analysts at the financial services firm Allianz wrote in a note. But in the short term, they added, “we expect volatility to remain elevated and any flare up of A. I. fears will continue to stress markets or break some trades.”

Jason Karaian is a deputy business editor at The Times, based in London.

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

Another Hot Inflation Reading Keeps Fed on Track to Raise Rates Again

The New York Times November 25, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates next month.

By Colby Smith

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

The Federal Reserve received yet more discouraging news about the trajectory of inflation on Wednesday, when its preferred measure showed that price pressures remained elevated last month.

Consumer prices rose 3.8 percent in October from a year earlier, according to the latest Personal Consumption Expenditures price index released by the Commerce Department. That was significantly higher than the Fed’s 2 percent target and a pickup from September’s 3.6 percent annual pace.

Core prices, a measure that strips out the volatile food and energy categories, were up 3.3 percent from a year earlier, the fastest pace since 2023. On a three-month annualized basis, those prices are 3.6 percent higher. Policymakers at the central bank pay close attention to the core measure because it is viewed as a reliable gauge of where inflation is headed.

On a monthly basis, overall prices increased at a slightly more moderate pace than the previous period, rising 0.3 percent. Core prices increased by the same magnitude.

The latest data lends support to the view of most officials at the Fed that borrowing costs need to continue rising in order to bring inflation back down to the 2 percent target, a goal that has been missed for nearly six years.

Energy prices and those for other commodities have fallen in recent weeks, helping to account for the slower monthly pace of inflation in October. The impact of President Trump’s initial round of tariffs has also begun to fade. On Wednesday, however, the White House proposed a new set of levies targeting imports from dozens of countries, including China, Japan and members of the European Union.

For the Fed, the primary concern is that prices appear to be rising across a widening range of goods and services.

Still, policymakers have proceeded gradually with raising rates, delivering their first increase in years in September and voting to stand pat last month. The Fed is widely expected to raise rates again at its final gathering of the year on Dec. 8-9, which would lift them to a range of 4 percent to 4.25 percent.

The pace after that has become a matter of debate. Many officials have embraced the idea of raising rates at consecutive meetings, suggesting that an increase at the Fed’s subsequent gathering at the end of January is plausible. After that, the central bank next meets in March.

The main determinant is whether there is any improvement in inflation or price pressures continue to accelerate as they have in recent months amid the war with Iran, which appears no closer to a resolution, and the surge in spending by technology companies seeking to expand their artificial intelligence abilities.

Despite rising costs, consumer spending has remained solid, although in October, the pace stalled out once adjusted for inflation. According to a separate report released on Wednesday, the economy grew faster in the third quarter than initially reported. Gross domestic product rose at a 4.3 percent annual pace through the three months ending in September, the highest in three years.

One key driver of demand has been the sharp rise in wealth across the country stemming from stock market gains.

In recent weeks, those gains have seesawed as equity markets have whipped around because of concerns about the sustainability of A. I. investments that have been crucial to propping up the economy.

Recent tumult at Nvidia, the chip-making giant at the heart of the boom, has injected additional volatility. After a bruising sell-off last week, Nvidia’s stock on Monday surged alongside the broader market after Jensen Huang was reinstated as chief executive after Mr. Trump’s intervention over the weekend. Mr. Huang had resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U. S. officials had identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

Corporate Oversight Revs Up as Washington Turns Blue Again

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

After two years of deregulation, congressional committees led by Democrats will shine the spotlight back on corporate America.

By Alan Rappeport

Reporting from Washington

A new era of corporate oversight is about to unfold in Washington.

President Trump has spent the first half of his term rolling back regulations and injecting the federal government into the operations of companies such as Nvidia, Intel and U. S. Steel.

Now, Democrats are gearing up to begin holding businesses accountable for actions that harm consumers or threaten national security. As they retake control of Congress next year, top Democrats are devising plans to use their committee gavels to investigate Trump administration regulators and to shine a spotlight on corporate corruption. The scrutiny is poised to create a culture shock for businesses that have become accustomed to the Trump administration’s light regulatory touch but will now have to confront skeptical lawmakers.

A preview of the new power dynamic will be on display next week, when Jensen Huang, who was reinstated this week as chief executive of Nvidia, will appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify about the company’s sales of advanced chips to China. Mr. Huang resigned this month after it emerged that he was having an affair with a woman whom U. S. officials believed to be a Chinese asset, but he returned to the job after Mr. Trump urged the board to take him back.

Mr. Trump and his advisers have made deregulation a hallmark of the president’s agenda for spurring economic growth. Since retaking the White House, the administration has gutted the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, eased bank capital requirements, allowed cryptocurrencies to flourish and scaled back bank examinations and enforcement activity by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The Treasury Department in particular has been under fire for its failure to enforce the 2021 Corporate Transparency Act, a bipartisan law that was intended to increase scrutiny of the shadowy shell companies that criminals used to launder money and traffic drugs. In October, 21 states filed a lawsuit against the Treasury Department over its rollback of new requirements that forced companies to report their ownership structures.

A more assertive approach from Democrats has unfolded in the aftermath of their overwhelming success in the midterm elections. It is poised to affect industries across corporate America. While the executive branch has shown an ability to stonewall congressional investigations, corporate America tends to be more compliant.

“So here we are teetering on the edge of a financial crisis that could crash markets, wipe out retirement savings and cost millions of people their jobs,” Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Banking Committee, said last week as she grilled Mr. Trump’s nominees to assume senior roles at the Treasury Department and the S. E. C. “The Trump administration’s response is to say, ‘Lalala, I can’t hear you, everything is just fine.’”

This month, Senators Chris Coons, Democrat of Delaware, and Jeanne Shaheen, Democrat of New Hampshire, sent a letter to Elon Musk demanding that he and SpaceX preserve documents related to the recent disruption of Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite services.

“The conflicting statements and reports as to who ordered and approved of these restrictions only underscore the need for a comprehensive inquiry and full accounting of the facts,” said Mr. Coons and Ms. Shaheen, who both sit on the Foreign Relations Committee.

Top House Democrats are also gearing up to investigate agencies that they believe have been shirking their regulatory responsibilities and businesses that have benefited from the ties to the Trump administration.

Representative Maxine Waters, the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, who could become its chair next year, sent letters to nearly two dozen federal regulators last week ordering them to preserve documents as the committee prepares to conduct “rigorous oversight” of how the Trump administration’s policies have affected the soundness of America’s financial system. She is particularly concerned about the neutering of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, which has reduced staff and halted most enforcement work, and on Tuesday her committee will hold a hearing about the dismantling of the agency.

In an interview, Ms. Waters said that she planned to call executives from big banks, asset managers and private equity funds to testify before the committee next year. Oversight of financial institutions will give lawmakers a window into how the Trump administration has been managing some of its more opaque policies, such as oil revenue that the United States is collecting from Venezuela.

“We’re going to have to do investigations on this administration with Venezuela and both the banks that were interacting with them,” said Ms. Waters, who explained that she planned to use the subpoena power of Congress if necessary. “I want to ask the banks basically, what is their role in working with the president of the United States with oil ownership and acquisition.”

Investigations are also expected to look at artificial intelligence companies, health insurers and the nursing home industry.

Liberal advocacy groups have been mobilizing to encourage lawmakers to use their oversight powers to target companies that have ties to the Trump administration. The Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive think tank and advocacy group, has been circulating a 181-page memo that details firms that have made donations to Mr. Trump or his causes and went on to receive special treatment. The document includes suggested hearings and witnesses that lawmakers could summon.

“The Democrats are going to be pursuing their agenda through legislation and oversight, and they’re going to be focused on cost and corruption,” said Lindsay Owens, president and chief executive of the Groundwork Collaborative.

Ms. Owens said that the blue wave had already started a lobbying “bonanza” with new firms emerging or hiring staff that had ties to Democratic lawmakers. Her organization’s polling data found that voters were less interested in oversight related to issues such as the White House ballroom donations and more concerned about signs that the Trump administration was helping to enrich companies that ripped off consumers.

While Democrats might struggle to enact legislation because of Mr. Trump’s presidential veto power, their ability to conduct public hearings and use subpoenas to gather information can still be a powerful tool to shift corporate behavior and public opinion.

“Oversight of industry will likely result in more changes than oversight of the executive branch,” said Aaron Klein, a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, who worked on financial regulation policy at the Treasury Department under the Obama administration. “Companies will change their policies when spotlights are shown.”

The ascent of the Democrats will also put more pressure on top Trump administration officials to defend their policies while the White House looks for areas of bipartisan cooperation.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested on Friday that stock markets had been tumbling in the United States in anticipation of more regulation from Democrats but that the Trump administration was ready to work across the aisle.

“I can tell you that President Trump wants to work with the Democrats,” Mr. Bessent said. “We’ll see if they can work with themselves.”

Alan Rappeport is an economic policy reporter for The Times, based in Washington. He covers the Treasury Department and writes about taxes, trade and fiscal matters.

California’s Tides Are in ‘Uncharted Territory’ as Water Surges Higher

The New York Times November 25, 2026

West Coast Weather

Advertisement

Supported by

High tide records were broken in a San Diego neighborhood and in Santa Barbara on Wednesday.

By Judson Jones and Amy Graff

Judson Jones is a meteorologist and a reporter for The Times. Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team.

California was experiencing another day of extraordinarily high tides on Wednesday as a mix of seasonal king tides, an unusually strong El Niño and incoming Pacific swells began to push ocean water into coastal neighborhoods across the state.

“We’re kind of in uncharted territory,” said Robbie Munroe, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Los Angeles.

After a storm cleared out on Wednesday morning, the waves began cresting under sunny November skies, attracting gawkers and surfers. The tide in La Jolla, a neighborhood in San Diego, reached 8.11 feet in a preliminary measurement, breaking the record of 7.98 feet set on Oct. 27.

Santa Barbara also experienced its highest tide ever measured, though the data there dates back only to 1990. And the tide in Los Angeles preliminarily tied the record set on Oct. 27.

Wednesday morning’s high tides began arriving in the southern part of the state after 8 a. m., and they were expected to reach Northern California in the subsequent hours.

In San Francisco, Tuesday’s high tide appeared to reach just over 8.2 feet, enough to make it one of the highest there but falling short of the 8.82-foot record set in 1983.

On Tuesday, floodwaters inundated low-lying areas in Marin County, just north of San Francisco. In Humboldt County, more than 200 miles north of San Francisco, residents in the community of King Salmon were ordered to evacuate and told they might have to stay away until Friday. Tuesday’s high tide there reached just over 10 feet, the second highest on record.

In Santa Cruz County, just south of San Francisco, evacuation warnings were issued Tuesday afternoon for about 200 homes along a few coastal roads in anticipation of higher tides on Wednesday.

“Large waves have the potential to reach homes and cause dangerous coastal flooding and road closures,” the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office said.

In Southern California, high tides were paired with surging waves and threatened areas on Tuesday that were still recovering from high water levels over the past few months. That afternoon, evacuation warnings were issued in parts of Santa Barbara County along the coast and will remain in effect until further notice.

Valerie Cimmarusti, a homeowner in the Sunset Beach neighborhood of Huntington Beach, said she and her family had been working to prevent her house from flooding again after its garage had gotten three inches of water last month.

Water from a canal behind her home breached its wall on Tuesday, “but nothing like October, where it was coming over like a river,” she said.

King tide is a nonscientific term for the highest tides of the year. It was popularized by environmental efforts that sought to document dramatically high tides as a way to help communities conceptualize what sea level rise would look like in a changing climate.

King tides are caused by a unique alignment of the sun, moon and Earth that maximizes the gravitational pull on the oceans. Because El Niño has raised the sea level of the Pacific higher than normal, these winter tides have forced emergency officials in towns across the state to install temporary flood walls and pile sandbags, hoping to keep the water at bay.

On Wednesday, forecasters warned that unique weather conditions might nudge the already high tides even higher in Northern California, where a storm system that brought light to moderate rain early Wednesday had exited by late morning.

Scientists knew going into this winter that the strength of the El Niño pattern would probably lead to some of the highest tides on record. But in many ways, this week has exceeded their expectations.

“Typically with an El Niño in San Diego, you might get a half a foot to maybe a foot,” said Mark Merrifield, an oceanographer at the University of California, San Diego. “But we’re well above that with this El Niño event.”

He added that water levels were “higher than my expectations.” Tides at their peak in La Jolla were about a foot higher than experts had predicted going into the week. Mr. Merrifield said he expected that conditions would worsen on Thursday with the arrival of additional high swell waves.

Weather forecasters have issued rarely used coastal flood warnings through Thursday.

It isn’t just the travel disruptions that could come with flooded roads on Wednesday. Meteorologists in San Francisco and Los Angeles expressed concern for anyone heading to the beach over the holiday.

“When we get up to near 80 in late November, with water temperatures near 70, it’s pretty unheard-of in terms of beach conditions,” Mr. Munroe, the meteorologist in Los Angeles, said. “People will be probably be trying to head to the beach if they’re not taking our warning seriously.”

Cindy Palmer, a meteorologist with the Weather Service’s Bay Area office said the larger waves could push the already elevated tides farther up the beaches and even produce sneaker waves, which happen when wave energy combines and sends a sudden surge much farther up the shore than preceding waves.

Pounding waves on top of a high tide could erode beaches, making them more vulnerable to future storms, experts warned.

There are still two more rounds of king tides to come this winter, one during the week of Christmas and one in late January. Ms. Palmer said she expected the tides then could be even higher.

Vik Jolly and Nicole Stock contributed reporting.

Judson Jones is a meteorologist and reporter for The Times who forecasts and covers extreme weather.

Amy Graff is a Times reporter covering weather, wildfires and earthquakes.

Opposition Makes Progress Toward Ousting Netanyahu, Party Leader Says

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Israel’s Election

Advertisement

Supported by

Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, has set Dec. 6 as the deadline to form a new Israeli government. His ally, Avigdor Liberman, said Mr. Eisenkot was on track.

By David M. Halbfinger

Reporting from Jerusalem

Gadi Eisenkot, the Israeli opposition leader and former military chief, appears to be making progress toward ousting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and forming a new government that could include ultra-Orthodox Jewish lawmakers.

Mr. Eisenkot announced late Tuesday that he and Avigdor Liberman, the leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) party, had agreed to sign a deal formally bringing their two parties into coalition. That is a vital first step toward building a governing majority, but he still needs similar backing from other parties to complete it.

Mr. Liberman said in a radio interview on Wednesday that a new government could be formed by next week.

Mr. Eisenkot has set a goal of announcing a new government by Dec. 6, when his mandate from Israel’s president to form a governing coalition will expire unless an extension is granted. His allies are sounding increasingly optimistic that he will succeed.

The deadline carries much symbolism: Dec. 7 will be the third anniversary of the death of Mr. Eisenkot’s 25-year-old son, Gal, in combat in the Gaza Strip. Mr. Eisenkot has devoted himself to being “worthy of the sacrifice” made by his son and other fallen Israeli soldiers.

Here is a look at key aspects of the coalition talks underway.

Mr. Liberman, a savvy, secular lawmaker who had long been a leading critic of the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, made himself a pivotal figure by reversing himself: He is now pushing to form a government that includes the Haredim.

He said on Tuesday that such an outcome was growing more likely, after religious leaders behind one of the ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism, authorized talks with Mr. Eisenkot.

“There will be a government with a Jewish majority,” Mr. Liberman said in the interview with Kan, Israel’s public broadcaster.

Mr. Eisenkot has made clear that toppling Mr. Netanyahu is his overarching priority. Getting the Haredi parties to break their decades-old partnership with Mr. Netanyahu and turn against him would be a political coup.

But forming an alliance with the Haredi parties is not without complications. They have fought tooth-and-nail to prevent young Haredi men from being conscripted into the Israeli military or from being arrested if they dodge the draft.

Mr. Eisenkot and his allies promised they would end Haredi draft dodging, easing the burden of reserve military duty now borne by thousands of other Israelis.

United Torah Judaism, with seven seats in the Parliament was expected to help Mr. Eisenkot either by voting to support his effort to form a new government or at least by abstaining, according to two people briefed on the coalition talks who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations.

But the group is expected only to join a new government after a compromise is made on a draft law. A pact would cement the party’s alliance with Mr. Eisenkot and could give its leaders ministerial posts.

Until now, Mr. Liberman has rejected the idea of forming a government that relies on the support of an Arab-led party. He had also previously ruled out the idea of a so-called minority government, in which a plurality of Parliament members, but fewer than a 61-seat majority, vote to form the government.

But Mr. Liberman indicated for the first time on Wednesday that he could support a minority government as long as a majority of the Jewish lawmakers backed it.

And Mr. Eisenkot is already there: His party and his core allies — Mr. Liberman, the more centrist Beyachad (Together) party led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, and the left-wing Democrat party headed by Yair Golan — hold 48 seats versus the 46 held by Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies.

Gayil Talshir, a political science lecturer at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who is advising the opposition, said that by making a “Jewish majority” his bottom line, Mr. Liberman opened the door to a new government supported by the United Arab List, or Raam, which is led by Mansour Abbas.

Mr. Abbas made history by serving in a government led by Mr. Bennett and then Mr. Lapid in 2021 and 2022. The leader has made clear he hopes to join the next government as well. While that may not pan out, Ms. Talshir said, Raam was certain to support Mr. Eisenkot’s formation of a new government and could be expected to cooperate with him from outside the coalition if the party doesn’t formally enter the government.

Mr. Eisenkot, by most accounts, ran a lackluster political campaign and fell well short of his goals in the election on Oct. 27. But he appears to be faring better than anticipated at the crucial inside game of coalition building. (If Mr. Eisenkot fails to form a government, Mr. Netanyahu could be given a chance to try. If he doesn’t succeed, new elections could be called.)

Since receiving the mandate on Nov. 8 to form a government, Mr. Eisenkot has left open three possibilities: partnering with the ultra-Orthodox, joining forces with the Arab parties, or forming a unity government with Mr. Netanyahu and his Likud party.

None of those options have yet been ruled out. By keeping them open, Mr. Eisenkot can keep pressure both on his natural allies and on adversaries who conceivably could join him in a unity government, Ms. Talshir said.

Likud, for example, faces pressure to let Mr. Eisenkot have the first turn as prime minister if he and Mr. Netanyahu agree to a unity government with rotating leadership.

Shas, an ultra-Orthodox party that has so far refused to break with Mr. Netanyahu, faces pressure to do so or risk being left in the cold without the lucrative government financial benefits it has enjoyed for years.

And Mr. Bennett, who has adamantly opposed any coalition agreement with the Haredi parties, now faces pressure to bow to Mr. Liberman on that score or risk being blamed for failing to oust Mr. Netanyahu.

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

Turmoil at Nvidia

Supported by

The freshest measures of growth and hiring show a healthy economy. Struggling Americans aren’t seeing that.

By Audra D. S. Burch

For Austin George, the first hint that something was wrong with the economy — beyond the typical bumps — started during his girlfriend’s job hunt this spring.

It took months before Jessica Marmolejo settled for a pay cut from what she had earned at a dentist office and accepted a position at a lighting warehouse.

The couple delayed purchasing a house and held onto their down payment as a financial cushion to help them weather punishing inflation and uncomfortably high prices.

No matter how sturdy the economy might appear on paper, Mr. George, 41, who lives in Fairfield, Calif., with Ms. Marmolejo and their eight-year-old son, believes the country is in a recession — or barreling toward one.

Economic indicators show quite the opposite. The nation’s economy grew at an annualized rate of 4.3 percent from June to September, the highest in three years, figures released Wednesday show. But such macroeconomic figures don’t reflect the experiences of Mr. George or many others who registered their dismay with President Trump and his party earlier this month at the polls.

To people like him, the more relevant number on Wednesday was 3.8 percent. That’s how much consumer prices rose in October from a year earlier, according to the latest Personal Consumption Expenditures price index released by the Commerce Department, and it marked a pickup from September’s 3.6 percent annual pace.

“The warning lights are blinking,” Mr. George said. “I think we have reached the tipping point and things could get ugly real quick.”

The country is far from a recession, which economists define as two consecutive quarters of negative growth measured by real gross domestic product. Yet a clear majority of Americans — about 61 percent across political parties — believe the United States is in a recession, according to a Harris Poll conducted for the Guardian in October.

For those Americans, the word simply captures the persistent pessimism they feel about their personal finances and future.

Unemployment is low at 4.1 percent and consumer spending has remained solid, although in October, the pace stalled out once adjusted for inflation, Wednesday’s numbers indicated.

But the economy’s strength is not equally distributed. Many high-income households are thriving with a rising stock market while lower-income households tread water or fall behind. And, the economy is vulnerable to cost of living pressures, government spending and growth tied to the artificial intelligence build out.

The divergence suggests there are two economies, one for the elite and one for the rest.

That was made all the more stark by the saga of Jensen Huang, the billionaire chief executive of Nvidia, one of the major technology companies in the artificial intelligence boom. He was reinstated less than two weeks past his resignation after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U. S. officials had identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

“It all points to an economy working for the rich and selling out the average American,” said Mr. George.

This is not the first time the public has declared a “vibecession” despite metrics showing otherwise, most recently during the Biden presidency.

“You and your family struggling might suggest that it’s an individual level experience,” said Erin Hatton, a professor of sociology at the State University of New York at Buffalo who studies the labor market, “but by calling it a recession, they’re saying, no it’s not just me. They are pointing to how widespread it is and that it’s a structural issue.”

After enduring more than a year of stiff trade tariffs and shocks related to the war in Iran, many Americans have lost faith.

They view the slashes they made to their household monthly budgets as an indicator of a personal recession. They fret over planning for the future when so much feels out of reach. And they remember the stress of past recessions — the short pandemic-induced downturn of 2020 and the financial crisis that began in late 2007.

The new macro data doesn’t reflect the real-world mismatch between slow wage growth and increasing expenses. Almost half of Americans struggle to pay for at least one of their basic needs, a recent study by the Pew Research Center found. Nearly three-quarters of lower-income adults reported difficulty covering the cost of basic necessities such as daily transportation, housing, groceries or health care.

Don Crafton, a longtime Democrat who switched to the Republican Party and supported Mr. Trump in the last two presidential elections, questioned the statistics projecting a healthy economy.

What he knows for sure is the $3,500 that he and his girlfriend bring home in pay each month is just enough to get by. But not much more.

To Mr. Crafton, describing the economy as in a recession or headed that way, seems beside the point.

“The economy is terrible. Everything is expensive and it doesn’t have to be that way. We live paycheck to paycheck,” said Mr. Crafton, 56, who works in a school district maintenance department and lives in Belle Vernon, Pa. “We don’t go without, but we can’t put any money in the bank for if something happens.”

Financial pressure, along with fear of a recession, has forced Americans to rethink their spending.

Spencer Smith, 39, a company manager for a Broadway show in New York City, said he began thinking a downturn might be imminent after watching the impact of the tariffs and war on the economy.

He began preparing for a “worst-case” scenario by cutting monthly costs and building his savings to cover about six months of living expenses.

That meant delaying a nonemergency foot surgery that could include out-of-pocket physical therapy fees. He decided against taking a vacation to Mexico City planned for January. He swapped pricey Uber rides for the subway. And he dialed back on dining out where the tab can easily top $100.

“I am asking myself the question that I think Americans are all asking themselves: Is this something that I need to do or is this something that I can reduce in order to save money?” he said. “I am now in a budget mind-set.”

When Democrats take control of Congress in January, many voters say they are expecting them to advance an ambitious agenda to lower costs by ending the Iran war, reversing tariffs and undoing much of the president’s signature domestic policy law, including cuts to Medicaid and food aid, and tax cuts for the rich.

Mr. Smith said he was also hopeful Democrats would reinstate expired health insurance subsidies under the Affordable Care Act.

“I don’t want to see a food fight in the party arguing over who is the most right on some issue,” he said. “It’s time to get some stuff done and try to help people who are suffering.”

Megan Irving, 51, a psychotherapist who lives on the Oregon coast, is convinced that parts of the country are already experiencing a recession based on some economic forecasts and what she sees firsthand at her grocery store.

Routine shopping, she said, tells a different story than what the top lines suggest.

“I am shopping and I see lots of calculators and coupons and moms telling their kids to put something back because they can’t afford it right now,” she said. “This feels like a recession or something close to it. It walks and talks like a recession.”

Kitty Bennett and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

Audra D. S. Burch is a national reporter, based in South Florida and Atlanta, writing about race and identity around the country.

Senator Chris Van Hollen says his move to replace Senator Chuck Schumer as party leader isn’t about Israel, but his sharply critical stance toward the Jewish state has become a major fault line in the race.

Senator Chris Van Hollen has played a prominent role in seeking to condition the sale of offensive weapons to Israel over the past several years, a position that increased his popularity with progressives. Credit... Haiyun Jiang for The New York Times

Supported by

By Annie Karni

Reporting from Washington

The divide among Democrats on Israel is hanging over a tense fight about who should lead the party in the Senate next year, pitting Chris Van Hollen, one of the most vocal critics of the Jewish state in the chamber, against Chuck Schumer, one of its most ardent backers.

Mr. Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, was elected to Congress two decades ago as a candidate who accepted contributions from donors to AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group. He led campaign committees in both the House and Senate, where he backed candidates funded by the group. But in recent years, he turned sharply against Israel — even before others in his party — as its right-wing government instituted hard-line policies and carried out an aggressive military campaign in Gaza after the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

Over the past several years, Mr. Van Hollen has played a prominent role in seeking to condition the sale of offensive weapons to Israel, a position that increased his popularity with progressives. He had recently been exploring a presidential run, which he said he abandoned in order to seek the Senate leadership post.

Now the issue has become a subtext of his drive to replace Mr. Schumer, the New York Democrat, after a midterm campaign shaped in part by the Democratic split over Israel and ahead of a new Congress where that divide is likely to persist.

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, frames his run as an attempt to upend the status quo in Washington. In an interview, he said the leadership race was not about Israel. But he conceded that criticism of the Jewish state and powerful players aligned with it resonated with voters who want to get big money and special interests out of politics.

“A couple of members have raised to me the fact that they’ve gotten calls from AIPAC members urging them to vote for the current leader,” he said, referring to Mr. Schumer. “AIPAC is an example of a special interest working to try to get their way, in this case provide unconditional American taxpayer support to the government of Israel. It’s one piece of a much larger set of issues.”

One accusation that Mr. Van Hollen has repeatedly made to justify challenging Mr. Schumer is that he “joined with AIPAC and crypto” to try to defeat Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who has been harshly critical of Israel, in the state’s competitive primary. Mr. Van Hollen says Democrats should no longer accept money from the group or its donors.

(Mr. Schumer did not officially back a candidate in Michigan’s primary, and he spent almost $70 million to boost Mr. El-Sayed’s general election bid. But he had privately supported Representative Haley Stevens, a vocally pro-Israel Democrat, in the primary.)

Mr. Schumer, who has insisted that he has secured enough private commitments from fellow Democrats to be elected majority leader in a vote that is set for Tuesday, declined to comment for this article. He has laid out an agenda to his colleagues that includes quick action on a stock trading ban, restoring the Affordable Care Act health subsidies and addressing tariffs and data centers.

Mr. Van Hollen, the self-proclaimed underdog in the race, is running an outside campaign for the internal position, seeking to leverage the support of progressive activists and build a public case to persuade senators to back him instead.

“I do think that people should have a say in the future direction of our caucus,” Mr. Van Hollen said.

On Monday night, Mr. Van Hollen participated in a Zoom call organized by Our Revolution, a progressive organization aligned with Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent. Attendees on the call were encouraged to put senators on blast and demand new leadership.

The secret-ballot election is for a position that is mostly about managing the 56 senators set to be in the Democratic caucus next year — including two independents who align with them — many of whom have presidential-sized egos and ambitions. Mr. Schumer, who orchestrated a $550 million push to put more Senate seats in play this year and recruited many of the candidates who flipped seats, is seen by his supporters as the coach who won the Super Bowl and earned his right to keep his job.

On most issues, Mr. Schumer and Mr. Van Hollen may favor different tactics but are not so far apart. Both support ending the war with Iran and regulating artificial intelligence. Mr. Van Hollen has pressed for a discussion about changing filibuster rules to push through major legislation, a move that Mr. Schumer has said should be a caucus decision.

But Israel has emerged as a fault line.

Mr. Schumer has long taken pride in being the highest-ranking Jewish official in the country. While he was one of the first to call for new leadership in Israel, Mr. Schumer has opposed measures to cancel arms sales to Israel. Last year, he refused to endorse Zohran Mamdani, who became the first Muslim mayor of New York City and has leftist views, particularly on Israel.

Mr. Van Hollen has emerged as one of the loudest voices in the Senate advocating Palestinian rights, criticizing many of Israel’s policies and actions and calling out what he has described as the failures of American administrations. Since Oct. 7, he has voted to block some arms sales to Israel and led a vote this fall to force the Trump administration to produce a human rights report examining violence by Israel in the West Bank, including the deaths of Palestinian American citizens. The measure was blocked, but it attracted support from almost the entire Democratic caucus, including from Mr. Schumer.

Mr. Van Hollen has also visited the Rafah crossing on Gaza’s southern border, which Israel shut down in 2024, trapping many Palestinians inside and stranding others outside.

“I was incredibly alarmed that the U. S. had become complicit in what was happening for the destruction of Gaza,” he said.

The visit was in line with Mr. Van Hollen’s approach of creating moments of confrontation to press for change. Last year, he traveled to El Salvador to push for the release of Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia, the Maryland man mistakenly deported by the Trump administration.

“I just got mad,” he said of his decision to visit Mr. Abrego Garcia in El Salvador.

He also made a showy motion last year to bring back 400 books that had been banned by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which included Maya Angelou’s “I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.”

“I actually brought it with me to the first meeting of the Naval Academy Board and put it on the table and said we need to reverse it,” he recalled. “I do think this moment calls for a different kind of approach.”

A majority of the books on the list were reinstated.

Jeremy Ben-Ami, the president of the liberal-leaning pro-Israel group J Street, which is not supporting a candidate in the leadership race, credited Mr. Van Hollen with leading on the issue of Israel “before the window really opened to make it politically acceptable. Van Hollen was out front and almost a step ahead on this issue before it was politically safe.”

And while Mr. Van Hollen may not be making his leadership bid about Israel, some of his supporters and detractors say his stance on the issue is a factor.

Mr. Sanders said Israel was just one issue in a race that was mostly about rejecting the status quo, but he praised Mr. Van Hollen as someone who has “been a leader in the effort to end military aid to the extremist government in Israel.”

He added: “He went last year to Gaza. His view on that is very different from Senator Schumer. It’s one of the issues that differentiates Chris from Chuck.”

Mr. El-Sayed, who is also backing Mr. Van Hollen, said that Mr. Schumer was out of step with his own caucus on Israel, and “even the caucus position has been out of step with the country. We should not be continuing to support a foreign government that has used our money to commit war crimes,” he said in an interview.

And while he said he had a good relationship now with Mr. Schumer and would support whoever emerged on Tuesday as leader, Mr. El-Sayed gave the New York Democrat little credit for getting behind him after his primary.

“I was the nominee in Michigan,” Mr. El-Sayed said. “I could have been a stale piece of bark and he would have supported me.”

Some staunch backers of Israel have taken the opposite view. Senator John Fetterman, the Pennsylvania Democrat who is an unyielding defender of the Jewish state, said recently on Fox News that Mr. Van Hollen became a “progressive darling” primarily because of his views on Israel.

“Other than that, I can’t really think of what Van Hollen’s known for,” he said, adding, “It would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen, that has really made his name being very anti-, hostile, to Israel.”

For others, Israel is low on the list of considerations as they select their leader. Senator Peter Welch, Democrat of Vermont, called Mr. Schumer “an outlier in our caucus” on the issue and said he was “totally aligned” with Mr. Van Hollen on it.

But Mr. Welch, who would not say whom he was planning to support for leader, said the contest was not about that.

“There are significant policy differences, but a major role of the leader is to make space for all the members to have a voice and their view,” he said.

Michael Gold contributed reporting.

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

Bizarre Material May Herald the Future of Computer Chips

The New York Times November 25, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Unlike copper, newly described “nanoribbons” conduct electricity better as they shrink. If refined, the material could usher in a supercharged generation of microchips.

By William J. Broad

The modern world runs on copper. Today, miles of thin copper wires link up the tens of billions of transistors that empower silicon microchips in things like cellphones and artificial intelligence data centers.

Making the chips even more powerful has historically relied on miniaturization. But standard copper wiring gets worse at conducting electricity as it gets smaller, creating a bottleneck to progress.

Now, a new generation of microchips is taking shape. If perfected, the chips could hold a trillion transistors each, researchers reported on Wednesday in the journal Nature. The key is swapping out copper wires for a type of “nanoribbon” that, in a twist, conducts electricity even better as it shrinks in size.

If refined in the coming years, the newly developed wire, made of niobium phosphide, could lead to chips that are smaller, faster, more powerful and, by reducing their heat emissions, less wasteful.

Ultimately, experts say, the new material might help to shrink the size of A. I. data centers and decrease their need for cooling water, reducing their environmental footprints.

“This could be a game changer,” said Laura H. Greene, the chief scientist at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory and a past president of the American Physical Society who was not involved in the research.

Eric Pop, the senior author on the Nature paper and a professor of electrical engineering at Stanford University, characterized his team’s finding as “a breakthrough,” partly because its fabrication steps align with existing industry methods, making it easier to commercialize.

“We’ve taken some really cool physics and ported it into the applied electronics world,” Dr. Pop said last year while giving the public a glimpse of his team’s research.

In an interview, he added that after that brief look, “our phones started ringing from industry people” eager to learn more about the new method of wire miniaturization.

The subject of the Stanford research is a material known as a topological semimetal. It possesses bizarre qualities that were presaged a decade ago by a Nobel Prize in Physics, which went to three scientists who found that extreme states of matter could produce strange effects that overpower the constant jostling of atoms in normal states.

The odd but defining characteristic of the niobium wire is that its outer parts conduct electricity better than its innards. So, if miniaturized, its outer parts contribute more to the electrical flow and, overall, the minuscule wire conducts better. Its behavior, in other words, is the exact opposite that of copper.

Last year, Dr. Pop’s team released a report in the journal Science that told of turning the niobium into thin films that had low electrical resistance. The Nature paper takes things a step further by achieving the same reduction in actual wires, which the team called nanoribbons because they’re flat.

The new report pushes back the frontiers of “nanoscale” engineering, in which the dimensions range from 1 nanometer to 100 nanometers, or billionths of a meter. The width of a human hair is about 100,000 nanometers.

Today, the smallest widths of copper wires in microchips run from roughly 16 to 10 nanometers. Dr. Pop’s team used its new material to produce nanowires that had widths as small as roughly six nanometers — considered the start of industry goals for the miniaturization of microchip wires in the next decade.

Dr. Pop sees the research as potentially leading to a new chip generation.

Judy J. Cha, a materials scientist at Cornell University who also studies chip miniaturization, cautioned that “many questions remain” in the field’s implementation of its rudimentary ideas.

“It requires further study,” Dr. Cha said of the Stanford work. “Students might think it’s all proven.” Asked if China, which is racing ahead in materials science, had developed an edge over America in such esoteric research, she said no. “The United States still leads.”

In an interview, Dr. Pop said the production of practical results in the form of a new generation of factory-made chips might take another five to 10 years. But he said such predictions were inherently imprecise.

“That’s the part that’s really hard to say,” he remarked. “If I had a solution today, they’d want it yesterday,” referring to the industry’s appetite for miniaturization. Overall, Dr. Pop added, the use of copper in microchips is “creating more and more headaches.”

A current frontier of his team’s research, he said, is to better understand the mechanism at work behind the material’s resistance drop.

“We keep asking ourselves, ‘What’s going on?’” he noted. Learning the details of the invisible process, Dr. Pop added, “will tell us how to improve the mechanism,” and that in turn may ultimately make the trillion-transistor chip a reality.

William J. Broad has reported on science at The Times since 1983. He is based in New York.

Trump Administration Unveils New Tariffs for Dozens of Countries, Citing Unfair Practices

The New York Times November 25, 2026

U. S. Tariffs and Trade

Advertisement

Supported by

The latest escalation came as the administration confronts continued legal obstacles and new scrutiny from an incoming Democratic-led Congress.

By Tony Romm and Ana Swanson

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration proposed a slate of new tariffs on Wednesday targeting imports from dozens of countries, including China, Japan and the members of the European Union, marking the latest expansion of a global trade war that faces mounting obstacles in Congress and the courts.

The administration framed the duties as a response to unfair trade practices, as it accused some of its closest economic partners of overproducing certain products, undercutting American businesses and contributing to a swelling U. S. trade deficit.

The newly unveiled roster of tariffs included a 20 percent tax on some imports from China, which the Trump administration signaled it could ratchet up — to 40 percent — if Beijing does not hew to the terms of a trade truce it has struck with Washington.

The Trump administration also proposed similarly high and potentially escalating rates on goods from the 27 members of the European Union and other trading partners including Cambodia, India, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. Some of those duties could reach up to 20 percent as well. And it coupled the sweeping action with a separate, specific proposal seeking to raise rates on Brazil, targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.

Before the new tariffs take effect, the administration must fulfill a set of final regulatory requirements, which would include seeking public feedback, according to Jamieson Greer, the U. S. trade representative, who appeared Wednesday on CNBC. He described the approach as “targeted,” but noted that discussions continued with each of the affected trading partners.

In many cases, though, Mr. Greer said the tariffs would not stack on top of those that the administration had already put in place. That included duties that President Trump has applied on national security grounds to products such as steel and cars. He said the White House also sought to keep its tariffs in line with the trade agreements it had already brokered.

The battery of new tariffs nonetheless arrived at a precarious political moment for Mr. Trump, who has continued to engage in a strategy of aggressive trade brinkmanship even after the Supreme Court struck down his initial slate of country-by-country duties this year.

Mr. Trump has long portrayed tariffs as essential for boosting domestic manufacturing, raising revenue and fostering better trade deals. But his shifting policies have still counted among the many forces driving up prices for consumers and business, feeding a public backlash that ultimately stripped Republicans of their congressional majorities in the midterm election.

Still, the White House risked touching off a widespread backlash — angering Congress, as Democrats prepare to take control of the House and the Senate, and rattling Wall Street, where stocks fell sharply to open trading on Wednesday. It coincided with the government’s release of a key gauge of inflation, which showed that prices rose 3.8 percent in October from a year earlier, marking a pickup from September.

President Trump’s administration eyed a new set of rates that could exceed those struck under its recent trade deals, unless other countries change their manufacturing practices.

Note: Final rates may be lower. The tariffs do not stack with many other duties, and there are exceptions for certain products

Source: U. S. Trade Representative.

Tony Romm/The New York Times

The announcement also appeared to rankle the country’s closest allies and trading partners. Some had already struck deals with Mr. Trump to avert higher tariffs — or were in the midst of negotiations — when the administration signaled Wednesday that it could raise rates even higher.

In the European Union, officials said they would study the Trump administration’s findings but disputed that Europe was the source of overproduction. Olof Gill, a spokesperson for the bloc, said E. U. members expected “any measure from this investigation to respect” the trade deal between Brussels and Washington.

Mr. Trump’s newly proposed tariffs on the European Union would be set at 15 percent, as the agreement between trans-Atlantic partners had stipulated. But the administration also warned it could raise rates as high as 25 percent if it found compliance was “unsatisfactory.”

In China, meanwhile, officials also reacted forcefully to the White House’s latest tariff actions, just days after the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, hosted Mr. Trump for another round of trade talks. “The so-called overcapacity is a false proposition, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation,” said Guo Jiakun, spokesman for China’s foreign ministry.

The Trump administration said it would enforce the new duties under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the U. S. government to investigate unfair trade practices abroad and impose tariffs in response to its findings. It is a power that presidents of both parties, including Mr. Trump, have invoked successfully in the past.

Under Section 301, the government can impose tariffs only after investigating and uncovering evidence that other countries discriminated or impeded U. S. industries. The administration announced two such inquiries in March, as it sought ways to resuscitate the tariffs that the Supreme Court had invalidated.

One of those inquiries focused on dozens of countries for failing to crack down on forced labor. Those tariffs, which took effect in July, sparked a swift court challenge — and now await a verdict from a panel of judges that recently seemed poised to rule against the administration.

The second investigation targeted what the administration has described as “excess capacity.” At the time, Jamieson Greer, the U. S. trade representative, said the inquiry would focus on the extent to which dozens of countries had unfairly boosted their manufacturing sectors and overproduced goods to the detriment of American industry.

On Mr. Greer’s radar was a wide range of foreign practices, including other countries’ use of state subsidies; their currency management; their support for state-owned enterprises; and their economic, labor and environmental regulations. For the administration, the main concern was that these practices gave foreign industry an unfair advantage over American manufacturers while driving up the nation’s trade deficit, which Mr. Trump has struggled to reduce.

This month, the government reported that the deficit reached $105 billion in September, a slight decrease from August yet still the second-largest total since Mr. Trump returned to office. A key force behind that imbalance is artificial intelligence, a priority for Mr. Trump, as U. S. firms snap up expensive semiconductors and other computing components from abroad.

Some business owners criticized the tariffs, saying that Americans were already struggling with affordability concerns and that new tariffs could force them to raise prices again.

Anne-Marie De Witt, the chief executive of Fireside Games, a board game publisher in Austin, Texas, said the move was “especially disheartening after the electorate spoke extremely clearly about the hardship tariffs are placing on the budgets of all Americans.”

She issued the criticism alongside We Pay the Tariffs, a coalition of small businesses that has fought Mr. Trump’s trade policies. In response to the announcement on Wednesday, Ms. De Witt added, “We have all suffered enough.”

Other groups welcomed the move. In a release, the United Steelworkers union called the crackdown “long overdue" and said that extended global dialogues in recent years had failed to make progress on excess capacity in a range of industries, from steel and aluminum to chemicals, tires and ships.

“America’s manufacturing workers have been under attack for far too long, and now we have an opportunity to start restoring fair markets,” said Roxanne Brown, the president of United Steelworkers International.

Absent from the tariffs unveiled on Wednesday were Norway and Mexico, which had been among the countries that the Trump administration investigated. A senior official said reviews continued with respect to both trading partners.

“The problem of global structural overcapacity is very real for many American companies and industries,” said Timothy Brightbill, a top trade lawyer at the law firm Wiley Rein. He explained that other countries’ overproduced goods also affected global markets “where U. S. companies would like to be able to export but can’t due to unfair competition.”

“There are likely challenges in quantifying the amount of structural overcapacity in particular industries, but there is no doubt that this problem is real and growing,” Mr. Brightbill continued.

Sui-Lee Wee and Jeanna Smialek contributed reporting.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.
