Why Aren’t the Midterms Over in Louisiana? Ask the Supreme Court.

The New York Times November 25, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

A landmark Supreme Court ruling reshaped the state’s congressional map and set up runoffs for two open seats.

By Tim Balk

The midterm elections may be over in most of the country, but in Louisiana another round of voting is about to begin.

Democrats, having already secured their largest House majority in decades, are aiming to build on their gains by recording upsets in two unresolved Louisiana races that were reshaped and extended by redistricting.

The first day of early voting for both contests is Saturday, and Election Day is scheduled for Dec. 12. The rare Christmastime election stems from a U. S. Supreme Court decision less than three weeks before Primary Day in May that prompted Louisiana to redraw its congressional map and delay its House primaries to the fall.

Republicans have advantages in the races, which are in districts drawn by Republican state lawmakers to benefit their party. But Democrats have pulled off several upsets in the South in the midterms, and they’re aiming for more in Louisiana, where they narrowly lost the Senate race.

Here’s what to know about the House races.

In late April, the Supreme Court, weakening the Voting Rights Act, declared that Louisiana state lawmakers had improperly considered race when drawing the congressional map to include a second majority-Black district.

Gov. Jeff Landry, a Republican, ordered that the state’s House primaries be moved to Nov. 3 from May 16 to give the State Legislature, which is controlled by Republicans, time to redraw district lines. (Other races unaffected by the congressional map proceeded as scheduled.)

The state’s Sixth Congressional District, represented by Cleo Fields, a Democrat from Baton Rouge, changed drastically, and he decided not to run for re-election. Other candidates, though, piled into the races.

The Nov. 3 House elections were open to candidates regardless of party, and candidates could win outright by capturing a majority of the vote. If nobody won a majority, the top two candidates regardless of party advanced to a runoff.

Louisiana has had December elections before: The state for decades usually used the unusual all-party primary system, and had planned to move away from it starting this year — but the Supreme Court decision altered those plans.

This year in four of Louisiana’s six House districts, candidates won their races outright; three Republicans and a Democrat won seats. But in the Baton-Rouge area Sixth District and in the deeply rural Fifth District, which includes Monroe, no candidate came close to a majority.

In each of those districts, a Democrat and a Republican advanced.

In the Sixth District, where Republicans hope to use new lines to flip a seat, Chauna Banks, a Democrat and a former member of the East Baton Rouge Metropolitan Council, received the most votes in the primary. State Senator Blake Miguez, a Republican, finished right behind her. Both won about 19 percent of the vote.

In the Fifth District, which Republicans are defending, State Representative Patricia Moore, a Democrat, finished first, winning about 18 percent of the vote. She advanced along with State Representative Gabe Firment, a Republican, who had about 17 percent of the vote. They are running for the redrawn district of Senator-elect Julia Letlow, a Republican who challenged the Republican senator Bill Cassidy instead of defending her House seat.

Both districts were graded as solidly Republican by the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster.

The primary results underscored the challenge facing Democrats: Republican candidates combined to win about 57 percent of the primary vote in Mr. Fields’s district, and 63 percent of the vote in Ms. Letlow’s.

Mr. Firment said that those numbers encouraged him, but that he was still contending with “concerning” levels of voter apathy and frustration with the high costs affecting farmers.

“We’re really starting from scratch,” Mr. Firment said of the runoff, adding, “I’m not taking anything for granted.”

His opponent, Ms. Moore, said that the map made her race difficult, but that voters in the district were “sick and tired of what’s going on in D. C.”

Democrats won several midterm races in the South, as rural voters recoiled at gasoline and fertilizer prices, which have been driven up by the Iran war. Black voters have also appeared motivated after the Supreme Court’s ruling on the Voting Rights Act.

In Louisiana’s Senate race, Jamie Davis, a Democrat and farmer whose campaign ran just two TV ads, came within two percentage points of defeating Ms. Letlow. He would have been the first Black senator representing Louisiana.

Although Mr. Davis vastly outperformed national Democrats’ expectations, his showing hasn’t inspired a heavy investment by Democrats in the two House races. AdImpact, a media tracking firm, said Tuesday that it had recorded $273,000 in Republican TV spending in the runoffs, and no Democratic TV spending.

Still, Ms. Banks, the Democratic candidate in the Sixth District, said that she hoped to “ride the wave” of Democratic enthusiasm, and predicted that candidates would have to remind voters that the midterms were not over.

“The whole country’s moved on, and you’re dealing with the holidays,” Ms. Banks said, adding, “The question is going to be: Who gets the most vote out?”

Families are messy and entertaining. He showed how compelling dysfunction could be long before it was everywhere.

Maury Povich’s career has doubled as a tour through more than six decades of media history, from anchor to daytime talk show host to podcaster. Credit... Clement Pascal for The New York Times

Supported by

By Matt Flegenheimer

They gazed at each other from behind their microphones and smiled — the stately former host of a less stately daytime talk show and the internet-famous mustachioed comic who tells sex jokes in tracksuits.

Maury Povich, 87, and Stavros Halkias, 37, had been filming a recent episode of Povich’s post-daytime podcast, “On Par with Maury Povich,” inside a Midtown Manhattan recording studio, meditating on the guest’s favorite pursuits.

“You like weed,” Povich said, faux-interrogating, sounding something like the high-school principal who isn’t like those other high-school principals.

“I do like weed, Maury,” Halkias confirmed.

“Do you know that there’s a strain named after my wife?” Povich asked. “The Connie Chung weed.”

Halkias vowed, cackling, to “roll up a nice spliff of your wife tonight, Maury. Out of respect.”

And this respect makes some sense. It is not merely that a generation of pod-comics a half-century his junior once delighted in watching Povich deliver on-air paternity results (“You are NOT the father!”) while they were home sick from school.

It is that Povich registers clearly now, with the ring light of hindsight, as both their seen-it-all peer and their essential forerunner.

He is, in a sense, the father of an everything-is-content entertainment moment in which no consideration — expertise, relevance, good taste — is an industry obstacle for the right kind of talker.

Or, at minimum, he is not not the father.

“Look, everybody in the country is going to have a podcast,” Povich said in an interview, sitting cross-legged inside the Upper West Side apartment he shares with Chung, the pioneering broadcast journalist and his wife of more than 40 years. “It’s OK. It’s fine.”

In many ways, Povich’s career has doubled as a tour through more than six decades of media history and canny national pulse-reading.

He has toggled from smoke-on-the-air anchorman (“I wasn’t Ron Burgundy, but…”) to eponymous daytime talk show franchise (1991 to 2022) to the final form: podcaster.

He has reclaimed a place in the cultural firmament by doing a version of what he has always done, sensing where the audience was headed and steering himself there.

There was a time, not so long ago, when on-air paternity tests were considered by some to be society’s rock bottom, not a quaint and nostalgic relic of linear television.

In non-retirement, Povich is a still-talking reminder that everything and nothing has changed.

“The whole ‘Housewives’ franchise, the Kardashians, ‘Jersey Shore,’ you name the reality show — it all came out of those daytime shows,” he said. “These themes are so classic. I mean, they’re Shakespearean. They go all the way back centuries. People are interested in the same themes that Shakespeare was, whether it be betrayal or love or lust or greed.”

Povich is one of those interested people. He has stuck around long enough to be simultaneously ubiquitous in the manner of a 2026 celebrity and a 1996 celebrity while retaining the newsman’s timbre and resilient hairline of a 1966 celebrity.

He is a TikTok neophyte now TikTok-famous to users who have never touched a remote control.

Accounts for the daytime show and its host have more than 10 million followers across platforms like Facebook, Instagram and YouTube. Throwback clips still circulate, frequently and virally, exposing Povich to viewers whose parents watched him counsel parents, unruly teenagers, ecstatic non-fathers, guests with bespoke phobias.

“Millions and millions of views on the pickle lady and the olive lady,” Povich said approvingly, as his golden retriever, Taxi, pawed for attention.

Reruns also air the old-fashioned way on about 150 stations, he said.

The most popular episodes of the podcast, which airs weekly and began last year, draw a more modest six-figure viewership on YouTube, where ad breaks tend to proceed with a knowing wink:

“Throughout my career I’ve always been about the results. And so I demand that same level of truth when it comes to my own skin care …”

To admirers past and present, Povich’s durability is proof that the camera can keep rolling, that the ’90s daytime boom is not entirely through with us yet, that fatherhood is to be cherished, sure — he speaks warmly and often of his three children — but that not-the-fatherhood can move people to celebration, too.

“Legend,” said Adam Friedland, the consciously off-kilter comedian and podcaster who has sat with Povich as both host and guest.

“Iconic,” Justina Valentine, a television and internet personality, said of Povich, whom she labeled “White Chocolate” in a clip she posted of the two rapping together last year after her “On Par” appearance.

“It’s bizarre to me,” Chung said of Povich’s kinship with the millennial-and-younger podcast class.

But it is not unfamiliar. She recalled the recurring scenes through the years at airports, Knicks games, anywhere.

“These college students would come,” Chung said. “‘Maury, say it! Say it, Maury! Say it!’ And he’d agree to do it: ‘You are NOT the father.’”

To Povich, who will still say it, his podcast has two more basic functions.

The first is as his “great Alzheimer’s test,” he said, with the hope that the show might keep him as sharp and engaged as possible for as long as possible. (The disease runs in the family.)

The second purpose is perhaps more complicated.

“More than anything else,” Povich said flatly, “it’s an attempt to stay relevant.”

Asked why this mattered, he seemed confounded by the premise: “Well, because I’m alive.”

Some online commenters have professed surprise, if relief, to learn this.

“Maybe,” Povich wondered, saluting a departed peer, “they thought I was Jerry Springer.”

A few years ago, a stand-up comedy clip was making the internet rounds.

“Maury is such an ally to the Black community,” the comedian Josh Johnson began, to a burble of bemused chuckles.

In Povich’s decades on the air, the comic reasoned, he had never mispronounced a guest’s name.

“‘Dontuavius’?” asked Johnson, who is Black, as the room caught up with him. “Says it like it’s nothing!”

Povich’s daughter Susan saw the video and shared it. Soon enough, Povich and Chung were traveling to see Johnson perform in Connecticut. The men hit it off.

Povich said Johnson reminded him of George Carlin, whom he had interviewed many jobs ago. He invited Johnson on “On Par” for what would become one of the podcast’s most viewed episodes.

Johnson, a correspondent on “The Daily Show,” seemed to have an almost anthropological interest in Povich’s old show.

When it filmed, before a rollicking studio audience consistently stirred by the chaos arrayed before it, “Maury” had often betrayed a self-aware trashiness: “DNA Will Prove I Had a Baby With Your Uncle!” “I’m Terrified of Spiders, Lizards … and Olives!” “My Stepson Slept With My Wife … Is He My Daughter’s Father?”

“My favorite program was: ‘Is it a man or is it a woman?’” Chung said. “Or fat babies.”

That the guests were often Black had long provoked uncomfortable questions about whether the show was trafficking in exploitative stereotypes, especially in its paternity episodes.

Johnson saw it differently.

“At the end of the segment, he’s always like, ‘What are we going to do?’” Johnson said in an interview. “You could tell the arc of whatever the show was doing was resolution. The arc of a lot of reality TV that came after was imagined conflict.”

At times, Povich has likewise suggested that the show, and its host, were at least a little misunderstood.

He really was trying to make families whole, he still insists. If people enjoyed watching what that looked like in his hands, then that was nice, too.

“He took it seriously,” said Geraldo Rivera, a longtime TV counterpart. “Even if we didn’t.”

Povich recalled receiving letters from prisoners (who apparently had sufficient television access) wondering if they might be the father of certain guests’ children. He shared proudly that pro athletes had reported delaying practice to see a paternity question settled on their locker room screens. (Shaquille O’Neal has said he placed four-figure bets on the answers.)

The host was sent up on “Curb Your Enthusiasm” and “South Park,” cheered by 50 Cent, floated as the face of a national stamp campaign on “Saturday Night Live.”

“I know he’s white,” Michael Che, a “Weekend Update” anchor on “S. N. L.,” said of Povich years ago. “But he’s brought more Black families together than anyone I can think of. And he’s set more Black men free than Abraham Lincoln himself.”

Angela Yee, a radio personality who co-hosted “The Breakfast Club” for over a decade, said Povich’s appeal was rooted in a sort of reflexive non-judgment.

He “wasn’t trying to fix people,” she said. But there was something resonant about watching him watch them raise hell while remaining calm.

“He just wanted people to tell their stories,” Yee said, after appearing as an “On Par” guest. “We can never forget that he really is a journalist.”

Early on, Povich was a local reporter and anchorman in Washington, the area where he was raised. In 1986, he began hosting “A Current Affair,” a television newsmagazine whose topics included the tabloid doings of Donald J. Trump, a sporadic former golf companion of Povich’s.

Povich counts journalists of very different generations, like Tony Kornheiser and Pablo Torre, as friends. In 2007, he and Chung founded a newspaper, The Flathead Beacon, in the Flathead Valley of Montana, where they spend much of the year.

Straighter news ran in the family. Povich’s father, the sportswriter Shirley Povich, worked for most of the 20th century at The Washington Post.

Chung, a journalist’s journalist, is quick to remind her husband’s newer fans that he once had standing in that world, too: covering Kennedy’s funeral, conflict in Lebanon, the Berlin Wall.

“I want everybody out there in podcast-land to know,” she told “On Par” listeners last year, as his inaugural guest.

Povich sighed performatively.

“You were not determining the paternity of every child in America,” she continued.

“Oh, God.”

“You were interviewing everybody from world leaders to Watergate figures,” she said. “You were the go-to.”

At the end of the episode, which focused largely on Chung’s path and her 2024 memoir, Povich asked if there was anything she might like to ask him.

“Are you OK with retiring from your talk show?” she said.

“That was two years ago,” he said. “Don’t you think you could have asked me earlier?”

“Well,” she said, deadpanning, “you didn’t have a podcast.”

Last month, Povich and his team set off on a well-worn bit: teaching an old man new words.

“Maury Povich Learns Gen Z Slang,” the video’s title read.

A young associate producer tried to define the term “stan” for him, describing an obsessive fan.

“For example, Maury, who is your favorite musical artist?” she asked.

“They’re all dead,” he said.

The lesson ended quickly.

When “Maury” stopped production, Povich said he assumed he would follow the example of a hero, Johnny Carson, who was scarcely heard from again after leaving “The Tonight Show.”

Povich has instead become the kind of person who talks to his guests about the power of reinvention.

“Why do you think I’m doing this podcast, huh?” he asked Valentine in their episode. “You think all I can do is read DNA tests?”

What he is doing, mostly, is conducting wandering conversations about his life and his guest’s, with a gimmick segment here or there (“On Par or off the rails!”) and a bit of improvisation.

It is, in short, a podcast.

“I know I made the right decision because I feel inspired,” he said. “It’s nice to be inspired at 87.”

If the guest roster has at times skewed toward younger comedians, Povich said he had always been fascinated by the profession, conducting long-ago interviews with Don Rickles, Richard Pryor and Mel Brooks.

He has become part of the loose affiliation of algorithmically linked comedy-adjacent podcasts, driving eyeballs to his show by appearing on more popular shows hosted by well-known internet figures like Friedland, Nick Cannon and Caleb Pressley.

Cannon and Friedland have in turn appeared on “On Par,” whose name comes from Povich’s golf fanaticism. “To them, I guess I’m still relevant,” he said of his younger counterparts, smiling again.

Chung said that she skips episodes only “if I’m not interested in the person or have never heard of the person,” which is not never.

She was asked if she and her husband had ever considered a joint podcast venture. This was a no. “When we work together,” she said, “I find him extremely annoying.”

Povich has found eager collaborators elsewhere. He is a regular fixture in Interview Magazine, a publication that pairs interviewers of note with interviewees of note in the hope that someone might say something of note. Earlier this year, Povich joined Friedland for a conversation that devolved into a worthy parable for the podcast age: Each man initially believed he was the interviewee.

The two merrily talked at each other before eventually diagnosing the confusion. (Povich was supposed to do the interviewing, they were told, but no one appeared to terribly mind the outcome.)

“Obviously this old guy got an email from something called Interview Magazine and his assumption was that he was being interviewed,” Friedland said. “So it wasn’t much of a stretch.”

Other sessions have been smoother, enshrining Povich as a common modern podcast creature: dishy, digressive, mining his own faults for the cause.

“Even in the talk show, it was about their stories,” Povich said. “I never revealed myself.” Now he cannot stop.

In a reciprocal appearance recently on Halkias’s podcast, “Stavvy’s World,” Povich detailed his college exploits at the University of Pennsylvania during a Philadelphia nurses’ convention (“What can I tell ya?”), noted the discrepancy in academic regard for him and Chung (“My wife’s got all these honorary degrees, I got bupkis”) and considered the host’s most sobering question.

“Maury,” Halkias said, sounding almost serious, “who was president the first time you saw breasts?”

Eisenhower, Povich ruled. “Thank god it wasn’t Kennedy.”

A short time later, Halkias said that Povich’s visit marked an important first:

“This might be the only time I’ve ever respected a guest.”

Matt Flegenheimer is a correspondent for The Times focusing on in-depth profiles of powerful figures.

Our 30 Easiest Thanksgiving Recipes for Busy People

The New York Times September 28, 2026

These simple recipes for roast turkey, stuffing, pie crust and more will set you up for a spectacular meal.

By Margaux Laskey and Sharon Attia

Published Nov. 6, 2020 Updated Sept. 28, 2026

Between work deadlines and family obligations, holiday travel or hosting relatives, spending hours cooking Thanksgiving dinner can feel impossible. But there’s no need to panic. Plan ahead, keep it simple and delegate when necessary. Below are 30 foolproof recipes to guarantee a memorable meal for you and your guests.

Depending on the size of your crowd, serve this succulent turkey breast from Sarah DiGregorio as a simple substitute for a whole roast turkey. The herby dry brine helps ensure moistness and flavor, so don’t skip it. The recipe tester called results “really, really good. So juicy, tender and not at all dry.”

Recipe: Slow-Cooker Turkey Breast

Is it stuffing, or is it dressing? Whatever you call it, it’s arguably the best part of the Thanksgiving table. This simple version from Lidey Heuck works with almost any kind of bread, even the store-bought stuffing cubes. (Just make sure you get the plain, unseasoned kind.)

Recipe: Easy Herb Stuffing

More than the sum of their parts, these potatoes from David Tanis are extremely simple to make, but deeply satisfying. Boiling the potatoes with eight garlic cloves and then mashing them with olive oil, some cooking liquid and plenty of salt results in the “lightest and fluffiest mashed potatoes ever made.”

Recipe: Olive Oil Mashed Potatoes

According to Melissa Clark, brussels sprouts are one of the best vegetables you can make in an air fryer because the little leaves turn brittle and delightfully crunchy. In this recipe, you get the bonus addition of garlic slivers, which turn into flavorful chips. Dress everything with balsamic vinegar simmered until thick and then spiked with lime juice and soy sauce for freshness and umami.

Recipe: Air-Fryer Brussels Sprouts With Garlic, Balsamic and Soy

Store-bought pizza dough infused with loads of softened butter makes these rolls from Melissa Clark both fast and flavorful. The trick to a fluffy, pillowy texture is to cover the pan with foil straight out of the oven, allowing the batch to steam as it cools.

Recipe: Easy Parker House Rolls

Gather your cranberries, orange juice, orange zest and sugar. Simmer until the berries burst. That’s it. If you’d like, Sam Sifton said you could add an allspice clove or two, a little freshly grated ginger or a handful of chopped nuts.

Recipe: Cranberry Sauce

For a lovely sweet-and-sour side dish to serve as a lively counterpart to the rest of the brown foods on the table, try this Priya Krishna recipe for butternut squash gently stewed with spices, tomatoes and brown sugar.

Recipe: Kaddu (Sweet and Sour Butternut Squash)

Save yourself the stress of trying to make gravy under the hungry eyes of your waiting guests. This one from Mark Bittman can be made ahead, so all you have to do is heat it over low heat and add some drippings from the turkey before transferring it to Grandma’s gravy boat.

Recipe: Make-Ahead Gravy

In the category of bright and snappy, serve up a big bowl of green beans like these from Kia Damon. Skip the big pots of boiling water, and cook the beans in a little butter and olive oil, so the beans will release their natural water content in a smart combination of steaming and sautéing.

Recipe: Sautéed Green Beans

Julia Moskin’s brilliant recipe has over 15,000 ratings and is easy as can be. Whiz together some cottage cheese, milk and seasonings in a blender, combine with uncooked pasta and grated Cheddar, and then bake until golden and bubbly.

Recipe: Creamy Macaroni and Cheese

“This was a bright and crunchy alternative to all usual heavy dishes and it was great in turkey leftover sandwiches the next day!” one reader wrote about Hetty Lui McKinnon’s autumnal salad. The 20-minute recipe features shaved brussels sprouts, apples, shallots, pecorino cheese and slivered almonds in a sweet-tart maple-mustard dressing.

Recipe: Crunchy Brussels Sprouts and Apple Slaw

“This pie got rave reviews at our Thanksgiving!” one happy reader wrote about Melissa Clark’s much-praised pumpkin pie. Yes, you can roast and purée your own butternut squash, but the canned pumpkin purée (not pumpkin pie filling) will do just fine. The spice combination and two tablespoons of brandy (budget tip: buy an airplane bottle) are what make it really special.

Recipe: Brandied Pumpkin Pie

Ina Garten’s festive holiday drink can be made quickly: Throw dried cranberries, cranberry juice cocktail, good vodka, Triple Sec and some ice into a large shaker and shake when guests arrive. It’s the perfect accompaniment to the annual “going around the table and sharing what you’re thankful for.”

Recipe: Cranberry Martinis

For a foolproof, 45-minute (really!) roast turkey, try Mark Bittman’s spatchcock version. Cut out the backbone — or ask your butcher to do it for you — and spread the bird out flat before roasting. If you want an organic, farm-raised bird, be sure to place your order a few weeks in advance, and invest in both oven and meat thermometers. (Accurate oven temperature is a key to success here.)

Recipe: Roast Spatchcock Turkey

“This dish was a big hit at our traditional Thanksgiving dinner, loved by adults and toddlers alike!” one reader wrote about Yossy Arefi’s sheet-pan side. Carrots get a head start in the oven, to make sure they get all nice and caramelized, and the kale is sliced thinly and massaged with oil and salt before cooking.

Recipe: Easy Roasted Carrots and Crispy Kale

In Puerto Rico, yuca is one of the most popular viandas, a regional word for starchy fruits and vegetables, such as plantain and taro. It has a subtly sweet and somewhat nutty flavor that’s complemented nicely by a garlicky citrus mojo dressing in this recipe from Von Diaz.

Recipe: Yuca con Mojo

Swirl cranberry sauce into a light and tangy mixture of whipped cream and Greek yogurt, and you’ve got yourself an easy, cooling dessert to finish off the big meal. For a little crunch, Ali Slagle recommends pairing it with gingersnaps, or adding a dollop atop slices of pie.

Recipe: Cranberries and Cream

Naz Deravian’s buttermilk biscuits come together quickly in one bowl — no rolling required. The batter is spread over a pool of melted butter in a baking pan, which is where the name comes from. While the biscuits bake, they absorb all the buttery goodness and crisp up around the edges.

Recipe: Butter Swim Biscuits

An artfully arranged platter of deviled eggs is always a welcome — maybe a little nostalgic? — addition to the holiday table. This recipe, which was adapted from “U. S. A. Cookbook,” by Sheila Lukins, an author of the Silver Palate cookbooks that were popular in the 1980s and ’90s, is pretty much perfect.

Recipe: Classic Deviled Eggs

You could go to all the trouble of mashing a bunch of sweet potatoes and covering them with a blanket of marshmallows, but it’s not necessary. In this simple recipe from Lidey Heuck, cubed (peeled or not) sweet potatoes are roasted on a sheet pan until crisp-edged and soft-centered.

Recipe: Roasted Sweet Potatoes

When you’re cooking what feels like a zillion homemade things for Thanksgiving dinner, a bag of frozen hash browns is your best friend. Also known as funeral potatoes, this creamy, cheesy casserole from Naz Deravian is made by combining the hash browns with cheese, sour cream and homemade cream of chicken soup, and then baking until brown-edged and bubbly.

Recipe: Hash Brown Casserole

Broccoli roasts beautifully in the air fryer, and frees up precious oven space. Eleanore Park’s five-ingredient, 15-minute recipe gives the veg a hit of umami from soy sauce, which is bolstered in the high heat, resulting in nutty, salty and deeply caramelized flavor.

Recipe: Air-Fryer Broccoli

Do not fear making your own pie crust. Melissa Clark’s recipe is hard to mess up and works with practically whatever kind of pie you like on your Thanksgiving table.

Recipe: Pie Crust

For perfectly moist and tender meat, brine your turkey first. This recipe is for a classic wet brine, which was adapted from an old Yankee Magazine recipe for a traditional New England roast turkey. (We also have a dry-brined turkey recipe.)

Recipe: Turkey Brine

Like a fresher, deconstructed version of classic green bean casserole, this dish from Kay Chun features green beans simmered in a classic flour-butter-broth gravy swirled through with miso, sour cream and lemon juice. Top with the classic French fried onions, of course.

Recipe: Miso Gravy-Smothered Green Beans

Salty, crispy and cheesy, these petite appetizers from Melissa Knific are precisely what you’ll want to nibble on while you sip an Old Fashioned as the turkey rests. They’re not at all sophisticated, and that’s part of the charm: Squares of white bread are spread with a savory combination of butter, Cheddar, egg, heavy cream, Worcestershire sauce, garlic powder and dry mustard, and then baked until warm and browned on top.

Recipe: Cheese Dreams

Real talk: Samantha Seneviratne’s apple crumble tastes just as good as pie, and it’s so much easier to make. When shopping for apples, select a combination of tart and sweet, like Granny Smith and McIntosh. They’ll cook and soften at slightly different rates, which will make the filling jammy and pleasantly firm all at once.

Recipe: Apple Crumble

If you love pecan pie, but the thought of eating an entire piece after the feast seems impossible, serve these treats, adapted from Hannah Kaminsky, a columnist at VegNews Magazine, for an adorable and slightly boozy finish to the meal. Combine pecans, graham cracker crumbs, brown sugar, maple syrup, bourbon and vanilla, shape them into balls, and then dip them into dark chocolate. Brown the butter first, as some readers do, for a nuttier, toastier flavor.

Recipe: Pecan Pie Truffles

Hungry guests are not happy guests. While you put the finishing touches on the meal, set out a platter of something that isn’t too filling and that tastes completely different from the rest of the menu, like Alexa Weibel’s bright, spicy marinated feta with herbs and peppercorns. (It takes just a few minutes to set up the night before.)

Recipe: Marinated Feta With Herbs and Peppercorns

Alexa Weibel took baked Brie and brilliantly made it into a vegetarian Thanksgiving centerpiece packed with roasted butternut squash, seared mushrooms, herbed brussels sprouts and tangy red onions. Cook the individual components in the days leading up to the holiday to make assembly and baking a breeze.

Recipe: Baked Brie and Caramelized Vegetable Pie

What Are King Tides, and Why Is Everyone Talking About Them?

The New York Times November 20, 2026

West Coast Weather

Advertisement

Supported by

Because of El Niño, the Pacific Ocean is already higher than normal. This year, that could lead to some especially high tides.

By Amy Graff

Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team. She is based in San Francisco.

Every fall and winter along the West Coast of the United States, the ocean swallows beaches. The Pacific lifts up and over the shore, and salt water spills onto roads and pathways. Hours later, it pulls back, exposing broad expanses of beach, seafloor, rocks and marine life that are usually covered by water.

This dramatic display comes from the highest and lowest tides of the year, commonly called “king tides” by the people who experience them. Usually, they bring only minor flooding and inconvenience. But the damage can become more serious when the high tides coincide with rain, winds and waves.

This winter, forecasters have warned that with sea levels along the West Coast higher than normal because of the strong El Niño climate pattern, these tides could reach their highest levels on record.

“King tide” is an informal, nonscientific term for the highest high tides of the year. It has no entry in the National Weather Service glossary of meteorological terms.

It was mentioned as early as the 1800s, in Australian newspapers; one, in 1868, described the tides as ebbing and flowing “with great violence.” In the early 21st century, an environmental effort in Australia thrust the term into the modern public eye, when the King Tides Project there sought to document dramatically high tides as a way to help communities conceptualize what sea level rise would look like in a changing climate.

Other countries and communities with vulnerable coastlines adopted similar programs, from New Zealand and Tuvalu to the Western United States.

Government agencies in the United States didn’t start using the term until recently. “It was not a thing when I left the N. W. S. at the end of 1997,” said Jan Null, a veteran meteorologist and former forecaster for the Weather Service.

“Somewhere in the last 20 years, the term has become more commonly used,” he said, citing its increasing popularity on social media.

Tides are vast waves rolling around the ocean that are generated by the gravitational attraction between the moon and the sun on Earth. The moon and the sun both tug at the Earth and its oceans as it spins around on its axis. The laws of physics take over, resulting in the high and low tides each day.

What people call the king tides occur when the gravitational pull between the sun, moon and Earth is at its maximum strength.

“A couple of times a year, the moon is closer to the Earth, which is a little more gravitational pull, and the moon and the Earth together are closer to the sun, and that adds to that gravitational pull,” said Gary Griggs, a professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

They happen on coastlines around the world during certain seasons. On the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts of the United States, that’s mainly during late summer and fall; on the West Coast, it’s during the winter.

Tides have already set records this fall in California, when October’s sent water over shorelines up and down the coast.

Many expect some of those records to be broken again.

The exact dates and times for the highest tides vary by location (look up those closest to you here). The California Coastal Commission, which runs the state’s King Tides Project, lists these dates for the state:

Nov. 24-26

Dec. 23-25

Jan. 21-22

Officials in Oregon and Washington list similar dates, but it is mostly in California where emergency officials and meteorologists are anticipating the kind of flooding that can affect daily life.

“Our coast is more sparsely populated than the coast of California,” said Noah Alviz, a meteorologist with the Weather Service office in Portland, Ore.

This will vary up and down the coast, but the short answer for some places is probably higher than ever before, experts warned.

King tides on the West Coast can be up to two feet higher than typical high tides.

But this year, the tides are hitting when the water levels along the coast are even higher because of El Niño. The climate pattern is defined by warm water in the Pacific Ocean, and as water warms, it expands, giving sea levels a little lift.

On top of that, the pulses of water known as Kelvin waves are arriving on the shores of the West Coast, sending sea levels even higher. (Go here for more on the science of a Kelvin wave.)

A few more of these waves of water will move across the ocean this winter, but they’re tricky to track in real time, Mr. Griggs said.

A worst-case scenario for residents and emergency officials would be a storm slamming the coast at the same time as the king tides. That would layer the tides, heavy rains and lashing waves on top of the already high sea levels.

“There are agencies that are trying to plan for a situation where all of these things happen at once,” said Karen Kavanaugh, an oceanographer at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

October’s record tides weren’t technically king tides, the Weather Service office in San Francisco noted, though many called them that anyway.

The city’s mayor, too, has embraced a more liberal definition.

Daniel Lurie, the mayor, said in a video last month that San Francisco was expecting 30 king tides between November and January. Even NOAA defines it just as “a nonscientific term people often use to describe exceptionally high tides.”

Some experts worry the term is being overused and, because of that, risks losing its power to raise awareness about the potential for flooding at the coast.

“It brings in warning fatigue,” said Todd Hall, a meteorologist with the Weather Service in Los Angeles. “If you call everything big, it brings in a different factor of, ‘Oh my goodness, this is going to be the worst ever.’”

There is no official scientific definition of king tides and it can be used loosely. Some meteorologists consider only the December tides, which will be the absolute highest, to be king tides. Others embrace the term because it helps them communicate when tides are going to be so much higher than normal. Regardless of what you call them, the experts agree the Thanksgiving week tides are going to be extremely high. They could bring significant flooding if they're layered on top of sea levels that are also elevated from the effects of El Niño and a storm, wind and waves. If you live on the coast what are you doing to prepare for the exceptionally high tides this year?

Amy Graff is a Times reporter covering weather, wildfires and earthquakes.

The Iowa Lead Detonation Happened. Now the Real Work Begins to Study It

Wired November 25, 2026

On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site.

But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days. A barrage of government, university, and citizen monitoring and testing projects are underway. Air, soil, and water samples they’ve collected will determine the extent of lead exposure, if any, in Middletown and the surrounding area.

The lead azide has been on the base near Middletown for decades, but recently the Army deemed it unstable and too dangerous to move and remediate. Poor communication between the Army and towns in the path of the fallout led to a public uproar. While the federal government stepped up its mitigation measures—the Army dug a dam around the detonation site, while NASA stepped in with research jets and satellites for monitoring—universities had already been swinging into action due to the chaotic rollout.

Several departments at the University of Iowa kicked into gear to begin to set up air and soil monitoring stations late last week. “Initially we did not know that [the] EPA or Army or anybody else was going to be doing anything,” says Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the university.

Scientists at Purdue University, nearly 300 miles away, also put out a call for soil samples from Middletown.

“We learned about the detonation late last week; once we learned of the initial delay in detonation date we decided to put forth the call,” says Ellen Wells, a professor of public health at Purdue who is helping lead the testing.

Surrounding towns were notified in late October that the Army wanted to conduct pre- and post-detonation soil sampling for “an intentional, controlled detonation” of a “quantity of lead azide”—seemingly the only notification that many towns in the initial modeled path of the fallout say they received before a press release issued by the Army days before the planned explosion.

The lack of communication has, understandably, instilled a lot of public distrust in the federal government, including agencies’ monitoring programs. Thorne says that efforts like the University of Iowa’s are not meant to displace federal monitoring, but rather to supplement and support it—and hopefully reassure the public.

“We and the EPA are doing similar exposure assessment efforts. If they agree, they can give us some confidence,” he says. “For people who might be concerned about the veracity of what the government tells them, if their findings are in alignment with ours, then I think that helps quell some of those concerns.”

Thorne says that the soil samples the University of Iowa scientists had measured before the detonation had low levels of lead. “If I saw something like a 10 fold increase in the amount of lead in the soil 20 miles downwind, I’d be concerned with that,” he says.

Some soil testing can be done instantaneously with devices that can image the soil’s surface, using a gun device that fires X-ray beams into a sample and measures the specific electromagnetic signature of lead atoms that bounce back. While Wells and her team don’t have those instruments in the field, they are planning on using them to analyze the samples they receive. More sensitive lab equipment can provide even more granular data, though Thorne estimates those results could take about a week.

In addition to monitoring being done by the Army and the EPA, which is maintaining a live website of air quality results, University of Iowa scientists are monitoring the plume to figure out where the highest concentration of lead may settle. They’re also collecting data on particulate matter in the air around the detonation site for analysis, sending air filters to the lab for more detailed results.

“As these data are compiled over the holiday week to the early next week, I think we'll start to have a bigger picture of roughly how much loading we have of the soil at various places downwind and what we can expect from that,” says Thorne.

A lot of concern online has centered around how additional lead in the soil may impact crops in Iowa, one of the central agricultural hubs for soybeans and corn. Jeffrey Catalano, a professor of earth and environmental sciences at Washington University in Saint Louis, says that there’s a large amount of research showing that plants like corn are actually pretty bad at absorbing lead.

“The hazard is more like, if soil with lead in it gets stuck to leaves, and you eat leaves that have lead-rich soil on them,” he says. “If you take some corn crops next year versus this year and measure their lead content, I don’t think you would see anything other than random variations. I’m not worried about food produced in Iowa.”

Municipal drinking water is also unlikely to be affected because most treatment plants are designed to remove lead from water supplies, says Patrick McNamara, a professor of environmental engineering at Marquette University. It’s more worrisome for private wells or streams on people’s property where livestock may drink. McNamara suggests that owners use at-home lead water tests for safety.

While the detonation and haphazard announcements leading up to it raised alarm bells, both Thorne and Catalano say that there are communities dealing with legacy pollution around the country that are exposed to dangerous levels of lead every day that deserve attention—and remediation.

“I've done work in places like East Chicago, Indiana, where they built a housing project and a school on the grounds of a former lead smelting plant—we were seeing soil lead levels that are roughly 10,000-fold higher than what we've measured in Iowa this week,” Thorne says. “There are a lot of places around the country where there's a much greater lead hazard than I'm going to anticipate what we’ll end up with here. I don't want to over-sell this one when we recognize that there are places where people are really suffering, and need to be remediated for the health of their children.”

How Jump-Roping Toy Soldiers Accidentally Took Over Your FYP

Wired November 25, 2026

Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”

He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage. And “experts” and “recent polling data,” “fans believe it is Holidave who holds the most whimsy” out of all the SeaWorld toy soldiers.

This is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando. Per toy soldier lore, in addition to Jackary Jingleson there’s also Sugarsnookie, Soulja Toy, Big Chestnut, and Frosty McSleigh. And all of the edits are the same: an AI-generated narrator recites stats about the toy soldiers, such as their net worth and their vertical leap, as if they were elite athletes and not niche theme park performers.

For the past two weeks, fan page videos featuring the jump-roping toy soldiers have been going viral, with @wejumprope_memes’ most popular video garnering 1.2 million views. In the comments sections, fans debate the merits and deficits of each toy soldier, declaring their allegiance to their favorite as if they were a ’90s boy band: “Jackery Jingleson is having a banner year! His speed is incomparable, his style undeniable, and his technique is utterly flawless,” reads one comment. Another disputes this, writing “Soulja Toy the underrated gem.”

Mostly, people seem confused as to why these videos keep showing up in their algorithm and why they keep watching them. “I have a PhD and lecture at a university. And yet here I am,” one commenter writes on a video about whether Major Bounce, a new toy soldier, will show up for the 2026 season. (In a November 20 Reel announcing “major news for the jump-roping toy soldier community,” he finally did.)

As it turns out, there’s a simple explanation for the virality. @wejumprope_memes is run by Devin Meek, an Orlando-based professional entertainer who works for WeFlip, a production company that produces acrobatics shows. But he’s now perhaps best known as his alter ego—Holidave.

What started just a few weeks ago as him making memes to make his coworkers laugh has metamorphosed into an internet sensation, with the toy soldiers amassing a genuine, and ardent, fandom. “I really just made these videos for my friends in the jump-roping community,” Meek tells WIRED. “But I guess they resonated with more people than I thought.”

The videos are piggybacking on a larger—and increasingly absurd—trend of seasonal theme park employees going viral. In September, as WIRED previously reported, SeaWorld Orlando enjoyed a bump in ticket sales thanks to Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-themed Halloween scare zone at SeaWorld Orlando that featured swaggering bad boys from the romantasy genre flirting with guests. And last month, women on TikTok swooned over Archer and Fryboy, two performers at Hersheypark Halloween known for sliding around in kneepads wearing tactical streetwear and clown makeup, a practice known as “sliding.”

Meek, who has been jumping rope for the past 20 years, was inspired to create the videos featuring Sugarsnookie, Jackary, and the like after seeing the success of Archer and Fryboy, who have a combined more than 3.1 million followers on TikTok. “It was such an interesting phenomenon, because I’m somebody who is in a very similar position where I work a few months out of the year as a holiday-themed performer,” he says. “So I got a kick out of it.”

Meek already had an account, @wejumprope_memes, where he posted jump-roping fails and compilations. He posted one video on November 13 featuring old footage from SeaWorld Orlando, where he’s been performing with the other toy soldiers for the past six years. (The group got started during the height of the Covid pandemic—hence, why they wear masks during their shows.) “Fryboy who? Move over, Archer,” it begins, before introducing the lore of Jackery Jingleson, the most “light-hearted, nonchalant” of the toy soldiers.

To Meek’s surprise, the video received almost a million views and 588 comments, most of which were not from fellow members of the jumping community but from total strangers. So Meek posted more toy soldier lore on his meme page, introducing Big Chestnut (“a powerful jumper”), Soulja Toy (the developer of the “Christmas Ice Storm 261”), Sugarsnookie (“the girl’s girl of the group,” who is dating Big Chestnut) and Frosty McSleigh (“he has the fastest salute time of all the toy soldiers.”)

Though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Big Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he says.

Though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

“This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he says. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”

Others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek says the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.)

What has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”

Essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he says.

So what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. Meek also shares that the toy soldiers will “likely cross state lines” in the coming months, including a stint at the Christmas market in Cullman, Alabama. Frosty McSleigh, renowned for his 0.08-second salute, plus a slew of new, yet-to-be-introduced toy soldiers will also make an appearance.

Though it may come as a disappointment to some that the roots of the toy soldier phenomenon were inorganic, Meek isn’t concerned. “The people are real. The athleticism is real. The lore is real,” he says. “For all of these people, jump rope is their life, and we’re super-dedicated to teaching it and sharing it. And I think people can feel that.”

Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

Wired November 25, 2026

In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

“Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.

“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.

To make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.

One company in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath says it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.

One pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.

“It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.

Cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he says. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.

The Best TVs We’ve Tested

Wired November 25, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Buying a new TV is always a big decision, namely because its a big piece of tech with a permanent place in your home that you'll be staring at for hours on end. Not to mention, some of the best of the best cost thousands of dollars. It doesn't help that most TVs look exactly the same and have nondescript names like the Samsung S95H—not great for narrowing your options.

Fear not. After stress-testing multiple TVs this year, I can attest to one simple truth: in 2026, you have more great options than ever. Art TVs and RGB TVs exploded onto the market and made the typical “just buy an OLED TV” advice seem like an ancient relic of a bygone. These top-performing televisions are my “desert island” picks, if said island had a power generator and good popcorn.

For more audio and home theater recommendations, check out related guides to the best OLED TVs, the best art TVs, the best RGB TVs, the best home theater projectors, and the best soundbars. If you truly don't know where to start, try our guide on how to buy a TV.

Update November 2026: We've revamped this entire guide, replacing nearly all of our top picks, Honorable Mentions, and Other TVs We've Tested.

What Size TV Should You Buy?

The great debate: which size television is best for your living room? Does it even matter? The first thing to consider is price: an 80-inch TV is going to cost significantly more than a 65-inch one. In some cases, that means an extra grand or two for the privilege of seeing the stubble on Spider-Man’s face in great detail. Broadly speaking, the larger the room, the more useful a large screen is. The most popular size is 65 inches, which is a great option for most medium sizes spaces.

Should You Buy an Art TV?

I’m partial to art televisions for one simple reason: They are useful even when they are turned off. Art TVs use an antireflective layer on top of the screen to create more realistic, textured still images like artwork or paintings. The best ones can replace a picture frame or wall art in any room, and double as great TVs.

Should You Pick an OLED or RGB TV?

TV tech has evolved in 2026, and the new kid on the block is RGB TVs. These new models shine red, blue, and green light through an LCD panel to create brighter, more vibrant color. OLED on the other hand can control the color of individual pixels and even turn them off completely, leading to excellent contrast and black levels.

Which one performs the best? That depends. RGB models like the LG Micro RGB Evo provide more control over picture quality, brightness, and contrast. OLED televisions like the Samsung S95H tend to look better on movie night, especially for nighttime scenes when inky blacks need to look realistic. If pressed, I’d pick an RGB TV model because you get more control over color, but that's just me.

Samsung

Amazon (65-Inch)

Best Buy (65-Inch)

Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) Specs

I picked Samsung's The Frame Pro (2026) as the best overall TV because it has stunningly good picture quality and looks incredible showcasing a masterpiece painting on your wall. I remember staring at the 65-inch model on the wall of my office for two months, just marveling at high-res shipwreck photos and the real wood bezels that encompass the screen (and snap easily into place, by the way). With just about every painting, The Frame Pro showed intricate and detailed textures, as though you could reach out and feel the waves of an ocean or curve of a face.

The Frame Pro is also an excellent choice for movies and shows. Because of the anti-glare screen and matte finish, the dark corridors of scenes in The Batman on HBO had extra depth and animated movies like Toy Story 5 on Disney+ popped with color. Sure, it doesn't have the true black pixels of an OLED screen, but its other capabilities more than make up for it.

Extra features included easy-to-install stands (no screws needed) and a breakout box called the Samsung Wireless One Connect that lets you connect streaming devices and a game console from across the room. That means fewer wires dangling on the wall.

TCL is a more budget-focused television maker that tends to undercut the price of brands like Samsung and LG. A good example of this is the TCL QM7L Mini-LED TV above, which has a budget-friendly price but anything but oriented picture quality. If anything, this QLED model competes with some OLED TVs for inky, deep blacks and rich color. Will you notice any contrast issues when you watch the latest Pixar film? Probably not, especially since the QM7L also looked exceptionally bright in our tests.

A few other extras to mention: We loved the backlit remote, which makes it easier to punch up the volume or adjust picture quality settings in a dark room. You might even be able to skip a soundbar with this TV—the internal Bang & Olufsen speakers sound nice and loud.

LG

Best Buy (75-inch)

LG (75-inch)

LG Micro RGB Evo Specs

Samsung, TCL, Hisense, and Sony released new RGB TVs this year, but it's the LG Micro RGB Evo that takes the crown, namely because you can tweak so many of its picture settings. In my tests, I could tweak the picture so much that movies and shows that mostly take place at night still looked visible, clear, and realistic. As one example among many, I remember tweaking settings for the movie Awake, a largely dark film, to the point where it looked clear and colorful. Other RGB models from Hisense and even Samsung struggled with those same dark scenes, no matter which setting I used.

Another major plus is that this model supports 100 percent of the color gamut specs for BT.2020, DCI-P3, and Adobe RGB. In layman's terms, if you watch a movie like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (which also matches those specs), you will see a true rainbow of every color available, with unmatched color vibrancy. This TV is so striking that I came away thinking that OLED TVs are no longer the obvious gold standard in 2026.

Samsung

Best Buy (65-Inch)

Samsung (65-Inch)

Samsung S95H Specs

Samsung made a big change to their flagship OLED model this year, the Samsung S95H. They ditch the Samsung One Connect breakout box that was required with previous models (and is still required on TVs like The Frame Pro). The TV now has ports directly on the panel, where you can connect video game consoles, streaming devices, or Blu-ray players directly. While that might create more cable clutter, I found it much easier to use than the previous Samsung S95F.

Perhaps more importantly, the S95H is a top performer when it comes to picture quality and settings. I could adjust the contrast and brightness to perfectly light famously dim shows like Game of Thrones. As an OLED, the blacks look richer and darker, more so than most RGB models. The AI optimization picture settings here are actually useful—during soccer matches, the TV adjust to make the pitch look even greener and minimizes background crowd noise, for example.

It's a bit pricey, but the overall brightness, contrast, color quality, and even built-in sound are all premium-grade.

Roku

Amazon (65-Inch)

Amazon (55-Inch)

Roku Pro Series OLED Specs

The company famous for streaming sticks released its first OLED TV this year, and it follows the brand's formula of low-cost simplicity. Roku has, up until this point, stuck with LED TV models with average performance. Wonder of wonders, the Pro Series is not bad at all, making even dark scenes in movies like Solo: A Star Wars Story look vibrant and colorful. Outside of picture quality, Roku makes things as easy as possible, with features like Smart Picture Max, which automatically tweaks picture settings for you, a simple TV operating system (Roku OS, of course), and an uncluttered remote.

I will say, the brightness and contrast are good for this price, but nowhere near the cinema-quality color of something like the premium Samsung S95H. I think it's a great option for anyone on a budget or for people who only watch TV occasionally.

Amazon

Amazon (65-inch)

Amazon (55-inch)

Amazon Ember Artline Specs

The Samsung The Frame Pro (2026) is my TV of the year, but the Amazon Ember Artline is also a capable, significantly cheaper, art TV. Just don't expert as premium of an image in movies and TV shows.

Art televisions use a matte finish on the screen to help make paintings look more realistic and textured. The Ember Artline achieves this look, and even includes frame bezel that snap into place around the screen (these are sold separately on Samsung's Frame TVs). I loved looking at painting on this TV, including some animated ones Amazon offers in the catalog. Using the TV is simple, and the improved Alexa+ voice assistant is useful for changing the volume (hands free) or finding obscure sci-fi films.

Image quality isn't the big selling point of this TV: the art, aesthetic, and low price are. Gamers will find the 60 Hz refresh rate lacking, especially for twitchy action titles. Contrast and brightness are okay, but not nearly as impressive as something like the Samsung The Frame Pro. But keep in mind: this TV is far, far cheaper than premium options.

Sony

Best Buy (65-inch)

Sony (65-inch)

Sony Bravia 9 II Specs

While the LG Micro RGB Evo is endlessly tweakable and outperformed every other RGB model I tested for picture quality, the Sony BRAVIA 9 II RGB TV still takes the cake when it comes to gaming. That’s especially true if you own a Sony PlayStation 5, since the TV will automatically adjust the picture quality and latency to match the game console. I tested it mostly using a high-end PC, and at a 120 Hz refresh rate, latency felt non-existent to me.

I also found this TV to be a capable alternative to a premium OLED. Red, green, and blue colors are almost infinitely adjustable. During a scene in Toy Story 5 by a tree in a field, the sun creates splashes of color that look incredibly lush and vivid. Watching Game of Thrones, I found I could enable a special black level setting to make night battles look more realistic.

The Bravia 9 II uses Google TV OS and Google Gemini voice assistant, which both run simply, smoothly, and with no weird hiccups. While the LG Micro RGB Evo is a better performer for color and contrast, the BRAVIA 9 II’s gaming features, fast performance, high-end speakers, and deep blacks are exceptional.

Hisense UR9 RGB Mini-LED: My top pick for a midrange RGB, the Hisense UR9 has rich colors thanks to RGB tech shining red, green, and blue pixels. Some scenes, including ones in the movie The Last Duel, looked extra crisp and colorful. But it's not quite as excellent as my top picks.

LG B6 OLED: The LG B6 is a great budget-friendly OLED TV that performed very similarly to the Roku Pro Series OLED. Either one of them would serve you well, but we gave the nod to the Roku TV for it's lower price, simpler remote, and easy to use Roku operating system.

Samsung Micro RGB R95H: Samsung's Micro RGB display tech didn’t make the Samsung Micro RGB R95H stand out from the competition as much as I'd hoped. In fact, the LG Micro RGB Evo responded much better to picture quality adjustments, and while shows and movies looked colorful and clear, they weren't quite as jaw-dropping as similarly priced RGB and OLED competitors.

Sony Bravia 7 II: The Sony Bravia 7 II is unfortunately outclassed by the other midrange RGB TV on this list: the Hisense UR9. It is more expensive, it's harder to set up, and the picture quality doesn't quite match that of the Hisense TV.

Sony Bravia 8 II: Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata tested this stunning high-end OLED, and praised it's top-notch image quality and processing. That said, the Samsung S95H is newer, about the same price, and has a more striking, glare-free image than the Sony Bravia 8 II.

TCL Nxtvision Series Art: This budget art TV simply cannot compete with similarly low-priced art TVs like the Amazon Ember Artline TV and Hisense Class S7 CanvasTV. Both offer better picture quality and a better general user experience. You can read my full review here.

TCL RM9L RGB Mini-LED: The TCL RM9L RGB TV is huge and hugely expensive. The $6,000 85-inch is the smallest and cheapest model you can get, and it is generally outclassed by the LG Micro RGB Evo.

The WIRED reviews team is busy testing the ever-popular midrange LG C6 and premium LG G6. Given past performances from LG C and G-series TVs, we expect them to be strong contenders for top accolades in this guide.
